proposals.reason: Section 20 allows release to the Crown in whole sections while preventing a partial release that leaves less than one section unless total surrender occurs.

proposedGroups.titleSuggestion: Release or surrender of permit or lease area
proposedGroups.reason: Section 20 allows release to the Crown in whole sections while preventing a partial release that leaves less than one section unless total surrender occurs.
proposedGroups.approximateLearningGoal: Recall when a permittee or lessee may release area to the Crown and the minimum-area limit on release.

proposals.reason: Section 21 grants exclusive production rights to permittees or lessees and requires oil and natural gas to be produced first in specified overlapping-resource circumstances.

proposedGroups.titleSuggestion: Production rights and priority for oil or natural gas
proposedGroups.reason: Section 21 grants exclusive production rights to permittees or lessees and requires oil and natural gas to be produced first in specified overlapping-resource circumstances.
proposedGroups.approximateLearningGoal: Recall the exclusive production rights of permittees or lessees and when oil or natural gas must be produced first.

proposals.reason: Section 23 allows pre-commercial-production rental reductions for allowable exploration expenditures, carry-forward of unused credits, and ends reductions after commercial production begins.

proposedGroups.titleSuggestion: Rental reductions for lease exploration work
proposedGroups.reason: Section 23 allows pre-commercial-production rental reductions for allowable exploration expenditures, carry-forward of unused credits, and ends reductions after commercial production begins.
proposedGroups.approximateLearningGoal: Recall when lease rentals may be reduced for exploration expenditures and when reductions no longer apply.

proposals.reason: Section 24 has two forfeiture tracks: failure to make deposits or pay rentals and other violations of the Act or regulations.

proposedGroups.titleSuggestion: Cancellation for unpaid deposit or rental
proposedGroups.reason: These subsections govern default notices and cancellation for unpaid deposits or rentals.
proposedGroups.approximateLearningGoal: Recall the notice and cure period before cancellation for unpaid deposits or rentals.

proposedGroups.titleSuggestion: Cancellation for other Act or regulation violations
proposedGroups.reason: These subsections govern notices and cancellation for other violations.
proposedGroups.approximateLearningGoal: Recall when other Act or regulation violations can lead to cancellation of a lease, development permit, or licence to search.

proposals.reason: Section 26 allows Minister entry and work, use of security deposits, continuing liability, and debt recovery for unpaid costs.

proposedGroups.titleSuggestion: Minister action and cost recovery for non-compliance
proposedGroups.reason: Section 26 allows Minister entry and work, use of security deposits, continuing liability, and debt recovery for unpaid costs.
proposedGroups.approximateLearningGoal: Recall what the Minister may do after non-compliant operations and how security deposits, liability, and Crown debt operate.

proposals.reason: Section 27 is a broad enforcement provision with separate Minister possession powers, obedience and production-control rules, cost or proceeds handling, and residual liability.

proposedGroups.titleSuggestion: Minister enforcement possession and operational control
proposedGroups.reason: The first two subsections authorize Minister seizure or control of operations and require personnel to obey directions.
proposedGroups.approximateLearningGoal: Recall the Minister enforcement powers to take possession or control of bituminous shale operations and require obedience.

proposedGroups.titleSuggestion: Produced materials, proceeds, and costs during enforcement
proposedGroups.reason: These subsections govern produced materials, costs, proceeds, and net proceeds during Minister control.
proposedGroups.approximateLearningGoal: Recall how bituminous shale produced during enforcement is dealt with and how costs and net proceeds are paid.

proposedGroups.titleSuggestion: Residual enforcement cost liability
proposedGroups.reason: Subsection 27(7) applies security-deposit and further-liability rules when proceeds are insufficient.
proposedGroups.approximateLearningGoal: Recall how unpaid enforcement costs are recovered when production proceeds are insufficient.

proposals.reason: Section 28 requires written notice before exploratory work and Minister approval, with possible conditions, before production schemes or operations begin.

proposedGroups.titleSuggestion: Notification and approval before exploration or production
proposedGroups.reason: Section 28 requires written notice before exploratory work and Minister approval, with possible conditions, before production schemes or operations begin.
proposedGroups.approximateLearningGoal: Recall the notice and approval required before bituminous shale exploration or production work begins.

proposals.reason: Section 29 contains distinct rules for Minister approval, recording and effectiveness, execution formalities, bank security registration, and transfers to self or co-holders.

proposedGroups.titleSuggestion: Approval, recording, and effectiveness of title instruments
proposedGroups.reason: The first five subsections govern approval, recording prerequisites, effective time, effect between parties, and fees for title instruments.
proposedGroups.approximateLearningGoal: Recall how transfers and assignments of bituminous shale authorizations are approved, recorded, and made effective.

proposedGroups.titleSuggestion: Execution formalities and bank security registration
proposedGroups.reason: These subsections address execution by individuals or corporations and registration of bank security instruments.
proposedGroups.approximateLearningGoal: Recall the execution formalities and bank security registration rules for bituminous shale title instruments.

proposedGroups.titleSuggestion: Valid transfers to self, co-holders, or fiduciaries
proposedGroups.reason: Subsection 29(8) permits certain direct, co-holder, and fiduciary transfers.
proposedGroups.approximateLearningGoal: Recall the special valid-transfer rules for holders, co-holders, trustees, executors, and administrators.

proposals.reason: Section 30 opens title records to inspection while protecting designated technical data and giving that protection precedence over conflicting right-to-information law.

proposedGroups.titleSuggestion: Public title records and confidential technical data
proposedGroups.reason: Section 30 opens title records to inspection while protecting designated technical data and giving that protection precedence over conflicting right-to-information law.
proposedGroups.approximateLearningGoal: Recall which bituminous shale records are publicly inspectable and when geological or other data remains confidential.

proposals.reason: Section 36 allows specified production or processing cost deductions and authorizes agreements for royalty amounts and calculation methods for unitized or conservation operations.

proposedGroups.titleSuggestion: Royalty deductions and royalty agreements
proposedGroups.reason: Section 36 allows specified production or processing cost deductions and authorizes agreements for royalty amounts and calculation methods for unitized or conservation operations.
proposedGroups.approximateLearningGoal: Recall when royalty deductions may be allowed and when an agreement may set royalty amount and calculation method.

proposals.reason: Section 37 assigns different offence categories for regulation violations, address-registration failures, unauthorized exploration or entry, confidentiality or non-interference failures, and disobedience during enforcement control.

proposedGroups.titleSuggestion: Regulation offences and registration offence
proposedGroups.reason: The first three subsections cover offences for regulation violations and failure to comply with address-registration duties.
proposedGroups.approximateLearningGoal: Recall the offence categories for regulation violations and failure to register an address for service.

proposedGroups.titleSuggestion: Unauthorized exploration, entry, or order offences
proposedGroups.reason: Subsection 37(4) groups category E offences tied to unauthorized exploration, entry, notification or approval failures, and orders.
proposedGroups.approximateLearningGoal: Recall the category E offences under the Bituminous Shale Act.

proposedGroups.titleSuggestion: Confidentiality, non-interference, and enforcement obedience offences
proposedGroups.reason: The final subsections assign categories for confidentiality, non-interference, and failure to obey Minister directions during enforcement control.
proposedGroups.approximateLearningGoal: Recall the category F and category I offences for confidentiality, non-interference, and enforcement obedience failures.

proposals.reason: Section 6 separates the basic right to apply, the list of applicants for parcels, public highway applications, and joint applications.

proposedGroups.titleSuggestion: Application to confirm a parcel boundary
proposedGroups.reason: These subsections state the basic application trigger and who may apply respecting a parcel.
proposedGroups.approximateLearningGoal: Recall who may apply to confirm the location of a parcel boundary when doubt exists.

proposedGroups.titleSuggestion: Public highway and joint boundary applications
proposedGroups.reason: These subsections provide for public highway applications and joint applications where multiple applicants agree on all boundaries.
proposedGroups.approximateLearningGoal: Recall who may apply about a public highway boundary and when joint applications may be made.

proposals.reason: Section 7 includes application materials, further information demands, refusal to proceed on non-boundary issues, and written notice of refusal.

proposedGroups.titleSuggestion: Materials accompanying a boundary application
proposedGroups.reason: The first two subsections state what must accompany an application and what additional material the Registrar General may require.
proposedGroups.approximateLearningGoal: Recall the plan, information, material, fee, and additional-information requirements for a boundary application.

proposedGroups.titleSuggestion: Refusal to proceed with non-boundary issues
proposedGroups.reason: These subsections allow refusal to proceed where issues go beyond boundary location and require written notice with reasons.
proposedGroups.approximateLearningGoal: Recall when the Registrar General may refuse to proceed and what notice must be given.

proposals.reason: Section 8 allows the Registrar General to start a boundary proceeding without an application, engage a surveyor, and terminate before notice if no boundary should be confirmed.

proposedGroups.titleSuggestion: Registrar General initiated boundary proceedings
proposedGroups.reason: Section 8 allows the Registrar General to start a boundary proceeding without an application, engage a surveyor, and terminate before notice if no boundary should be confirmed.
proposedGroups.approximateLearningGoal: Recall when the Registrar General may initiate or terminate a boundary confirmation proceeding without an application.

proposals.reason: Section 9 requires applicant or Registrar General notice and specifies notice contents: reasons, deadline for objections, and inspection location for the plan.

proposedGroups.titleSuggestion: Notice of boundary application or proceeding
proposedGroups.reason: Section 9 requires applicant or Registrar General notice and specifies notice contents: reasons, deadline for objections, and inspection location for the plan.
proposedGroups.approximateLearningGoal: Recall who gives notice of a boundary application or proceeding and what that notice must contain.

proposals.reason: Section 10 separates written objections, the consequences of receiving or not receiving objections, parties to hearings, and notice-of-hearing contents.

proposedGroups.titleSuggestion: Written objection and hearing trigger
proposedGroups.reason: The first two subsections state how to object and require a hearing when a timely written objection is delivered.
proposedGroups.approximateLearningGoal: Recall how a person objects to boundary confirmation and when that objection triggers a hearing.

proposedGroups.titleSuggestion: No objection and discretionary hearing
proposedGroups.reason: Subsection 10(3) states when the Registrar General may confirm without a hearing or hold one despite no objection.
proposedGroups.approximateLearningGoal: Recall what the Registrar General may do if no timely objection is delivered.

proposedGroups.titleSuggestion: Hearing parties and notice of hearing
proposedGroups.reason: The last three subsections define hearing parties and required notice-of-hearing contents.
proposedGroups.approximateLearningGoal: Recall who is a party to a boundary hearing and what the notice of hearing must specify.

proposals.reason: Section 11 allows summonses, oaths, contempt proceedings, recording oral evidence, and providing recordings to parties.

proposedGroups.titleSuggestion: Registrar General hearing powers and record
proposedGroups.reason: Section 11 allows summonses, oaths, contempt proceedings, recording oral evidence, and providing recordings to parties.
proposedGroups.approximateLearningGoal: Recall the Registrar General hearing powers for witnesses, oaths, contempt proceedings, and recording evidence.

proposals.reason: Section 12 allows the Registrar General after hearing to confirm boundaries, require amended or new plans, refuse confirmation, and send the order to parties and specified persons.

proposedGroups.titleSuggestion: Registrar General orders after a boundary hearing
proposedGroups.reason: Section 12 allows the Registrar General after hearing to confirm boundaries, require amended or new plans, refuse confirmation, and send the order to parties and specified persons.
proposedGroups.approximateLearningGoal: Recall what orders the Registrar General may make after a boundary hearing and who receives the order.

proposals.reason: Section 13 distinguishes non-appealable preliminary refusals, binding agreed orders, Court of King’s Bench appeals, Court remedies, and further appeals on law.

proposedGroups.titleSuggestion: Final non-appealable and agreed boundary decisions
proposedGroups.reason: The first two subsections identify decisions with no appeal and parties bound by written agreement.
proposedGroups.approximateLearningGoal: Recall which Registrar General boundary decisions are final with no appeal.

proposedGroups.titleSuggestion: Court of King’s Bench appeal from Registrar General order
proposedGroups.reason: These subsections set the Court appeal route, deadline, service, and possible Court orders.
proposedGroups.approximateLearningGoal: Recall how a party appeals a Registrar General boundary order and what the Court may order.

proposedGroups.titleSuggestion: Further appeal to the Court of Appeal
proposedGroups.reason: Subsection 13(7) creates a further appeal on a point of law.
proposedGroups.approximateLearningGoal: Recall when a further appeal lies to the Court of Appeal.

proposals.reason: Section 14 requires certification after appeal periods or appeals are complete and makes certification conclusive proof that required procedural steps occurred.

proposedGroups.titleSuggestion: Certification of confirmed boundaries
proposedGroups.reason: Section 14 requires certification after appeal periods or appeals are complete and makes certification conclusive proof that required procedural steps occurred.
proposedGroups.approximateLearningGoal: Recall when the Registrar General certifies confirmed boundaries and the proof effect of that certification.

proposals.reason: Section 15 requires filing of a certified plan of survey and deems the confirmed boundaries to be the boundaries while superseding earlier plans or descriptions.

proposedGroups.titleSuggestion: Filing and legal effect of confirmed survey plans
proposedGroups.reason: Section 15 requires filing of a certified plan of survey and deems the confirmed boundaries to be the boundaries while superseding earlier plans or descriptions.
proposedGroups.approximateLearningGoal: Recall how a confirmed plan of survey is filed and what legal effect it has on boundaries and prior plans or descriptions.

proposals.reason: Section 16 separates authority to order a corrected plan, the limit that correction cannot affect confirmed boundary location, and filing or notation effects for corrected plans.

proposedGroups.titleSuggestion: Ordering a corrected plan of survey
proposedGroups.reason: The first three subsections state when the Registrar General may order a corrected plan, whether notice is needed, and the boundary-location limit.
proposedGroups.approximateLearningGoal: Recall when a corrected plan of survey may be ordered and what boundary-location limit applies.

proposedGroups.titleSuggestion: Filing and notation for corrected plans
proposedGroups.reason: The last three subsections state filing, application of section 15(2), and notation on the earlier plan.
proposedGroups.approximateLearningGoal: Recall how corrected plans of survey are filed and how the superseded plan is noted.

proposals.reason: Section 18 establishes the Boundaries Confirmation Fund and identifies its purposes, custodian and trust status, account use, charge on the Fund, and regulation-based administration.

proposedGroups.titleSuggestion: Boundaries Confirmation Fund purpose and administration
proposedGroups.reason: Section 18 establishes the Boundaries Confirmation Fund and identifies its purposes, custodian and trust status, account use, charge on the Fund, and regulation-based administration.
proposedGroups.approximateLearningGoal: Recall the purpose, custody, payment, and administration rules for the Boundaries Confirmation Fund.

proposals.reason: Section 19 allows the Registrar General to reduce excessive prescribed fees and order recovery of the difference from the Fund.

proposedGroups.titleSuggestion: Reduction of prescribed fees
proposedGroups.reason: Section 19 allows the Registrar General to reduce excessive prescribed fees and order recovery of the difference from the Fund.
proposedGroups.approximateLearningGoal: Recall when prescribed fees may be reduced and how the difference may be recovered from the Fund.

proposals.reason: Section 20 makes applicants liable by default while allowing the Registrar General to order costs paid by or to parties or from the Fund.

proposedGroups.titleSuggestion: Liability and allocation of boundary proceeding costs
proposedGroups.reason: Section 20 makes applicants liable by default while allowing the Registrar General to order costs paid by or to parties or from the Fund.
proposedGroups.approximateLearningGoal: Recall who is liable for boundary application costs by default and how the Registrar General may reallocate costs or use the Fund.

proposals.reason: Section 5 is a large order-power provision with separate target-supported topics: contaminant-release orders, triggering opinions, persons to whom orders may be directed, compliance orders, source and works orders, public-health waterworks orders, and construction-schedule contents.

proposedGroups.titleSuggestion: Contaminant-release order directions
proposedGroups.reason: Subsection 5(1) lists the directions the Minister may include in an order responding to contaminant releases.
proposedGroups.approximateLearningGoal: Recall the kinds of contaminant-release control, investigation, reporting, cleanup, and remedial directions that may be ordered under subsection 5(1).

proposedGroups.titleSuggestion: Circumstances for contaminant-release orders
proposedGroups.reason: Subsection 5(2) separately states the Ministerial opinions and release circumstances that can support a contaminant order.
proposedGroups.approximateLearningGoal: Recall the release-rate, prohibited-release, and public-interest circumstances that may justify a contaminant order.

proposedGroups.titleSuggestion: Persons who may receive contaminant-release orders
proposedGroups.reason: Subsection 5(3) is a distinct list of possible recipients of a subsection 5(1) contaminant-release order.
proposedGroups.approximateLearningGoal: Recall who a contaminant-release order may be directed to under subsection 5(3).

proposedGroups.titleSuggestion: Compliance orders after Act or regulation violations
proposedGroups.reason: Subsection 5(4) creates a separate order power tied to violations or failures to comply with the Act or regulations.
proposedGroups.approximateLearningGoal: Recall when the Minister may issue a compliance order and what that order may direct.

proposedGroups.titleSuggestion: Source, wastewater works, and waterworks modification orders
proposedGroups.reason: Subsections 5(5) and 5(6) deal together with orders requiring investigations or modifications of a source, wastewater works, or waterworks despite an approval.
proposedGroups.approximateLearningGoal: Recall when the Minister may order investigation or modification of a source, wastewater works, or waterworks despite an approval.

proposedGroups.titleSuggestion: Public-health waterworks construction or operation orders
proposedGroups.reason: Subsection 5(7) is specifically about orders to a local government after public-health notification concerning waterworks construction, modification, or operation.
proposedGroups.approximateLearningGoal: Recall when public-health notification may lead to a local-government waterworks construction, modification, or operation order.

proposedGroups.titleSuggestion: Wastewater treatment facility or waterworks order contents
proposedGroups.reason: Subsection 5(8) identifies additional contents that may be included in orders requiring installation, replacement, or alteration of wastewater treatment facilities or waterworks.
proposedGroups.approximateLearningGoal: Recall the information requirements and compliance schedule that may be included in wastewater treatment facility or waterworks orders.

proposals.reason: Section 13 is a focused register provision requiring the Minister to maintain a register for authorization applications and making it open for inspection on payment of the prescribed fee.

proposedGroups.titleSuggestion: Register for authorization applications and inspection
proposedGroups.reason: The two subsections work together by requiring a register of application information and providing public inspection access subject to a prescribed fee.
proposedGroups.approximateLearningGoal: Recall what register the Minister must maintain for authorization applications and when it is open for inspection.

proposals.reason: Section 14 lists separate appeal rights for authorization decisions, designation-order exemption refusals with special Natural Resources substitutions, and responsible-party declarations.

proposedGroups.titleSuggestion: Appeals from authorization suspensions, cancellations, and refusals
proposedGroups.reason: Subsection 14(1) identifies the appeal right for specified decisions about registrations, licences, permits, and approvals.
proposedGroups.approximateLearningGoal: Recall which authorization suspensions, cancellations, and refusals may be appealed under subsection 14(1).

proposedGroups.titleSuggestion: Appeals from wetland or coastal exemption refusals
proposedGroups.reason: Subsections 14(2) and 14(3) address appeals from refused designation-order exemption requests and the substitutions that apply when the exemption was granted by the Minister of Natural Resources.
proposedGroups.approximateLearningGoal: Recall the appeal right for refused wetland or coastal exemption requests and the Natural Resources substitutions for certain appeals.

proposedGroups.titleSuggestion: Appeals by declared contaminated-site responsible parties
proposedGroups.reason: Subsection 14(4) creates a separate appeal right for persons declared responsible parties under section 4.6.
proposedGroups.approximateLearningGoal: Recall that a person declared a responsible party under section 4.6 may appeal that decision in the prescribed manner.

proposals.reason: Section 15 is a focused agreement-making power for the Minister, with Lieutenant-Governor in Council approval, to enter agreements that carry out the Act's intent and support committees, consultation, and advice on policies and programs.

proposedGroups.titleSuggestion: Minister agreements to carry out Act objectives
proposedGroups.reason: The provision identifies possible agreement parties and the agreement purposes related to implementing programs, continuing consultation, and advice on Act objectives.
proposedGroups.approximateLearningGoal: Recall with whom the Minister may enter agreements under section 15 and what those agreements may establish to carry out the Act's intent.

proposals.reason: Section 16 is a cohesive provision establishing an environmental council and setting membership, chair and vice-chair designation, quorum, term, expenses, and allowances.

proposedGroups.titleSuggestion: Environmental council establishment and membership rules
proposedGroups.reason: The subsections together define how the environmental council is created, who may serve, officer designations, quorum, term, and compensation-related rules.
proposedGroups.approximateLearningGoal: Recall how the environmental council is established and governed for membership, officers, quorum, terms, expenses, and allowances.

proposals.reason: Section 29 is a cohesive evidentiary provision for analyst certificates, including admissibility and proof, cross-examination with leave, and notice before production.

proposedGroups.titleSuggestion: Analyst certificate evidence, cross-examination, and notice
proposedGroups.reason: The subsections work together on how analyst certificates are used in prosecutions and what procedural protections apply to the opposing party.
proposedGroups.approximateLearningGoal: Recall when an analyst certificate is admissible and proof, and how cross-examination and notice requirements apply.

proposals.reason: Section 33 combines offence liability and fine rules with a separate evidentiary-document regime for prosecutions.

proposedGroups.titleSuggestion: Offence liability, fine ranges, daily fines, and pesticide charges
proposedGroups.reason: Subsections 33(1) through 33(3) identify what conduct is an offence, the fine ranges for individuals and others, the multiplier for continuing violations, and the charging rule for overlapping Pesticides Control Act offences.
proposedGroups.approximateLearningGoal: Recall the Clean Environment Act offence, fine, continuing-violation, and Pesticides Control Act charging rules.

proposedGroups.titleSuggestion: Minister documents and statements in offence prosecutions
proposedGroups.reason: Subsections 33(4) through 33(6) set evidentiary treatment for Minister documents, statements, and certified copies, plus notice and cross-examination requirements.
proposedGroups.approximateLearningGoal: Recall how Minister documents and statements may be used in prosecutions and what notice and cross-examination protections apply.

proposals.reason: Clean Water Act section 3 is a cohesive conflict-of-law provision stating the Act's general priority, the Public Health Act exception, and the validity of measures that could also have been taken under the Clean Environment Act.

proposedGroups.titleSuggestion: Clean Water Act priority, public health exception, and Clean Environment Act overlap
proposedGroups.reason: The subsections work together to resolve conflicts with other legislation, carve out public-health matters, and preserve Clean Water Act measures despite Clean Environment Act overlap.
proposedGroups.approximateLearningGoal: Recall how Clean Water Act conflicts are resolved, when the Public Health Act prevails, and why Clean Water Act measures remain valid despite Clean Environment Act overlap.

proposals.reason: Clean Water Act section 4 is a large order-power provision with separate target-supported topics for contaminant-release directions, triggering circumstances, possible recipients, compliance orders, facility order contents, order form and scope, compliance responsibility and access, duration, appeal effect, and successor binding.

proposedGroups.titleSuggestion: Water contaminant-release order directions
proposedGroups.reason: Subsection 4(1) lists the directions the Minister may include in an order responding to contaminant releases into or upon water.
proposedGroups.approximateLearningGoal: Recall the release control, investigation, reporting, cleanup, and remedial directions that may be ordered for contaminants released into or upon water.

proposedGroups.titleSuggestion: Circumstances for water contaminant-release orders
proposedGroups.reason: Subsection 4(2) separately states the Ministerial opinions and release circumstances that can support a contaminant order under the Clean Water Act.
proposedGroups.approximateLearningGoal: Recall the release-rate, prohibited-release, and public-interest circumstances that may justify a water contaminant order.

proposedGroups.titleSuggestion: Persons who may receive water contaminant orders
proposedGroups.reason: Subsection 4(3) is a distinct list of possible recipients of a subsection 4(1) contaminant-release order.
proposedGroups.approximateLearningGoal: Recall who a Clean Water Act contaminant-release order may be directed to.

proposedGroups.titleSuggestion: Compliance orders and facility order contents
proposedGroups.reason: Subsections 4(4) and 4(5) cover compliance orders for violations or failures to comply and the additional information and schedule requirements that may be included in wastewater treatment facility or waterworks orders.
proposedGroups.approximateLearningGoal: Recall when the Minister may issue a Clean Water Act compliance order and what information or schedule may be included in facility orders.

proposedGroups.titleSuggestion: Order scope, written reasons, compliance responsibility, and access
proposedGroups.reason: Subsections 4(6) through 4(9) govern order scope, writing and reasons outside emergencies, each directed person's responsibility and expense, and access needed to implement an order.
proposedGroups.approximateLearningGoal: Recall how Clean Water Act orders may cover multiple contaminants or persons and how writing, reasons, responsibility, expense, entry, and access rules operate.

proposedGroups.titleSuggestion: Order duration, appeal effect, and successor binding
proposedGroups.reason: Subsections 4(10) through 4(12) state how long an order lasts, that an appeal does not suspend compliance, and who remains bound by the order.
proposedGroups.approximateLearningGoal: Recall when a Clean Water Act order ends, why appeal does not remove compliance, and how it binds heirs, successors, executors, administrators, and assigns.

proposals.reason: Clean Water Act section 5 is a focused follow-up order and non-compliance provision, covering additional remedial orders when existing action is inadequate and Ministerial entry to effect compliance after failure or refusal.

proposedGroups.titleSuggestion: Additional remedial orders and action after non-compliance
proposedGroups.reason: Both subsections address what the Minister may do after existing action is inadequate or a directed person fails or refuses to comply with an order.
proposedGroups.approximateLearningGoal: Recall when the Minister may order further remedial action or enter premises to effect compliance with a Clean Water Act order.

proposals.reason: Clean Water Act section 6 contains two separable cost-liability topics: Minister cost liability and recovery from liable persons, and ordered-person cost recovery with preserved responsibilities after settlements or liability determinations.

proposedGroups.titleSuggestion: Minister cost liability after water-release response action
proposedGroups.reason: Subsections 6(1) and 6(2) identify who is liable to pay Minister-incurred costs for water-release response action and how the Minister may recover from multiple liable persons.
proposedGroups.approximateLearningGoal: Recall who is liable for Minister-incurred water-release response costs and how recovery may proceed when more than one person is liable.

proposedGroups.titleSuggestion: Ordered-person cost recovery and continuing water-release responsibilities
proposedGroups.reason: Subsections 6(3) and 6(4) address recovery of costs incurred by a person acting under an order and confirm that settlement or other liability determinations do not remove order, restoration, or payment responsibilities.
proposedGroups.approximateLearningGoal: Recall how Clean Water Act section 6 protects ordered-person cost recovery and preserves responsibilities despite settlements or liability determinations.

proposals.reason: Clean Water Act section 7 separates the Minister's direct entry-and-action power from the owner access duty, the public-interest and order-ineffectiveness conditions for using that power, and the link to subsection 4(1) action types.

proposedGroups.titleSuggestion: Minister entry and direct action for water contaminant releases
proposedGroups.reason: Subsections 7(1) and 7(2) pair the Minister's direct entry-and-action authority with the access duty imposed on owners, persons in charge, employees, and agents.
proposedGroups.approximateLearningGoal: Recall the Minister's entry and direct-action authority for water contaminant releases and the corresponding duty to permit access.

proposedGroups.titleSuggestion: Conditions for Minister direct action for water releases
proposedGroups.reason: Subsection 7(3) states the Ministerial opinions and circumstances that must support taking direct action, including public interest, owner-control problems, and inability to deal effectively by order.
proposedGroups.approximateLearningGoal: Recall the circumstances that allow the Minister to take direct action for a water contaminant release whether or not an order has been issued.

proposedGroups.titleSuggestion: Actions available by reference to subsection 4(1)
proposedGroups.reason: Subsection 7(4) defines the range of direct actions by incorporating subsection 4(1) action types.
proposedGroups.approximateLearningGoal: Recall that Minister direct actions under Clean Water Act section 7 may include the action types set out in subsection 4(1).

proposals.reason: Clean Water Act section 8 is a large recovery-cost provision. The operative recovery rules are clear, but the target text ends with an apparent stray heading marker, so confidence is medium.

proposedGroups.titleSuggestion: Crown debt recovery, notice, directions, and carriage for water-release costs
proposedGroups.reason: Subsections 8(1) through 8(4) set the court-debt route for unrecovered Minister costs, require notice before another person pursues related costs, allow Minister directions within sixty days, and permit the Minister to assume carriage of an action that includes a Crown claim.
proposedGroups.approximateLearningGoal: Recall the court action, notice, direction, and carriage rules for recovering unrecovered Clean Water Act Minister costs.

proposedGroups.titleSuggestion: Unrecovered-cost certificate, judgment, and appeal
proposedGroups.reason: Subsections 8(3.1) to 8(3.3) form a certificate mechanism that can become a court judgment but is delayed if the named person appeals liability or amount.
proposedGroups.approximateLearningGoal: Recall how a Clean Water Act unrecovered-cost certificate is issued, filed as a judgment, and affected by an appeal.

proposedGroups.titleSuggestion: Insurance proceeds for water-release response costs
proposedGroups.reason: Subsections 8(5) through 8(7.1) address when an insurer must pay Minister costs, how insurance proceeds may be shared, how payments are characterized, and the coverage-limit ceiling.
proposedGroups.approximateLearningGoal: Recall the insurer payment, proceeds-sharing, deemed-payment, and coverage-limit rules for water-release response costs.

proposedGroups.titleSuggestion: Cost certificate evidence and modified application
proposedGroups.reason: Subsection 8(8) gives evidentiary effect to a Minister-signed cost certificate, while subsection 8(9) extends the section, with modifications, to listed Minister costs under regulations, failures to comply, investigations, and inspections.
proposedGroups.approximateLearningGoal: Recall how a Minister cost certificate proves Clean Water Act costs and how section 8 applies with modifications to other Minister-incurred costs.

proposals.reason: Section 10 separates contaminant designation for potable water by the Minister of Health from contaminant designation and permissible-level orders for non-potable water by the Minister, plus the Regulations Act exclusion.

proposedGroups.titleSuggestion: Minister of Health contaminant designation for potable water
proposedGroups.reason: Subsection 10(1) specifically addresses the Minister of Health's order power for contaminants in potable water or classes of potable water.
proposedGroups.approximateLearningGoal: Recall how the Minister of Health may designate contaminants for potable water or classes of potable water.

proposedGroups.titleSuggestion: Minister contaminant designation and permissible levels for non-potable water
proposedGroups.reason: Subsection 10(2) addresses the Minister's order powers for non-potable water, including contaminant designation and maximum permissible amounts, levels, or concentrations.
proposedGroups.approximateLearningGoal: Recall how the Minister may designate contaminants and set permissible levels for water that is not potable water.

proposedGroups.titleSuggestion: Regulations Act exclusion for section 10 orders
proposedGroups.reason: Subsection 10(3) separately states the legal treatment of orders made under section 10.
proposedGroups.approximateLearningGoal: Recall that the Regulations Act does not apply to Clean Water Act section 10 orders.

proposals.reason: Section 11 contains distinct water-testing duties for well drillers, owners of newly worked wells, private well owners, and public water supply system owners.

proposedGroups.titleSuggestion: Water well driller report and testing fee duties
proposedGroups.reason: Subsection 11(1) imposes reporting and fee duties on persons who bore, drill, dig, or redrill another person's well.
proposedGroups.approximateLearningGoal: Recall the report filing and testing fee duties for persons who bore, drill, dig, or redrill another person's well.

proposedGroups.titleSuggestion: Testing and notice duties for owners of newly worked wells
proposedGroups.reason: Subsection 11(2) requires the owner of a well worked by another person to have water tested and notify consumers and intended consumers of results.
proposedGroups.approximateLearningGoal: Recall the testing and consumer-notice duties of owners whose wells have been bored, drilled, dug, or redrilled by another person.

proposedGroups.titleSuggestion: Private well and public water supply testing rules
proposedGroups.reason: Subsections 11(2.1) and 11(3) distinguish optional private well testing from mandatory public water supply system testing.
proposedGroups.approximateLearningGoal: Recall how private well testing differs from mandatory public water supply system testing under section 11.

proposals.reason: Section 12 contains three distinct target-supported rules: the prohibition on harmful contaminant releases into water without legislative authority, the ability to order or act despite such authority, and the pesticide-control bar on specified orders and actions.

proposedGroups.titleSuggestion: Water contaminant release prohibition absent legislative authority
proposedGroups.reason: Subsection 12(1) states the basic prohibition and exception for releases into or upon water that would or could affect water quality, health, property, plant life, visibility, transport, business, or enjoyment of life or property.
proposedGroups.approximateLearningGoal: Recall when section 12 prohibits contaminant releases into or upon water unless the person acts under and complies with legislative authority or permission.

proposedGroups.titleSuggestion: Orders and Minister action despite legislative authority
proposedGroups.reason: Subsection 12(2) separately confirms that legislative authority or permission does not prevent orders or other Minister action respecting contaminant releases.
proposedGroups.approximateLearningGoal: Recall that authority or permission under another Act does not by itself prevent Clean Water Act contaminant-release orders or Minister action.

proposedGroups.titleSuggestion: Pesticides Control Act bar on specified water-release orders
proposedGroups.reason: Subsection 12(3) identifies the pesticide-control circumstances in which the Minister of Health or Minister must not make the listed Clean Water Act orders or take the listed actions.
proposedGroups.approximateLearningGoal: Recall when Pesticides Control Act orders or steps bar specified Clean Water Act contaminant-release orders or actions.

proposals.reason: Section 13 contains substantial operative significant-health-risk rules despite a repeal-only content flag; subsection 13(1) is repealed, but the remaining target text supports several distinct study groups.

proposedGroups.titleSuggestion: Supplying water that poses a significant health risk
proposedGroups.reason: Subsection 13(2) is the direct prohibition on supplying water to consumers from listed systems when the water poses a significant health risk.
proposedGroups.approximateLearningGoal: Recall the prohibition on supplying water that poses a significant health risk from a well, public water supply system, or water supply system other than a private well.

proposedGroups.titleSuggestion: Source-contaminant significant health risk orders
proposedGroups.reason: Subsection 13(3) addresses significant health risks caused by contaminants at the source and the Minister's orders to close access, provide water, eliminate the risk, install a new well or alternate source, or take further measures.
proposedGroups.approximateLearningGoal: Recall the orders available when water poses a significant health risk because of a contaminant at the source.

proposedGroups.titleSuggestion: Point-of-consumption significant health risk orders
proposedGroups.reason: Subsection 13(4) addresses significant health risks at the point of consumption and the Minister of Health's orders for access, temporary water, notice, safe water, new systems, and further measures.
proposedGroups.approximateLearningGoal: Recall the orders available when water poses a significant health risk because of a contaminant at the point of consumption.

proposedGroups.titleSuggestion: Future significant health risk prevention at source or consumption point
proposedGroups.reason: Subsection 13(5) separately addresses possible future significant health risks and divides authority between the Minister for source risks and the Minister of Health for point-of-consumption risks.
proposedGroups.approximateLearningGoal: Recall how possible future significant health risks at the source or point of consumption may be prevented, eliminated, minimized, or otherwise addressed.

proposedGroups.titleSuggestion: Private well notice, no-liability rule, and modified application
proposedGroups.reason: Subsections 13(6) through 13(8) address private-well notice, the no-liability effect while the risk is restricted to the private well, and the modified application of related order and cost provisions.
proposedGroups.approximateLearningGoal: Recall the private well notice duty, no-liability rule, and modified application of related provisions for significant-health-risk orders.

proposals.reason: Section 14 is a large protected-area Designation Order provision with distinct topics for designation authority, order requirements and contents, publication, filing and registers, and compliance by affected persons.

proposedGroups.titleSuggestion: Designation of protected watershed, aquifer, or recharge areas
proposedGroups.reason: Subsections 14(1) and 14(2) establish the authority to designate protected areas used as public water supply sources and require a commencement date.
proposedGroups.approximateLearningGoal: Recall how the Minister may designate protected watershed, aquifer, or ground water recharge areas and must provide a commencement date.

proposedGroups.titleSuggestion: Protected-area requirements, schedules, and plans
proposedGroups.reason: Subsections 14(3) and 14(4) identify the requirements a Designation Order may impose and the schedule and protected-area description or plan it must include.
proposedGroups.approximateLearningGoal: Recall the requirements, schedule, and plan or description that may or must appear in a protected-area Designation Order.

proposedGroups.titleSuggestion: Publication, filing, registration, notice, and registers for Designation Orders
proposedGroups.reason: Subsections 14(4.1) through 14(7) cover publication alternatives, pre-commencement filing and registry-office registration, newspaper notice, notice contents, and public inspection registers.
proposedGroups.approximateLearningGoal: Recall the publication, filing, registration, notice, and register requirements for protected-area Designation Orders.

proposedGroups.titleSuggestion: Compliance with protected-area Designation Order requirements
proposedGroups.reason: Subsections 14(8) and 14(9) distinguish compliance duties for persons already affected on commencement and persons who later acquire, propose, or commence affected activities, things, or uses.
proposedGroups.approximateLearningGoal: Recall when existing and later-affected persons must comply with protected-area requirements and how exemptions affect that duty.

proposals.reason: Section 15 is a large watercourse and wetland alteration provision with distinct topics for planning and permits, owner maintenance and specification duties, Minister inspection and repair orders, non-compliant alteration orders, and public-interest removal when the owner cannot be ascertained.

proposedGroups.titleSuggestion: Watercourse or wetland alteration planning, permits, terms, and exemptions
proposedGroups.reason: Subsections 15(1), 15(1.01), and 15(1.1) govern pre-project plan submission, permit requirements, permit terms and conditions, and regulatory exemptions or waivers.
proposedGroups.approximateLearningGoal: Recall the planning, document, permit, permit-term, and exemption rules before undertaking watercourse or wetland alteration projects.

proposedGroups.titleSuggestion: Owner duties to meet specifications and maintain structures
proposedGroups.reason: Subsections 15(1.2) and 15(2) impose ongoing owner duties to meet original, permit, and approved specifications and maintain projects or structures in good repair.
proposedGroups.approximateLearningGoal: Recall the ongoing owner duties to meet specifications and keep watercourse or wetland projects and structures in good repair.

proposedGroups.titleSuggestion: Minister inspection, information, repair, and compliance orders
proposedGroups.reason: Subsection 15(3) authorizes Minister orders for inspection, documents and information, repairs or modifications, and compliance with permit terms or specifications.
proposedGroups.approximateLearningGoal: Recall the inspection, information, repair, modification, and specification-compliance orders available for watercourse or wetland projects or structures.

proposedGroups.titleSuggestion: Orders for non-compliant watercourse or wetland alterations
proposedGroups.reason: Subsection 15(4) separately addresses orders when an alteration or related work is not commenced, made, or carried out in compliance with the Act, regulations, permit terms, or Minister orders, directions, or demands.
proposedGroups.approximateLearningGoal: Recall what the Minister may order when a watercourse or wetland alteration is not compliant.

proposedGroups.titleSuggestion: Public-interest removal when alteration or structure owner cannot be ascertained
proposedGroups.reason: Subsection 15(5) is a separate removal power for public-interest removal of an alteration, structure, or thing from a watercourse or wetland when the owner cannot be ascertained.
proposedGroups.approximateLearningGoal: Recall when the Minister may order public-interest removal from a watercourse or wetland at provincial expense because the owner cannot be ascertained.

proposals.reason: Section 17 contains distinct inspector topics: Minister designation, broad inspection powers, private-dwelling entry limits, and detention of evidence.

proposedGroups.titleSuggestion: Inspector designation and Clean Water Act inspection powers
proposedGroups.reason: Subsections 17(1) and 17(2) establish inspector designation and the inspection, testing, entry, and sampling powers used to administer the Act, including protected-area inspection powers.
proposedGroups.approximateLearningGoal: Recall how inspectors are designated and what entry, inspection, testing, and sampling powers they have under the Clean Water Act.

proposedGroups.titleSuggestion: Private dwelling limits on Clean Water Act inspector entry
proposedGroups.reason: Subsection 17(3) separately limits inspector entry into private dwellings to emergency, adult occupant consent, or Entry Warrants Act warrant situations.
proposedGroups.approximateLearningGoal: Recall the emergency, consent, and entry-warrant bases that allow a Clean Water Act inspector to enter a private dwelling.

proposedGroups.titleSuggestion: Inspector detention of evidence discovered under section 17
proposedGroups.reason: Subsection 17(4) identifies what an inspector may detain, the evidentiary purpose, and the reasonable-grounds connection to a violation or failure to comply.
proposedGroups.approximateLearningGoal: Recall what Clean Water Act inspectors may detain as evidence after discovering it while acting under section 17.

proposals.reason: Section 22 is a cohesive evidentiary provision for Minister statements and documents in prosecutions, including admissibility and proof, notice before production, and cross-examination with leave.

proposedGroups.titleSuggestion: Minister documents and statements in Clean Water Act prosecutions
proposedGroups.reason: The subsections work together on how Minister documents, statements, and certified copies are used in prosecutions and what procedural protections apply to the opposing party.
proposedGroups.approximateLearningGoal: Recall how Minister documents and statements may be used in Clean Water Act prosecutions and what notice and cross-examination protections apply.

proposals.reason: Clean Water Act section 23 is a cohesive evidentiary provision for analyst certificates, including admissibility and proof, cross-examination with leave, and notice before production.

proposedGroups.titleSuggestion: Analyst certificate evidence, cross-examination, and notice
proposedGroups.reason: The subsections work together on how analyst certificates are used in prosecutions and what procedural protections apply to the opposing party.
proposedGroups.approximateLearningGoal: Recall when an analyst certificate is admissible and proof in Clean Water Act prosecutions, and how cross-examination and notice requirements apply.

proposals.reason: Clean Water Act section 24 is a focused service provision identifying sufficient service methods for orders, notices, and other documents and deeming registered-mail service after five days.

proposedGroups.titleSuggestion: Service methods and registered-mail deeming rule
proposedGroups.reason: The two subsections specify acceptable service methods and when service by prepaid registered mail is deemed effective.
proposedGroups.approximateLearningGoal: Recall how Clean Water Act orders, notices, and other documents may be served and when registered-mail service is deemed effective.

proposals.reason: Clean Water Act section 25 is a cohesive offence and fine provision covering offences, fine ranges, daily multiplication for continuing violations, and the Pesticides Control Act charging rule.

proposedGroups.titleSuggestion: Clean Water Act offence liability, fine ranges, daily fines, and pesticide charges
proposedGroups.reason: The subsections identify what conduct is an offence, the fine ranges for individuals and others, the multiplier for continuing violations, and the charging rule for overlapping Pesticides Control Act offences.
proposedGroups.approximateLearningGoal: Recall the Clean Water Act offence, fine, continuing-violation, and Pesticides Control Act charging rules.

proposals.reason: Clean Water Act section 26 is a cohesive enhanced-fine provision for offences committed for financial advantage or to avoid compliance costs, with a prosecutor notice prerequisite.

proposedGroups.titleSuggestion: Enhanced fines for financial advantage or avoided compliance costs
proposedGroups.reason: The two subsections work together by authorizing fines beyond ordinary maxima in specified financial-benefit circumstances and requiring advance prosecutor notice.
proposedGroups.approximateLearningGoal: Recall when a judge may impose an enhanced Clean Water Act fine for financial advantage or avoided compliance costs and what notice must be given.

proposals.reason: Section 31 is a cohesive establishment and governance provision for the Land and Water Advisory Committee, including definition, membership, officers, quorum, procedure, and tenure.

proposedGroups.titleSuggestion: Land and Water Advisory Committee establishment and governance
proposedGroups.reason: The subsections define the Committee and set how it is established, who is appointed, officer designations, quorum, procedural rules, and service at pleasure.
proposedGroups.approximateLearningGoal: Recall how the Land and Water Advisory Committee is defined, established, appointed, chaired, quorate, procedurally governed, and held at pleasure.

proposals.reason: Section 32 covers both the Land and Water Advisory Committee's substantive duties and its supporting powers for submissions, expenses, special-knowledge services, and annual reporting.

proposedGroups.titleSuggestion: Land and Water Advisory Committee department definition and duties
proposedGroups.reason: Subsections 32(1) and 32(2) define department for the section and list the Committee's duties relating to land and water use information, recommendations, conflict resolution, Act review, Minister requests, and regulated duties.
proposedGroups.approximateLearningGoal: Recall the definition of department and the Land and Water Advisory Committee's duties concerning land and water use.

proposedGroups.titleSuggestion: Committee submissions, expenses, special knowledge, and annual report
proposedGroups.reason: Subsections 32(3) through 32(6) provide supporting powers and duties for receiving submissions, paying expenses, engaging special knowledge, submitting an annual report, and legislative tabling.
proposedGroups.approximateLearningGoal: Recall the Committee's powers and duties for submissions, expenses, expert services, annual reporting, and tabling.

proposals.reason: Section 34 is a focused agreement-making power for the Minister, with Lieutenant-Governor in Council approval, to enter agreements that carry out the Act's intent and support committees, consultation, and advice on policies and programs.

proposedGroups.titleSuggestion: Minister agreements to carry out Clean Water Act objectives
proposedGroups.reason: The provision identifies possible agreement parties and the agreement purposes related to implementing programs, continuing consultation, and advice on Act objectives.
proposedGroups.approximateLearningGoal: Recall with whom the Minister may enter agreements under section 34 and what those agreements may establish to carry out the Act's intent.

proposals.reason: Community Planning Act section 1 is a large definitions and interpretation section. Its current target-defined terms support separate study groups for institutions and officials, planning instruments and local-government geography, and development, land, and subdivision concepts.

proposedGroups.titleSuggestion: Community planning institutions, officials, and roles
proposedGroups.reason: These definitions identify the committees, tribunal, inspectors, local-government officials, Crown, development officer, Director, Minister, planner, and registrar roles used in the Act.
proposedGroups.approximateLearningGoal: Recall the Community Planning Act meanings of advisory committee, Board, building inspector, clerk, council, Crown, development officer, Director, Minister, planner, and registrar.

proposedGroups.titleSuggestion: Planning instruments, regional bodies, and local-government interpretation
proposedGroups.reason: These definitions and the interpretation rule explain the planning instruments, regional and rural entities, statement of public interest, local-government meaning, and context-dependent reference to the body corporate or area.
proposedGroups.approximateLearningGoal: Recall the Act's meanings for planning instruments, regional and rural entities, statement of public interest, regional service commissions, and references to local government.

proposedGroups.titleSuggestion: Development, land, registration, non-conforming use, and subdivision definitions
proposedGroups.reason: These definitions govern core land-development concepts, public-purpose land, registration offices, non-conforming uses, streets, subdivision, and the distinction between type 1 and type 2 subdivisions.
proposedGroups.approximateLearningGoal: Recall the Act's meanings for development, land for public purposes, land registration office, non-conforming use, street, subdivide, type 1 subdivision, and type 2 subdivision.

proposals.reason: Section 3 is an operative advisory-committee establishment provision, though its content flag marks commencement-only; the target text supports authoring with caution.

proposedGroups.titleSuggestion: Planning advisory committee by-law establishment and validity
proposedGroups.reason: The two subsections require councils providing their own land use planning service to establish a planning advisory committee by by-law and state the validity and filing-based commencement requirements for that by-law.
proposedGroups.approximateLearningGoal: Recall when a council must establish a planning advisory committee and what makes the by-law valid and in force.

proposals.reason: Section 5 is a cohesive membership provision for advisory committees, covering committee size, appointment and removal by council, council or employee participation limits, voter eligibility, and residence.

proposedGroups.titleSuggestion: Planning advisory committee membership, appointment, and eligibility
proposedGroups.reason: The subsections work together to define membership size ranges, appointment and removal authority, composition limits, and eligibility requirements.
proposedGroups.approximateLearningGoal: Recall how planning advisory committee membership is sized, appointed, removed, composed, and limited by voter eligibility and residence.

proposals.reason: Section 6 contains distinct advisory-committee term topics: ordinary and initial staggered terms, changes in membership size, loss of council or employee status, mid-term succession, and holdover when successors are not appointed.

proposedGroups.titleSuggestion: Advisory committee member, chair, vice-chair, and staggered terms
proposedGroups.reason: Subsections 6(1) through 6(5) set ordinary terms, officer terms, initial staggering, and adjustments when membership increases or decreases.
proposedGroups.approximateLearningGoal: Recall the ordinary, officer, staggered, increased-membership, and decreased-membership term rules for advisory committees.

proposedGroups.titleSuggestion: Advisory committee replacement and holdover rules
proposedGroups.reason: Subsections 6(6) through 6(8) address what happens when council or employee status ends, when a member dies, resigns, becomes ineligible or is removed, and when council fails to appoint a successor.
proposedGroups.approximateLearningGoal: Recall the advisory committee rules for replacement, remainder terms, and holdover when a successor has not been appointed.

proposals.reason: Section 9 contains separate Provincial Planning Director topics: appointment, development-officer role in specified local-government situations, and delegation, technical assistance, and assigned planning powers.

proposedGroups.titleSuggestion: Provincial Planning Director appointment and development-officer role
proposedGroups.reason: Subsections 9(1) and 9(2) address appointment of the Director and the Director's development-officer role for specified village or rural community subdivision by-law or regulation contexts.
proposedGroups.approximateLearningGoal: Recall how the Provincial Planning Director is appointed and when the Director acts as development officer.

proposedGroups.titleSuggestion: Director delegation, technical assistance, and assigned planning duties
proposedGroups.reason: Subsection 9(3) separately identifies the Director's delegation authority, technical assistance role, and Minister-assigned community-planning powers and duties.
proposedGroups.approximateLearningGoal: Recall the Director's authority to delegate administrative powers, provide technical planning assistance, and perform assigned community-planning duties.

proposals.reason: Section 10 is a cohesive local-government planning director provision, covering employment or engagement of planning personnel, appointment of a planning director, the development-officer effect, and special village or rural community Director roles.

proposedGroups.titleSuggestion: Local government planning director and development-officer roles
proposedGroups.reason: The subsections work together to set staffing authority, planning director appointment, development-officer status, and special Director appointment or subdivision-regulation roles for villages and rural communities.
proposedGroups.approximateLearningGoal: Recall how local governments providing their own planning service appoint planning directors and assign development-officer roles.

proposals.reason: Section 12 is a focused content provision for design review committee by-laws, but the target text includes apparent stray part headings after subsection 12(2).

proposedGroups.titleSuggestion: Content of design review committee by-laws
proposedGroups.reason: The operative subsections list the membership, officer, term, remuneration, expense, duty, procedure, review-matter, and appointment-by-resolution provisions a design review committee by-law may include.
proposedGroups.approximateLearningGoal: Recall what a design review committee by-law may provide about membership, officers, terms, remuneration, expenses, duties, procedure, review matters, and appointment by resolution.

proposals.reason: Section 13 is a cohesive statement-of-public-interest provision covering establishment by regulation, required content, and optional consultation before establishment or amendment.

proposedGroups.titleSuggestion: Establishing statements of public interest
proposedGroups.reason: The subsections work together to require a regulation establishing a statement of public interest, define what the regulation must do, and permit Minister consultation before establishment or amendment.
proposedGroups.approximateLearningGoal: Recall how statements of public interest are established, what they must identify or establish, and when the Minister may consult.

proposals.reason: Section 15 is a cohesive consistency and consequence provision for planning instruments, by-laws, regulations, and building by-laws made or adopted after a statement of public interest comes into effect.

proposedGroups.titleSuggestion: Planning instruments and by-laws consistent with statements of public interest
proposedGroups.reason: The two subsections pair the consistency requirement with the legal consequence of inconsistency and the practical-reason exception for councils.
proposedGroups.approximateLearningGoal: Recall which planning instruments and by-laws must be consistent with statements of public interest and what effect inconsistency has.

proposals.reason: Section 16 is a cohesive enforcement provision allowing the Minister to direct amendments for consistency with a statement of public interest, requiring compliance within 24 months, and requiring revocation once a consistent amendment is made.

proposedGroups.titleSuggestion: Minister directions to enforce statement-of-public-interest consistency
proposedGroups.reason: The subsections form one enforcement workflow for Minister directions, local or regional compliance, and revocation after a consistent amendment.
proposedGroups.approximateLearningGoal: Recall how the Minister may direct amendments to achieve consistency with a statement of public interest and when the direction must be complied with or revoked.

proposals.reason: Section 17 is a focused review-timing provision for statements of public interest, but the target text includes apparent stray next-part headings after subsection 17(2).

proposedGroups.titleSuggestion: Review timing for statements of public interest
proposedGroups.reason: The operative subsections set the deadline to commence a review, the purpose of the review, and the deadline to conclude it.
proposedGroups.approximateLearningGoal: Recall when a statement-of-public-interest review must start, what it examines, and when it must conclude.

proposals.reason: Section 18 is a focused source on who may adopt and prepare regional land use plans for regions or parts of regions.

proposedGroups.titleSuggestion: Minister and preparers for regional land use plans

evidenceText: may adopt regional land use plans

proposedGroups.reason: Both subsections identify the Minister's adoption power and the bodies that may prepare regional land use plans.
proposedGroups.approximateLearningGoal: Recall who may adopt a regional land use plan, who may prepare it, and the regions or parts of regions it may cover.

proposals.reason: Section 21 combines the municipal council's five-year adoption duty with the Minister's assessment and approval role.

proposedGroups.titleSuggestion: Municipal plan adoption deadline and Minister approval

evidenceText: Within five years after the incorporation of a municipality

proposedGroups.reason: The two subsections describe the council's duty to adopt a municipal plan by by-law and the Minister's approval if requirements are met.
proposedGroups.approximateLearningGoal: Recall when a municipality must adopt a municipal plan and when the Minister must approve it.

proposals.reason: Section 22 is a coherent rule for responsible Crown actors considering municipal plans and obtaining approval for non-conforming construction.

proposedGroups.titleSuggestion: Crown development conformity with municipal plans

evidenceText: is required to obtain the approval of the Lieutenant-Governor in Council

proposedGroups.reason: The subsections cover consideration of the municipal plan, approval for specified non-conforming construction, and the repair or alteration exception.
proposedGroups.approximateLearningGoal: Recall how responsible Crown actors must consider municipal plans and when Lieutenant-Governor in Council approval is required or unnecessary.

proposals.reason: Section 23 addresses one enforcement topic: Ministerial action and cost recovery when council fails to adopt or amend a municipal plan.

proposedGroups.titleSuggestion: Minister adoption powers and municipal cost recovery

evidenceText: fails to make a by-law adopting a municipal plan

proposedGroups.reason: The subsections tie the Minister's replacement authority to notice, debt, arrears, and deduction from money owed to the municipality.
proposedGroups.approximateLearningGoal: Recall what happens when a council fails to adopt or amend a municipal plan, including notice, chargeable costs, debt, arrears, and deductions.

proposals.reason: Section 24 is a large municipal-plan source with distinct preparation/certification requirements and separate content, map, and budget rules.

proposedGroups.titleSuggestion: Municipal plan preparation, studies, consultation, and certification

evidenceText: shall certify that the content of the municipal plan complies

proposedGroups.reason: These subsections state who prepares the plan, the required planning direction, study report, consultation, certification, and planner considerations.
proposedGroups.approximateLearningGoal: Recall the preparation, study, consultation, certification, and planner-consideration requirements for municipal plans.

proposedGroups.titleSuggestion: Municipal plan map, policies, proposals, measures, and capital budget

evidenceText: A municipal plan shall contain the following

proposedGroups.reason: These subsections describe the attached zoning map, mandatory policy statements, implementation proposals and measures, the five-year capital budget, annual revision, and the budget-revision exception.
proposedGroups.approximateLearningGoal: Recall what a municipal plan must contain, how zoning maps and capital budgets fit into it, and what annual budget revision does not trigger.

proposals.reason: Section 25 is a coherent notice and objection process for proposed municipal plans before the section 111 process.

proposedGroups.titleSuggestion: Municipal plan public presentation notice and written objections

evidenceText: objections to the proposed plan may be made

proposedGroups.reason: The subsections state the timing and contents of the notice, permitted publication methods, inspection requirements, social media option, and written objection right.
proposedGroups.approximateLearningGoal: Recall how notice, public presentation, inspection availability, and written objections work before adopting a municipal plan.

proposals.reason: Section 26 provides substantive validity and commencement conditions for a municipal plan, not merely a cross-reference.

proposedGroups.titleSuggestion: Municipal plan validity conditions and filing commencement

evidenceText: no municipal plan is valid unless

proposedGroups.reason: The subsections identify certification, section 111 compliance, Ministerial filing compliance, and when the municipal plan comes into force.
proposedGroups.approximateLearningGoal: Recall the validity conditions for a municipal plan and when it comes into force after filing in the land registration office.

proposals.reason: Section 29 is a complete topic on secondary municipal plans: where they apply, why they exist, and which preparation rules carry over.

proposedGroups.titleSuggestion: Secondary municipal plan area, purpose, and preparation rules

evidenceText: applies, as part of the municipal plan, to a specific area

proposedGroups.reason: The subsections describe adoption for specific areas, the purpose of addressing local planning issues, and modified application of approval and preparation provisions.
proposedGroups.approximateLearningGoal: Recall when a secondary municipal plan may be used, its purpose, and which municipal-plan rules apply to its preparation and adoption.

proposals.reason: Section 32 is a single review workflow for municipal plans, with start, conclusion, and reporting duties.

proposedGroups.titleSuggestion: Municipal plan ten-year review, completion deadline, and report

evidenceText: a review of a municipal plan is commenced at least once every ten years

proposedGroups.reason: The subsections connect the ten-year review trigger, 36-month completion deadline, and duty to provide the review report to the Minister.
proposedGroups.approximateLearningGoal: Recall when municipal plan reviews must start, when they must conclude, and when the report goes to the Minister.

proposals.reason: Section 33 parallels municipal plan adoption for villages and is a focused adoption and approval rule for village rural plans.

proposedGroups.titleSuggestion: Village rural plan adoption deadline and Minister approval

evidenceText: Within five years after the incorporation of a village

proposedGroups.reason: The subsections state the village council's five-year adoption duty and the Minister's assessment and approval role.
proposedGroups.approximateLearningGoal: Recall when a village must adopt a rural plan and when the Minister approves it.

proposals.reason: Section 34 addresses one enforcement and recovery topic when a village council fails to adopt or amend a rural plan.

proposedGroups.titleSuggestion: Minister adoption powers and village cost recovery

evidenceText: fails to make a by-law adopting a rural plan

proposedGroups.reason: The subsections link the Minister's replacement authority with 30 days' notice, chargeable costs, debt, arrears, and deduction from money owed to the village.
proposedGroups.approximateLearningGoal: Recall what happens when a village council fails to adopt or amend a rural plan, including notice, cost debt, arrears, and deductions.

proposals.reason: Section 35 is a large village rural-plan source with distinct preparation/certification rules and separate content, zoning, and priority rules.

proposedGroups.titleSuggestion: Village rural plan preparation, studies, consultation, and certification

evidenceText: shall certify that the content of the rural plan for a village complies

proposedGroups.reason: These subsections state who prepares the plan, the planning direction, study report, consultation, and certification of compliance.
proposedGroups.approximateLearningGoal: Recall the preparation, study, consultation, and certification requirements for a village rural plan.

proposedGroups.titleSuggestion: Village rural plan policies, proposals, zoning provisions, and priority

evidenceText: A rural plan for a village shall contain

proposedGroups.reason: These subsections list required policy topics, proposals, implementation measures, zoning provisions, modified zoning rules, and priority of policy or proposal over zoning provisions.
proposedGroups.approximateLearningGoal: Recall what a village rural plan must contain and how its policies or proposals relate to its zoning provisions.

proposals.reason: Section 36 is a complete topic on secondary rural plans for villages, including authority, purpose, and applicable preparation rules.

proposedGroups.titleSuggestion: Secondary rural plan for a specific village area

evidenceText: applies, as part of the rural plan for the village, to a specific area

proposedGroups.reason: The subsections describe secondary rural plans as part of a village rural plan, their purpose for particular planning areas, and modified preparation and adoption rules.
proposedGroups.approximateLearningGoal: Recall when a village rural plan may include a secondary rural plan, why it is used, and which rules apply to its preparation and adoption.

proposals.reason: Section 39 is a focused village rural-plan notice and objection rule tied to the vote and substantial amendments.

proposedGroups.titleSuggestion: Village rural plan objections before adoption vote

evidenceText: shall not vote on adopting a rural plan until after the 14 days

proposedGroups.reason: The subsections require waiting until the 14-day objection period has passed, considering objections, and repeating the process for substantial amendments.
proposedGroups.approximateLearningGoal: Recall the objection period, voting limit, and substantial-amendment notice rule for village rural plans.

proposals.reason: Section 40 provides substantive validity and commencement conditions for a village rural plan.

proposedGroups.titleSuggestion: Village rural plan validity conditions and filing commencement

evidenceText: no rural plan for a village is valid unless

proposedGroups.reason: The subsections identify certification, section 111 compliance, Ministerial filing compliance, and when the plan comes into force.
proposedGroups.approximateLearningGoal: Recall the validity requirements for a village rural plan and when it comes into force after filing.

proposals.reason: Section 43 is a single village rural-plan review workflow with start, completion, and reporting duties.

proposedGroups.titleSuggestion: Village rural plan ten-year review, completion deadline, and report

evidenceText: review of a rural plan is commenced at least once every ten years

proposedGroups.reason: The subsections connect the ten-year review trigger, 36-month completion deadline, and duty to provide the report to the Minister.
proposedGroups.approximateLearningGoal: Recall when a village rural plan review must start, when it must conclude, and when the review report goes to the Minister.

proposals.reason: Section 44 is a large rural-community rural-plan source covering adoption, preparation, incorporation of other rules, and special zoning powers.

proposedGroups.titleSuggestion: Rural community rural plan adoption, preparation, studies, and certification

evidenceText: shall certify that the content of the rural plan for a rural community complies
