proposedGroups.reason: These subsections allow appointment of five advisory committee members when the Minister exercises council powers for a local government with its own planning service and allow the Minister to revest powers in council by notice and filing.
proposedGroups.approximateLearningGoal: Recall how advisory committee appointments and revesting of powers work when the Minister has taken over council powers.

proposals.reason: Section 133 is a coherent inspection workflow for suspected planning violations and resulting orders.

proposedGroups.titleSuggestion: Inspection of property, entry warrants, dwelling limits, and written orders

evidenceText: may, at all reasonable times

proposedGroups.reason: The subsections authorize entry with consent on reasonable grounds, allow entry warrant applications, restrict entry to private dwellings, and permit service of a written order after a violation is found.
proposedGroups.approximateLearningGoal: Recall who may inspect for suspected planning violations, when warrants or dwelling consent are needed, and when an order may be served.

proposals.reason: Section 134 is a substantial violation-order source with distinct topics for order powers, service and deadlines, and compliance or cost recovery.

proposedGroups.titleSuggestion: Violation orders to stop, alter, or restore development

evidenceText: may order

proposedGroups.reason: Subsection 134(1) identifies who may order cessation, alteration to remove a violation, or restoration after development violates the Act, by-laws, regulations, or imposed terms and conditions.
proposedGroups.approximateLearningGoal: Recall who may issue violation orders and what cessation, alteration, or restoration actions may be ordered.

proposedGroups.titleSuggestion: Written order contents, service, deadlines, cessation service, and deemed mail service

evidenceText: be in writing and signed

proposedGroups.reason: These subsections require signed written orders, service on owners, grounds and compliance periods, additional service for cessation orders, and deemed service four days after mailing.
proposedGroups.approximateLearningGoal: Recall how violation orders must be written, served, timed, and deemed served by registered mail.

proposedGroups.titleSuggestion: Owner compliance, action by Director or council, cost recovery, and lien

evidenceText: shall comply with the order at their own expense

proposedGroups.reason: These subsections require owner compliance at the owner's expense, allow the Director or council to undertake the ordered action and sue for costs, and make those costs a lien until recovered.
proposedGroups.approximateLearningGoal: Recall the owner's compliance duty and how costs of unmet violation orders may be recovered and secured by lien.

proposals.reason: Section 135 is a coherent court-enforcement application and order provision for violations, failures, and obstruction.

proposedGroups.titleSuggestion: Court orders for violations, failures, obstruction, removal, destruction, and costs

evidenceText: may make an application to The Court

proposedGroups.reason: The subsections identify who may apply to the Court for enforcement orders and list possible restraining, removal, destruction, enforcement, cost, and expense-recovery orders.
proposedGroups.approximateLearningGoal: Recall when local government, the Minister, or a designated person may seek court orders and what orders the judge may make.

proposals.reason: Section 136 is a coherent court power for directly affected persons or residents challenging or confirming local instruments, with a repeat-application refusal rule.

proposedGroups.titleSuggestion: Court orders quashing or declaring by-laws, resolutions, or orders

evidenceText: quash it in whole or in part for illegality

proposedGroups.reason: The subsections identify who may apply, the Court's power to quash for illegality or declare force and effect, and when the Court may refuse a repeat application raising substantially the same matters.
proposedGroups.approximateLearningGoal: Recall who may seek court review of a by-law, resolution, or order and what quashing, declaration, or repeat-application powers the Court has.

proposals.reason: Section 138 separates offence/category consequences from prosecution limits and appeal-related time extension.

proposedGroups.titleSuggestion: Offences, offence categories, and continued prosecution after conviction

evidenceText: commits an offence

proposedGroups.reason: These subsections make listed Schedule A violations offences, tie them to Provincial Offences Procedure Act categories, and state that conviction does not bar further prosecution for continued neglect or failure.
proposedGroups.approximateLearningGoal: Recall how offences are created and categorized under section 138 and why conviction does not bar further prosecution for continued non-compliance.

proposedGroups.titleSuggestion: Six-month prosecution limit and Board appeal extension

evidenceText: shall not be commenced after six months

proposedGroups.reason: These subsections set a six-month limit from discovery of the offence and extend that period by the time between notice of appeal and final disposition when a Board appeal is made.
proposedGroups.approximateLearningGoal: Recall the prosecution limitation period and how a Board appeal extends it.

proposals.reason: The section directs how claims are filed, discontinued, or determined by the Court.

proposedGroups.titleSuggestion: Filing and settling claims in abandoned-land proceedings
proposedGroups.reason: The provisions route claims to the Minister and unresolved claims to the Court of King's Bench.
proposedGroups.approximateLearningGoal: Determine how abandoned-land claims are filed, discontinued, or judicially settled.

proposals.source: Crown Lands and Forests Act s. 90
proposals.reason: The vesting order section separates prerequisites and contents from registration and proof effects.

proposedGroups.titleSuggestion: Order in Council declaring abandoned land vested in the Crown
proposedGroups.reason: These subsections authorize vesting when claims are absent or rejected and list required order particulars.
proposedGroups.approximateLearningGoal: Identify prerequisites and required contents of an abandoned-land vesting order.

proposedGroups.titleSuggestion: Registration and proof effect of abandoned-land vesting order
proposedGroups.reason: These subsections make registration vest land from the Gazette notice date and make the order proof in court.
proposedGroups.approximateLearningGoal: Explain the registration and evidentiary effects of an abandoned-land vesting order.

proposals.reason: The section vests real and personal property in personal representatives as trustees on death.

proposedGroups.titleSuggestion: Devolution of property to personal representatives
proposedGroups.reason: The rule covers property subject to debts and dispositions and general powers of appointment exercised by will.
proposedGroups.approximateLearningGoal: Explain how real and personal property devolves to personal representatives on death.

proposals.reason: The section provides separate post-one-year remedies for compelled conveyance and court-ordered sale.

proposedGroups.titleSuggestion: Court-ordered conveyance to person entitled to real property
proposedGroups.reason: This subsection allows an entitled person to seek conveyance or vesting after request and personal representative failure.
proposedGroups.approximateLearningGoal: Identify when the Court may order conveyance or vesting to the person entitled.

proposedGroups.titleSuggestion: Court-ordered sale when personal representative has not conveyed or sold
proposedGroups.reason: This subsection allows a beneficially interested person to seek sale and possible sheriff sale after non-compliance.
proposedGroups.approximateLearningGoal: Determine when the Court may order sale after personal representative inaction.

proposals.reason: The section distinguishes the concurrence requirement from court approval where concurrence is unavailable or incomplete.

proposedGroups.titleSuggestion: Concurrence requirement for distribution-only real property sales
proposedGroups.reason: These subsections require concurrence and deem it when an adult knowingly accepts purchase money.
proposedGroups.approximateLearningGoal: Recognize when a beneficiary is treated as concurring in a distribution-only sale.

proposedGroups.titleSuggestion: Court approval where beneficiaries cannot or do not concur
proposedGroups.reason: This subsection permits court approval binding persons lacking capacity, non-concurring adults, contingent interests, and unascertained beneficiaries.
proposedGroups.approximateLearningGoal: Apply the court approval route when concurrence is missing or impossible.

proposals.reason: Purchaser protection and continuing liability after conveyance to beneficiaries are separate rules.

proposedGroups.titleSuggestion: Good-faith purchaser protection from estate debts and beneficiary claims
proposedGroups.reason: This subsection protects good-faith value purchasers except for specific non-will charges and beneficiary claims in some sales.
proposedGroups.approximateLearningGoal: Recognize the protection given to good-faith purchasers of estate real property.

proposedGroups.titleSuggestion: Continuing liability of property conveyed to beneficiaries
proposedGroups.reason: This subsection keeps conveyed or vested property liable for deceased-owner debts and creates limited personal liability after value transactions.
proposedGroups.approximateLearningGoal: Determine how estate debts continue to affect property conveyed or vested in beneficiaries.

proposals.reason: The section separates the court order for sale free from curtesy or dower from the sale effect and compensation options.

proposedGroups.titleSuggestion: Court order for sale free from curtesy or dower
proposedGroups.reason: This subsection allows a personal representative to apply for a summary order with notice unless otherwise directed.
proposedGroups.approximateLearningGoal: Identify when a personal representative may seek sale free from curtesy or dower.

proposedGroups.titleSuggestion: Effect of sale and compensation for curtesy or dower interests
proposedGroups.reason: These subsections pass the interest without release and authorize gross-sum, annual-sum, income, and investment orders.
proposedGroups.approximateLearningGoal: Explain the effect of sale and compensation for curtesy or dower interests.

proposals.reason: The section combines a marital property definition with widow-share rules for different child scenarios.

proposedGroups.titleSuggestion: Marital property definition for widow intestacy shares
proposedGroups.reason: This subsection defines the property concept used in the widow-share rules.
proposedGroups.approximateLearningGoal: Identify the marital property concept used in section 22.

proposedGroups.titleSuggestion: Widow share when intestate leaves one child or children
proposedGroups.reason: These subsections assign marital property interests plus one-half or one-third of residue depending on number of children.
proposedGroups.approximateLearningGoal: Determine the widow share when an intestate leaves one child or multiple children.

proposedGroups.titleSuggestion: Widow share when a child predeceases leaving issue
proposedGroups.reason: This subsection treats a deceased child with living issue as living for the widow share calculation.
proposedGroups.approximateLearningGoal: Apply the widow-share rule when a child has died leaving issue.

proposals.reason: The advancement section has a hotchpot calculation rule plus valuation and proof rules.

proposedGroups.titleSuggestion: Accounting for advancement to a child in whole intestacy
proposedGroups.reason: This subsection reckons the advanced portion as part of the distributable estate and adjusts or excludes the child share.
proposedGroups.approximateLearningGoal: Determine how an advancement affects a child share in a wholly intestate estate.

proposedGroups.titleSuggestion: Valuation and proof of advancement
proposedGroups.reason: These subsections set value by writing or time advanced and place the proof burden on the asserting person.
proposedGroups.approximateLearningGoal: Apply the valuation and proof rules for alleged advancement.

proposals.reason: The Easements Act section creates different consequences after thirty and sixty years of enjoying profits or benefits.

proposedGroups.titleSuggestion: Thirty-year enjoyment protects profit or benefit claims from ancient-origin defeat
proposedGroups.reason: This subsection prevents defeat based only on lack of time-immemorial origin after thirty years uninterrupted enjoyment.
proposedGroups.approximateLearningGoal: Identify the effect of thirty years enjoyment on a profit or benefit claim.

proposedGroups.titleSuggestion: Sixty-year enjoyment makes profit or benefit rights indefeasible except written consent
proposedGroups.reason: This subsection makes the right absolute after sixty years unless enjoyment was under express deed or written consent.
proposedGroups.approximateLearningGoal: Apply the sixty-year rule and written-consent exception for profit or benefit claims.

proposals.reason: The general easement section uses separate twenty-year and forty-year thresholds.

proposedGroups.titleSuggestion: Twenty-year enjoyment protects general easement claims from ancient-origin defeat
proposedGroups.reason: This subsection protects claims to ways, easements, watercourses, and water use after twenty years enjoyment.
proposedGroups.approximateLearningGoal: Identify the effect of twenty years enjoyment on general easement and water-use claims.

proposedGroups.titleSuggestion: Forty-year enjoyment makes general easement rights indefeasible except written consent
proposedGroups.reason: This subsection makes the right absolute after forty years unless enjoyment was under express deed or written consent.
proposedGroups.approximateLearningGoal: Apply the forty-year rule and written-consent exception.

proposals.reason: The pleading section has separate rules for general allegations, enjoyment pleadings, and special pleading of exceptions.

proposedGroups.titleSuggestion: General allegation and evidence for easement claims
proposedGroups.reason: This subsection preserves general pleading and admits sections 1 to 3 matters to sustain or rebut it.
proposedGroups.approximateLearningGoal: Recognize when a general allegation of right is sufficient.

proposedGroups.titleSuggestion: Pleading enjoyment as of right instead of time immemorial
proposedGroups.reason: This subsection allows pleading enjoyment as of right for statutory periods rather than time immemorial.
proposedGroups.approximateLearningGoal: Identify how a claimant may plead enjoyment for statutory periods.

proposedGroups.titleSuggestion: Special pleading of exceptions, disabilities, agreements, or other matters
proposedGroups.reason: This subsection requires exceptions and similar matters to be specially alleged instead of raised under general denial.
proposedGroups.approximateLearningGoal: Apply the requirement to specially plead matters answering an easement claim.

proposals.reason: The section gives priority to other express electronic-information Acts and permits regulatory exclusions.

proposedGroups.titleSuggestion: Application limits where other Acts or regulations govern electronic information
proposedGroups.reason: The subsections address conflict with other Acts and exclusions by regulation.
proposedGroups.approximateLearningGoal: Determine when the Electronic Transactions Act gives way to another Act or regulation.

proposals.reason: The original requirement, integrity standard, and conversion rule are separate topics.

proposedGroups.titleSuggestion: Reliable assurance of integrity for electronic originals
proposedGroups.reason: These subsections require reliable assurance of integrity and define how integrity and reliability are assessed.
proposedGroups.approximateLearningGoal: Determine whether electronic information satisfies a legal requirement for an original.

proposedGroups.titleSuggestion: Converted information remaining an original
proposedGroups.reason: This subsection preserves original status through electronic and non-electronic conversion if requirements continue to be met.
proposedGroups.approximateLearningGoal: Recognize when converted information remains an original.

proposals.reason: The section states that an electronic signature satisfies a signature requirement and gives examples.

proposedGroups.titleSuggestion: Electronic signatures satisfying signature requirements
proposedGroups.reason: The examples include electronic representation of a manual signature or name information clearly provided as a signature.
proposedGroups.approximateLearningGoal: Identify how an electronic signature can satisfy a legal signature requirement.

proposals.reason: The section separates electronic retention conditions from non-electronic retention of initially electronic information.

proposedGroups.titleSuggestion: Conditions for retaining information electronically
proposedGroups.reason: This subsection requires format/content integrity, accessibility, and supplementary origin/destination/time information where applicable.
proposedGroups.approximateLearningGoal: Apply the conditions for electronic retention of information.

proposedGroups.titleSuggestion: Non-electronic retention of initially electronic information
proposedGroups.reason: This subsection permits non-electronic retention if the subsection (1) requirements are met.
proposedGroups.approximateLearningGoal: Recognize when initially electronic information may be retained non-electronically.

proposals.reason: The provision rule includes separate requirements for accessibility, multiple copies, and inhibited retention.

proposedGroups.titleSuggestion: Providing written information electronically
proposedGroups.reason: This subsection requires recipient accessibility and retention capability for later reference.
proposedGroups.approximateLearningGoal: Determine when electronic information satisfies a requirement to provide written information.

proposedGroups.titleSuggestion: Single electronic version and inhibited retention
proposedGroups.reason: These subsections satisfy multiple-copy requirements with one electronic version and negate retention if printing or storage is inhibited.
proposedGroups.approximateLearningGoal: Apply the multiple-copy and inhibited-retention rules.

proposals.reason: The section sets acknowledgement conditions for electronic registered mail.

proposedGroups.titleSuggestion: Electronic delivery satisfying registered mail requirement
proposedGroups.reason: The sender must request acknowledgement, the recipient must acknowledge, and electronic acknowledgement requires an electronic signature.
proposedGroups.approximateLearningGoal: Apply the acknowledgement and signature requirements for electronic registered mail.

proposals.reason: The responsible authority definition and the authority to set effective electronic means are separate concepts.

proposedGroups.titleSuggestion: Responsible authority definition for electronic means
proposedGroups.reason: These subsections identify responsible authorities for statutory powers, public bodies, Ministers, and related dealings.
proposedGroups.approximateLearningGoal: Identify who is the responsible authority for electronic means.

proposedGroups.titleSuggestion: Authority to set electronic information characteristics and conditions
proposedGroups.reason: These subsections allow determinations of form, technology, manner, terms, and conditions and make that use effective.
proposedGroups.approximateLearningGoal: Determine how a responsible authority can make electronic information effective.

proposedGroups.titleSuggestion: Other electronic means do not bind responsible authority
proposedGroups.reason: This subsection allows other acceptance but says private acceptance does not require authority acceptance.
proposedGroups.approximateLearningGoal: Recognize that other electronic means do not compel a responsible authority.

proposals.reason: The timing section has separate sending, receipt, and place-limitation rules.

proposedGroups.titleSuggestion: Time electronic information is sent
proposedGroups.reason: This subsection defines sending by system entry outside sender control or same-system accessibility.
proposedGroups.approximateLearningGoal: Determine when electronic information is sent.

proposedGroups.titleSuggestion: Presumed receipt of electronic information
proposedGroups.reason: This subsection presumes receipt based on designated or used systems and retrievability or addressee awareness.
proposedGroups.approximateLearningGoal: Determine when electronic information is presumed received.

proposedGroups.titleSuggestion: No place-of-sending or place-of-receipt rule
proposedGroups.reason: This subsection states that place of sending or receipt is not determined.
proposedGroups.approximateLearningGoal: Recognize that timing rules do not set legal place.

proposals.reason: The section defines electronic agent and validates contracts or transactions formed through agent interactions.

proposedGroups.titleSuggestion: Electronic agents entering contracts or transactions
proposedGroups.reason: The rule covers individual-agent and agent-agent interactions.
proposedGroups.approximateLearningGoal: Identify what an electronic agent is and how it may enter transactions.

proposals.reason: The human-error cancellation section has conditions, cancellation duties, and preserved remedies.

proposedGroups.titleSuggestion: Conditions for cancelling a transaction after human error
proposedGroups.reason: These subsections allow cancellation for material error with no correction opportunity, including by the represented person.
proposedGroups.approximateLearningGoal: Identify when human error with an electronic agent permits cancellation.

proposedGroups.titleSuggestion: Notice, return, destruction, and no-benefit duties after cancellation
proposedGroups.reason: These subsections require prompt notice, return or destruction steps, no material benefit, and reciprocal return or destruction.
proposedGroups.approximateLearningGoal: Apply duties that follow cancellation for human error.

proposedGroups.titleSuggestion: Other remedies preserved after electronic-agent error
proposedGroups.reason: This subsection preserves other remedies or recourse.
proposedGroups.approximateLearningGoal: Recognize that cancellation does not displace other remedies.

proposals.reason: The regulation section covers regulation subjects and the scope of general, specific, and consumer rules.

proposedGroups.titleSuggestion: Regulations for electronic information, consent, payments, exclusions, and consumer contracts
proposedGroups.reason: This subsection authorizes regulations on terms, electronic information, consent, payments, exclusions, consumer transactions, and implementation.
proposedGroups.approximateLearningGoal: Identify regulation subjects authorized under the Act.

proposedGroups.titleSuggestion: General, specific, and consumer-transaction regulatory scope
proposedGroups.reason: These subsections allow general or specific regulations and consumer rules on requirements, enforceability, and remedies.
proposedGroups.approximateLearningGoal: Recognize how regulations may vary by person, subject matter, and consumer transaction.

proposals.reason: The section authorizes Crown possession or recovery action for lands liable to escheat or forfeiture without inquisition.

proposedGroups.titleSuggestion: Crown possession or recovery of escheated or forfeited lands
proposedGroups.reason: The proceedings may resemble other land-recovery actions.
proposedGroups.approximateLearningGoal: Identify how the Attorney General may take possession or recover escheated or forfeited lands.

proposals.reason: The grants section separates grant purposes from grant mechanics and grantee recovery rights.

proposedGroups.titleSuggestion: Grants of escheated or forfeited lands for moral claims, contemplated dispositions, or discovery rewards
proposedGroups.reason: This subsection authorizes grants to restore property, carry out contemplated dispositions, or reward discovery.
proposedGroups.approximateLearningGoal: Identify purposes for which escheated or forfeited lands may be granted.

proposedGroups.titleSuggestion: Grant without entry or inquisition and grantee recovery proceedings
proposedGroups.reason: These subsections allow grants before entry or inquisition and allow grantee recovery if possession is withheld.
proposedGroups.approximateLearningGoal: Recognize when a grant may be made before possession and what recovery right follows.

proposals.reason: The section allows the Crown to waive or release forfeiture rights on terms to restore property interests.

proposedGroups.titleSuggestion: Waiver or release of Crown forfeiture rights
proposedGroups.reason: The waiver or release may be for consideration or otherwise and on terms set by the Lieutenant-Governor in Council.
proposedGroups.approximateLearningGoal: Identify how relief from forfeiture may restore property interests.

proposals.reason: The section authorizes sale of forfeited personal property and directs proceeds to the Consolidated Fund.

proposedGroups.titleSuggestion: Sale of forfeited personal property and Consolidated Fund proceeds
proposedGroups.reason: The Minister may sell by public auction or private sale and proceeds become part of the Consolidated Fund.
proposedGroups.approximateLearningGoal: Recognize who may sell forfeited personal property and where proceeds go.

proposals.reason: The section makes parties, represented persons, and spouses competent and compellable in court proceedings, subject to exceptions.

proposedGroups.titleSuggestion: Competency and compellability of parties and spouses in civil proceedings
proposedGroups.reason: Subsection 3(2) is repealed, while subsection 3(1) contains the operative rule.
proposedGroups.approximateLearningGoal: Identify who is competent and compellable to give evidence under section 3.

proposals.reason: The section allows solemn affirmation for persons unwilling to be sworn on conscientious grounds and gives it oath-equivalent force.

proposedGroups.titleSuggestion: Solemn affirmation instead of oath
proposedGroups.reason: The subsections state the affirmation words and the same force and effect as an oath.
proposedGroups.approximateLearningGoal: Identify when solemn affirmation may replace an oath and its legal effect.

proposals.reason: Prior-conviction questioning and proof by certificate are separate evidence rules.

proposedGroups.titleSuggestion: Questioning witness about prior conviction
proposedGroups.reason: This subsection allows questioning and proof if the witness denies or refuses to answer.
proposedGroups.approximateLearningGoal: Identify when a prior conviction may be proved after questioning a witness.

proposedGroups.titleSuggestion: Certificate as sufficient evidence of conviction
proposedGroups.reason: This subsection makes a conviction certificate sufficient evidence upon proof of identity without proof of signature or office.
proposedGroups.approximateLearningGoal: Apply the certificate rule for proving a witness prior conviction.

proposals.reason: The section allows unsworn evidence from a child of tender years if the court finds sufficient intelligence and truth understanding.

proposedGroups.titleSuggestion: Unsworn evidence of child of tender years
proposedGroups.reason: Subsection 24(2) is repealed, while subsection 24(1) supplies the operative conditions.
proposedGroups.approximateLearningGoal: Identify the conditions for receiving unsworn evidence from a child of tender years.

proposals.reason: The section separates authorized recording methods from admissibility of certified transcripts.

proposedGroups.titleSuggestion: Authorized methods for recording evidence and proceedings
proposedGroups.reason: This subsection permits shorthand, approved mechanical devices, and approved sound recording devices.
proposedGroups.approximateLearningGoal: Identify who may record evidence and what methods are authorized.

proposedGroups.titleSuggestion: Certified transcript admissibility despite approval or signature issues
proposedGroups.reason: This subsection makes certified transcripts admissible if otherwise admissible even without approval, reading, or signature.
proposedGroups.approximateLearningGoal: Determine when a certified transcript is admissible in evidence.

proposals.reason: The section covers covered bodies, destruction timing, and preservation orders.

proposedGroups.titleSuggestion: Application to tribunal and commissioner records
proposedGroups.reason: This subsection extends the section to evidence or proceedings before boards, commissions, tribunals, bodies, or commissioners.
proposedGroups.approximateLearningGoal: Identify the proceedings to which the record preservation section applies.

proposedGroups.titleSuggestion: Destroying or retaining records depending on transcript certification
proposedGroups.reason: These subsections set destruction timing after certified transcripts or prescribed retention for uncertified records.
proposedGroups.approximateLearningGoal: Apply destruction timing rules for records of evidence or proceedings.

proposedGroups.titleSuggestion: Preservation orders and service on record holders
proposedGroups.reason: These provisions allow preservation applications, identify the decision maker, authorize orders, and require preservation after service.
proposedGroups.approximateLearningGoal: Trace how an interested person obtains and enforces a record preservation order.

proposals.reason: The section separates the order to bring a prisoner witness from return, continuity, and immunity consequences.

proposedGroups.titleSuggestion: Order to bring prisoner or committed person as witness
proposedGroups.reason: This subsection allows a Court of King's Bench judge to order the person brought, with tender required for custody officer compliance.
proposedGroups.approximateLearningGoal: Identify the application, order, and tender requirements for bringing a prisoner as witness.

proposedGroups.titleSuggestion: Return, continuity of imprisonment, and officer immunity
proposedGroups.reason: These subsections require return after testimony, deem continuous imprisonment, and protect officers obeying the order.
proposedGroups.approximateLearningGoal: Recognize the return obligation, imprisonment-continuity rule, and officer immunity.

proposals.reason: Section 8 authorizes proceedings in the Minister's name for contract enforcement, highway damage recovery, and highway rights, while preserving Crown enforcement rights.

proposedGroups.approximateLearningGoal: Recall when proceedings may be instituted in the Minister's name and how Crown enforcement rights are preserved.

proposals.reason: Section 13 authorizes disposal of no-longer-required highway equipment, machinery, or implements by sale, lease, tender, or trade-in credit.

lease

proposedGroups.approximateLearningGoal: Recall how the Minister may dispose of or trade no-longer-required highway equipment, machinery, or implements.

proposals.reason: Section 15 covers designation of roads as highways, Royal Gazette notice, amendment of designations, deemed amendment after discontinuance, and inclusion of bridges and incidental structures.

proposedGroups.titleSuggestion: Filing and notice for highway designations

evidenceText: may designate roads as highways by filing
are highways for the purposes of this Act
publish in The Royal Gazette a notice

proposedGroups.reason: Subsections 15(1) to 15(3) explain how road designations are filed, what legal status follows, and what notice is published.
proposedGroups.approximateLearningGoal: Recall how the Minister designates roads as highways and gives Royal Gazette notice.

proposedGroups.titleSuggestion: Amending highway designations and included structures

evidenceText: may amend a designation
discontinued under section 33
includes bridges and other structures incidental to the highway

proposedGroups.reason: Subsections 15(4) to 15(6) address amending designations, automatic amendment on discontinuance, and what structures are included in a designated highway.
proposedGroups.approximateLearningGoal: Recall how highway designations may be amended, how discontinuance affects them, and what structures a designated highway includes.

proposals.reason: Section 17 is a coherent set of rules for acquiring land in a development area, leasing it back or otherwise until needed, and terminating those leases on notice.

proposedGroups.approximateLearningGoal: Recall how the Minister may acquire and lease land within a development area and how leases may be terminated.

proposals.reason: Section 18 gives an owner of land in a development area the right to request Ministerial purchase and removes the land from the declaration if it is not purchased within two years.

proposals.reason: Section 21 addresses compensation for expropriated development-area land and denies compensation for increased value caused by contravening section 19.

proposedGroups.titleSuggestion: Compensation for expropriated development-area land

evidenceText: compensated for that land as though the land were not in a development area

proposedGroups.reason: The subsections together state the baseline compensation rule and the contravention-based exclusion for increased value.
proposedGroups.approximateLearningGoal: Recall how compensation is calculated for expropriated development-area land and when increased value is excluded.

proposals.reason: Section 28 combines uncompensated highway-purpose removal and entry powers, a damage compensation exception for shore or bed materials, snow-fence powers, and a court-backed warrant process for resistance.

proposedGroups.titleSuggestion: Removal, material, and snow-fence powers without compensation

evidenceText: without compensating the owner
may remove for highway purposes
may take and carry away
may enter upon any lands adjacent to a highway

proposedGroups.reason: Subsection 28(1) lists the Minister or agent powers over materials, encroachments, shore or bed materials, fences, and snow fences, including the compensation exception for damage under paragraph (c).
proposedGroups.approximateLearningGoal: Recall the Minister or agent powers to remove materials or obstructions, use shore or bed materials, and handle fences or snow fences for highway purposes.

proposedGroups.titleSuggestion: Warrant process for resistance to highway removal or demolition

evidenceText: resistance or opposition

shall make a return of the warrant

proposedGroups.reason: Subsections 28(2) and 28(3) provide the judicial warrant and sheriff return process when removal or demolition under paragraph 28(1)(b) is resisted.
proposedGroups.approximateLearningGoal: Recall how resistance to authorized highway removal or demolition can be addressed through a court warrant and sheriff return.

proposals.reason: Section 30 covers width presumptions and requirements for highways, Lieutenant-Governor in Council authority to allow narrower highways, and the centre-line rule for boundary doubts or disputes.

proposedGroups.titleSuggestion: Highway width presumptions and minimum widths

evidenceText: deemed to have been laid out four rods in width

proposedGroups.reason: Subsections 30(1) to 30(3) address deemed width for existing highways, default width for new highways, and orders allowing narrower width.
proposedGroups.approximateLearningGoal: Recall the four-rod presumption, 20 m minimum, and 10 m lower limit for highway width.

proposedGroups.titleSuggestion: Centre line for disputed highway boundaries

evidenceText: doubt or dispute as to the boundaries of a highway
centre line of the travelled portion

proposedGroups.reason: Subsection 30(4) is a separate boundary rule based on the centre line of the travelled portion.
proposedGroups.approximateLearningGoal: Recognize how the centre line of a highway is determined when highway boundaries are in doubt or dispute.

proposals.reason: Section 31 authorizes Ministerial construction standards for roads and streets in specified local governments, exemptions where subdivision by-laws prescribe standards, and an offence for contravening applicable standards.

proposedGroups.titleSuggestion: Construction standards for village, rural community, and regional municipality streets

evidenceText: may establish the standards
may exempt the village, rural community or regional municipality
commits an offence

proposedGroups.reason: The subsections together set standards, possible local exemption, and offence consequences.
proposedGroups.approximateLearningGoal: Recall how road or street construction standards apply in villages, rural communities, and regional municipalities and when contravention is an offence.

proposals.reason: Section 32 combines a historical vesting declaration for soil and freehold with a current proclamation mechanism releasing highways to local government jurisdiction and vesting Crown-owned soil and freehold in that local government.

proposedGroups.reason: Subsection 32(1) is a distinct vesting declaration concerning abutting owners and successors in title.
proposedGroups.approximateLearningGoal: Recall the declared vesting of soil and freehold of certain highways in abutting owners and their successors.

proposedGroups.titleSuggestion: Proclamation releasing highways to local government control

evidenceText: cease to be under the control of the Minister
under the jurisdiction of the local government
vested in that local government

proposedGroups.reason: Subsections 32(2) and 32(3) cover proclamation-based transfer of highway control and Crown-owned soil and freehold to the named local government.
proposedGroups.approximateLearningGoal: Recall how a highway can cease to be under Ministerial control and how related Crown-owned soil and freehold vests in a local government.

proposals.reason: Section 33 covers discontinuance filing methods and effects, access protection before discontinuance, cessation of public passage rights, and ratification of earlier discontinuances.

proposedGroups.approximateLearningGoal: Recall the recording methods and highway-status effect of discontinuing a highway or road.

proposedGroups.titleSuggestion: Access protection and public rights after discontinuance

proposedGroups.reason: Subsections 33(2) and 33(3) address access safeguards and the cessation of public passage rights.
proposedGroups.approximateLearningGoal: Recall the adequate-access safeguard and the effect of discontinuance on public passage rights.

proposedGroups.titleSuggestion: Ratification of earlier highway discontinuances

proposals.reason: Section 34 authorizes the Minister to close highways by posted signs or notices, limit closure to vehicle classes, and makes operation on a closed highway an offence.

proposedGroups.titleSuggestion: Posted highway closures and offence for operating on closed highway

limit the closing
