proposedGroups.reason: The current subsections together cover the closure authority, vehicle-class limitation, evidentiary effect of posted signs, and offence for operating on a closed highway.
proposedGroups.approximateLearningGoal: Recall how highway closures are posted and proved, how they may be limited by vehicle class, and when operation on a closed highway is an offence.

proposals.reason: Section 35 states when roads constructed by others become highways and authorizes the Minister to accept roads or streets as highways despite the Community Planning Act.

proposedGroups.titleSuggestion: Ministerial certification accepting roads as highways

evidenceText: shall become a highway
until the Minister certifies
may accept a road or street as a highway

proposedGroups.reason: Both subsections depend on Ministerial certification and designation amendment for road or street acceptance as a highway.
proposedGroups.approximateLearningGoal: Recall when a road or street becomes a highway through Ministerial certification and designation amendment.

proposals.reason: Section 36 is a large height and weight restriction regime with definitions, imposition and proof of restrictions, offences and penalties, damage liability, special permits, and exemptions.

proposedGroups.titleSuggestion: Height and weight restriction definitions and posting
proposedGroups.reason: Subsections 36(1) to 36(6) define key restriction terms and explain how restrictions are imposed, amended, cancelled, noticed, and proved.
proposedGroups.approximateLearningGoal: Recall the definitions of height and weight restrictions and how Minister-posted restrictions take effect, are proved, and may be amended or cancelled.

proposedGroups.titleSuggestion: Offences, penalties, and damage liability for excess height or weight
proposedGroups.reason: Subsections 36(7) to 36(11) cover offences for exceeding restrictions, excess-weight penalties, and joint and several liability for resulting damage.
proposedGroups.approximateLearningGoal: Recall the offence, penalty, and damage-liability consequences of operating vehicles over height or weight restrictions.

proposedGroups.titleSuggestion: Special permits and exemptions from weight restrictions
proposedGroups.reason: Subsections 36(12) to 36(15) address special permits, their effect and liability limits, and exemptions for emergency or maintenance vehicles.
proposedGroups.approximateLearningGoal: Recall when special permits may authorize operation despite weight restrictions and which vehicles are exempt from bridge weight restrictions.

proposals.reason: Section 37 contains several distinct learning topics: weighing powers and offences, technician designation, evidentiary certificates, and the risk rule for unloaded material.

proposedGroups.titleSuggestion: Approved weighing device and qualified technician definitions
proposedGroups.reason: Subsection 37(1) defines the two terms that control the weighing and certificate rules in the rest of the section.
proposedGroups.approximateLearningGoal: Identify how approved weighing device and qualified technician are defined for vehicle weighing enforcement.

proposedGroups.titleSuggestion: Commercial vehicle weighing demands and stop directions
proposedGroups.reason: Subsections 37(2) to 37(5) set inspector powers to demand weighing, direct movement or unloading, signal stops, and create offences for non-compliance.
proposedGroups.approximateLearningGoal: Explain when commercial vehicle inspectors may demand weighing or issue stop directions and what non-compliance triggers.

proposedGroups.titleSuggestion: Designation and status of weighing-device technicians
proposedGroups.reason: Subsections 37(7) and 37(9) address who may operate or certify approved weighing devices and how that designation affects qualified-technician status.
proposedGroups.approximateLearningGoal: Describe how the Minister designates persons for approved weighing devices and how designation creates qualified-technician status.

proposedGroups.titleSuggestion: Weighing and registration certificate evidence
proposedGroups.reason: Subsections 37(10) to 37(15) set the evidentiary effect, notice, cross-examination, weighing-proof, and Registrar certificate rules for vehicle weight proceedings.
proposedGroups.approximateLearningGoal: Recognize what certificates and weighing results prove in vehicle weight proceedings and the notice and cross-examination limits.

proposedGroups.titleSuggestion: Risk for unloaded vehicle material
proposedGroups.reason: Subsection 37(16) separately assigns risk for material unloaded after an inspector directs movement or load removal.
proposedGroups.approximateLearningGoal: State who bears the risk for material unloaded after a commercial vehicle inspector direction.

proposals.reason: Section 39 is a broad controlled-access-highway regime with separable topics for the utility definition, access prohibitions and closure enforcement, permits, and preserved highway corporation access.

proposedGroups.titleSuggestion: Utility definition for controlled access highways
proposedGroups.reason: Subsection 39(1) defines utility for the controlled access highway section, including included public-service activities and excluded signal conveyance.
proposedGroups.approximateLearningGoal: Identify who is a utility for the controlled access highway rules.

proposedGroups.titleSuggestion: Prohibited access and closure orders for controlled access highways
proposedGroups.reason: Subsections 39(2) to 39(9) prohibit unauthorized access and set the Minister order, service, compliance, entry, cost recovery, and court-order mechanisms.
proposedGroups.approximateLearningGoal: Explain how unauthorized access to a controlled access highway is prohibited and enforced through Ministerial orders.

proposedGroups.titleSuggestion: Controlled access highway permits and farm crossings
proposedGroups.reason: Subsections 39(10), 39(13) to 39(16), and 39(18) provide permit pathways, cancellation and records, temporary access, legacy access permits, and farm crossings.
proposedGroups.approximateLearningGoal: Distinguish the controlled access highway permit pathways, permit records, cancellation, and farm-crossing authority.

proposedGroups.titleSuggestion: New Brunswick Highway Corporation access exception
proposedGroups.reason: Subsection 39(19) separately preserves New Brunswick Highway Corporation ability to construct, use, open, or permit access for highways under its administration and control.
proposedGroups.approximateLearningGoal: State how section 39 treats New Brunswick Highway Corporation access to highways under its administration and control.

proposals.reason: Section 43 covers advertisement regulation near highways, advertisement offences, Ministerial notice and removal powers, and the definition or carve-out for advertisements and traffic control devices.

proposedGroups.titleSuggestion: Advertisement regulations near highways
proposedGroups.reason: Subsection 43(1) authorizes regulations prohibiting or regulating advertisements at specified distances from highways and covering identification, compensation, costs, removal, relocation, disposal, and permits.
proposedGroups.approximateLearningGoal: Identify the highway-advertisement matters that may be regulated under section 43.

proposedGroups.titleSuggestion: Advertisement offences on or near highways
proposedGroups.reason: Subsections 43(2) to 43(4) create offences for unlawful advertisement activity, destroying or defacing advertisements, and failing to remove an advertisement after notice.
proposedGroups.approximateLearningGoal: Recognize the conduct involving highway advertisements that section 43 makes an offence.

proposedGroups.titleSuggestion: Notice and removal of unlawful or hazardous advertisements
proposedGroups.reason: Subsections 43(5) and 43(6) set service of removal notice and allow Ministerial removal of unlawful or immediately hazardous advertisements.
proposedGroups.approximateLearningGoal: Explain how notice is served and when the Minister may remove an advertisement.

proposedGroups.titleSuggestion: Meaning of advertisement and traffic control devices
proposedGroups.reason: Subsections 43(7) and 43(8) define advertisement broadly and preserve traffic control devices approved by the Minister.
proposedGroups.approximateLearningGoal: State what counts as an advertisement and why traffic control devices are unaffected.

proposals.reason: Section 45 is a cohesive rule on public utility obstructions in highways, including removal duties, Ministerial notice and recovery of expenses, franchise preservation, and Corporation substitution.

proposedGroups.titleSuggestion: Public utility obstruction removal from highways
proposedGroups.reason: All subsections address removal of utility objects obstructing or interfering with highway work or use and who exercises the Ministerial power.
proposedGroups.approximateLearningGoal: Explain when public utility objects must be removed from highways and how removal authority and costs operate.

proposals.reason: The section is a focused allocation of provincial-municipal highway construction, maintenance, local services, and prescribed additional services.

proposedGroups.titleSuggestion: Provincial-municipal highway service responsibilities
proposedGroups.reason: Subsections 47(1) to 47(3) allocate Minister and local government responsibilities for provincial-municipal highway work and related services.
proposedGroups.approximateLearningGoal: Distinguish the highway work the Minister may provide from the services a local government may provide on provincial-municipal highways.

proposals.reason: The section collects the Minister responsibilities and authorities for resource access road supervision, acquisition, and agreements.

proposedGroups.titleSuggestion: Resource access road supervision, acquisition, and agreements
proposedGroups.reason: All subsections address Ministerial control over construction and maintenance funds, land acquisition, and intergovernmental or other agreements for resource access roads.
proposedGroups.approximateLearningGoal: Explain the Minister powers over supervising, acquiring land for, and contracting about resource access roads.

proposals.reason: The section is a focused soil-rights and compensation rule following resource access road classification.

proposedGroups.titleSuggestion: Soil rights and compensation for resource access roads
proposedGroups.reason: Subsection 54(1) preserves existing soil rights after classification and subsection 54(2) requires compensation when the Minister has not acquired the soil rights.
proposedGroups.approximateLearningGoal: Explain how resource access road classification affects soil rights and when compensation is required.

proposals.reason: The section is a single resource access road use-restriction regime covering reasons for restrictions, posting, forms of restriction, and public use.

proposedGroups.titleSuggestion: Restrictions on use of resource access roads
proposedGroups.reason: The subsections together explain when the Minister may restrict resource access road use, how orders are posted, what restrictions may do, and the baseline public-use rule.
proposedGroups.approximateLearningGoal: Identify the grounds, posting methods, restriction types, and public-use rule for resource access roads.

proposals.reason: The section is a cohesive contract-penalty rule for highway construction or maintenance contracts involving the Minister.

proposedGroups.titleSuggestion: Penalty clauses in Minister highway contracts
proposedGroups.reason: The subsections identify when contract penalties may be used, how penalties are measured, and that penalty amounts may be withheld from Crown payments.
proposedGroups.approximateLearningGoal: Explain how penalty clauses may operate in Minister highway construction or maintenance contracts.

proposals.reason: The section is a focused rule for removing buildings from a highway right-of-way, including notice, removal methods, and compensation limits.

proposedGroups.titleSuggestion: Removing buildings from a highway right-of-way
proposedGroups.reason: All subsections address Ministerial removal of buildings from the highway right-of-way after notice, how removal may occur, and when compensation under section 24 is barred.
proposedGroups.approximateLearningGoal: Describe the notice, removal methods, and compensation limit for buildings in a highway right-of-way.

proposals.reason: Section 65 contains distinct control-line topics: the designated line and construction prohibition, continuing offence consequences, Ministerial closure power, and permit records.

proposedGroups.titleSuggestion: Control line distance and construction prohibition
proposedGroups.reason: Subsections 65(2) to 65(4) set the maximum control-line distance, prohibit structures and driveways inside the line, and preserve existing objects between the highway center line and control line.
proposedGroups.approximateLearningGoal: Explain how a control line limits construction or placement near an arterial or collector highway.

proposedGroups.titleSuggestion: Control line offences, closure power, and entrance permits
proposedGroups.reason: Subsections 65(5) to 65(8) address continuing offence fines, Ministerial closure of unlawful access, permits for entrance ways, permit cancellation, and public permit records.
proposedGroups.approximateLearningGoal: Recognize the enforcement, closure, permit, and record rules tied to control line violations.

proposals.reason: Section 67 combines a broad list of regulation-making subjects with separate land-registration and effectiveness rules for controlled access highway and control line regulations.

proposedGroups.titleSuggestion: Highway Act regulation-making subjects
proposedGroups.reason: Subsection 67(1) lists the subjects the Lieutenant-Governor in Council may regulate, including permits, penalties, weighing, controlled access highways, utilities, highway use, maintenance, control lines, forms, and transitional matters.
proposedGroups.approximateLearningGoal: Identify the main Highway Act subjects that may be governed by regulation.

proposedGroups.titleSuggestion: Registration and effect of controlled access and control line regulations
proposedGroups.reason: Subsections 67(2) to 67(9) set the plan or description requirements, registration, commencement, website notice, and validity rules for controlled access highway and control line regulations.
proposedGroups.approximateLearningGoal: Explain how controlled access highway and control line regulations are described, registered, take effect, and remain valid despite notice failures.

proposals.reason: Section 69 separates listed highway offences from the special vehicle-owner liability and charging rule.

proposedGroups.titleSuggestion: Listed highway obstruction and damage offences
proposedGroups.reason: Subsection 69(1) lists offence conduct involving encumbrances, water obstructions, altering highways or drains, disturbing ditch soil, damaging shoulders, traffic control devices, highways, bridges, culverts, and obstructing the Minister.
proposedGroups.approximateLearningGoal: Identify the highway obstruction, alteration, damage, and interference conduct made an offence.

proposedGroups.titleSuggestion: Vehicle owner liability and charging for weight violations
proposedGroups.reason: Subsections 69(2) and 69(3) address when a vehicle owner is deemed guilty of weight-related violations and how the owner may be charged.
proposedGroups.approximateLearningGoal: Explain how owner liability and charging work for vehicle weight violations.

proposals.reason: The section is a focused offence-classification provision for regulatory violations and Act provisions listed in Schedule A.

proposedGroups.titleSuggestion: Regulation violations and Schedule A offence categories
proposedGroups.reason: The three subsections make regulatory non-compliance an offence, make Schedule A listed provisions offences, and tie those listed offences to Provincial Offences Procedure Act categories.
proposedGroups.approximateLearningGoal: Explain how section 70 creates offences and links Schedule A provisions to offence categories.

proposals.reason: Schedule A is an authoritative table mapping Highway Act provisions to Provincial Offences Procedure Act offence categories.

proposedGroups.titleSuggestion: Schedule A offence category table

evidenceText: Column I
Category of Offence

proposedGroups.reason: The schedule consists of a two-column table identifying listed sections or paragraphs and their corresponding offence categories.
proposedGroups.approximateLearningGoal: Use Schedule A to match listed Highway Act offences with their category of offence.

proposals.reason: The section separates land brought under the Act from Registry Act recording restrictions and exceptions.

proposedGroups.titleSuggestion: Parcels subject to or excepted from the Act
proposedGroups.reason: These subsections set application to parcels, exception or inclusion by the Lieutenant-Governor in Council, and Crown binding.
proposedGroups.approximateLearningGoal: Explain what land the Act applies to and how parcels may be excepted or added.

proposedGroups.titleSuggestion: Registry Act recording limits and exceptions
proposedGroups.reason: These subsections restrict Registry Act recording for land titles land and set application-pending and Registrar General certificate exceptions.
proposedGroups.approximateLearningGoal: Identify when an instrument for land titles land may still be recorded under the Registry Act.

proposals.reason: Administrative section on appointment, powers, remuneration, fee handling, and pension coverage for officers.

proposedGroups.titleSuggestion: Registrar General, registrar, and deputy appointments
proposedGroups.reason: All subsections concern the appointment and status of the Registrar General, registrars, and deputies.
proposedGroups.approximateLearningGoal: Describe appointment, duties, remuneration, fee, and pension rules for land titles officers.

proposals.reason: The section separates access and evidentiary use of records from the definition of records.

proposedGroups.titleSuggestion: Inspection, copies, and evidentiary status of records
proposedGroups.reason: These subsections govern record inspection, sealed copies, an application-document exception, and certified evidence.
proposedGroups.approximateLearningGoal: Explain access to land titles records and when copies or reproductions are evidence.

proposedGroups.titleSuggestion: Definition of records for land titles evidence
proposedGroups.reason: Subsection 9(3) defines records across written, printed, photographic, magnetic, mechanical, electronic, and computer forms.
proposedGroups.approximateLearningGoal: Recognize what counts as records under section 9.

proposals.reason: The section separates application entitlement and contents from electronic submission, retention, and production duties.

proposedGroups.titleSuggestion: Application requirements to register unregistered land
proposedGroups.reason: These subsections identify who may apply and the required form, parcel identifier, fee, certificate of title, affidavit, and supporting information.
proposedGroups.approximateLearningGoal: Identify who may apply to register unregistered land and what must accompany the application.

proposedGroups.titleSuggestion: Electronic application duties and affidavit handling
proposedGroups.reason: These subsections govern electronic applications, certificate format, affidavit possession, fee payment, retention, and production.
proposedGroups.approximateLearningGoal: Explain subscriber duties for electronic applications to register land.

proposals.reason: The section has distinct stages for application handling, existing interests, and the Registrar General registration order.

proposedGroups.titleSuggestion: Forwarding, rejecting, or withdrawing applications
proposedGroups.reason: These subsections address complete applications, incomplete rejections with notice, and withdrawal before certificate issuance.
proposedGroups.approximateLearningGoal: Explain how an application is forwarded, rejected, or withdrawn.

proposedGroups.titleSuggestion: Existing interests when title is registered by order
proposedGroups.reason: These subsections direct handling of instruments evidencing interests and preserve their force after registration.
proposedGroups.approximateLearningGoal: Describe how existing interests are handled when title is registered subject to them.

proposedGroups.titleSuggestion: Registrar General order to register title
proposedGroups.reason: These subsections authorize an order based on the certificate of title and require delivery to the registrar.
proposedGroups.approximateLearningGoal: State when the Registrar General may order registration of title.

proposals.reason: Focused registration path where title is acquired or confirmed by court order or provincial enactment.

proposedGroups.titleSuggestion: Registering title acquired by court order or enactment
proposedGroups.reason: The text requires documentation and fee, forwarding to the Registrar General, and an order if title, land identification, and Community Planning Act compliance are satisfactory.
proposedGroups.approximateLearningGoal: Explain how title acquired or confirmed by court order or enactment may be registered.

proposals.reason: Central land titles rule that registration is needed to pass interests, with a lease exception and title limit.

proposedGroups.titleSuggestion: Registration required to pass estates or interests
proposedGroups.reason: The subsections state when instruments pass interests, the short-lease exception, registration effect according to tenor, and predecessor-title limits.
proposedGroups.approximateLearningGoal: Explain why registration is necessary to pass an estate or interest in registered land.

proposals.reason: The section separates effects of registration against adverse rights from court relief for prior unregistered access rights.

proposedGroups.titleSuggestion: Registration effect on adverse possession and prescription
proposedGroups.reason: Subsection 17(1) bars later adverse possession and limits prescriptive light, easement, right, or profit a prendre claims.
proposedGroups.approximateLearningGoal: Explain how registration affects adverse possession and prescriptive rights.

proposedGroups.titleSuggestion: Court relief for prior unregistered access rights
proposedGroups.reason: These subsections allow court relief for prior unregistered rights of way or access and identify rectification, compensation, costs, and limits.
proposedGroups.approximateLearningGoal: Describe court relief for prior unregistered rights of way or access.

proposals.reason: Central instrument-registration workflow with distinct receipt, rejection, title-record, and amendment or Registry Act document stages.

proposedGroups.titleSuggestion: Receipt, acceptance, registration, and rejection of instruments
proposedGroups.reason: These subsections cover assigned registration details, examination, acceptance, registration, refusal grounds, rejection records, notice, and the section 12(10) limit.
proposedGroups.approximateLearningGoal: Explain the registrar workflow for receiving, accepting, registering, and rejecting instruments.

proposedGroups.titleSuggestion: Title registration certificates, notices, and parcel identifiers
proposedGroups.reason: These subsections cover cancelling and issuing certificates, Registry Act notices when land enters the Act, and approved parcel identifiers in the title register.
proposedGroups.approximateLearningGoal: Describe the records created when land or title is registered under the Act.

proposedGroups.titleSuggestion: Amending instruments and Registry Act documents affecting registered land
proposedGroups.reason: These subsections allow amending instruments and Registrar General-ordered registration of Registry Act documents affecting registered land.
proposedGroups.approximateLearningGoal: Explain how registered instruments may be amended and when Registry Act documents can be registered.

proposals.reason: Focused priority rule based on registration number, date, and time, with loss of priority for rejected or terminated instruments.

proposedGroups.titleSuggestion: Priority based on registration order
proposedGroups.reason: The subsections state how priority is assigned and when it is cancelled or lost.
proposedGroups.approximateLearningGoal: Explain how registered instrument priority is determined and lost.

proposals.reason: Effect-of-transfer rule covering the absolute transfer default and estoppel preservation.

proposedGroups.titleSuggestion: Effect of a transfer of land
proposedGroups.reason: The subsections address the transferor title conveyed and confirm operation by estoppel is not precluded.
proposedGroups.approximateLearningGoal: Explain what title a transfer conveys and how estoppel is preserved.

proposals.reason: Operative rule for registering instruments granting easements or incorporeal rights against dominant and servient registered tenements.

proposedGroups.titleSuggestion: Registration of easements or incorporeal rights
proposedGroups.reason: Subsection 24(1) states where the granting instrument may be registered.
proposedGroups.approximateLearningGoal: Identify how an easement or incorporeal right may be registered.

proposals.reason: The mortgage section separates registration and legal effect from prescribed and optional covenant rules.

proposedGroups.titleSuggestion: Registration and effect of mortgages on registered land
proposedGroups.reason: These subsections explain mortgaging by registration, mortgage remedies, and that registration does not sever joint tenancy.
proposedGroups.approximateLearningGoal: Explain how registered land is mortgaged and what effect registration has.

proposedGroups.titleSuggestion: Prescribed and optional mortgage covenants
proposedGroups.reason: These subsections address deemed covenants, exclusion, optional covenants, and Registrar General numbering.
proposedGroups.approximateLearningGoal: Describe how prescribed and optional mortgage covenants are included, excluded, or numbered.

proposals.reason: Focused mortgage release rule covering discharge and release of covenantors.

proposedGroups.titleSuggestion: Discharge of registered mortgage and release of covenantor
proposedGroups.reason: The subsections allow mortgage discharge and covenantor release by prescribed-form registration.
proposedGroups.approximateLearningGoal: Explain how a registered mortgage or mortgage covenantor may be released.

proposals.reason: The lease section separates registration, covenant handling, and validity against encumbrancers or options.

proposedGroups.titleSuggestion: Registration or notice of lease for registered land
proposedGroups.reason: Subsection 27(1) states when a lease or notice of lease is required and excludes short occupied leases.
proposedGroups.approximateLearningGoal: Identify when a lease of registered land must be registered or noticed.

proposedGroups.titleSuggestion: Prescribed and optional lease covenants
proposedGroups.reason: These subsections cover deemed prescribed covenants, exclusions, optional covenants, and Registrar General numbering.
proposedGroups.approximateLearningGoal: Describe how prescribed and optional lease covenants are handled.

proposedGroups.titleSuggestion: Lease validity against encumbrancers and lease options
proposedGroups.reason: These subsections address encumbrancer consent or priority and how purchase, extension, or renewal options are shown.
proposedGroups.approximateLearningGoal: Explain when a lease binds an encumbrancer and how options are indicated.

proposals.reason: Focused surrender-of-lease rule with lessor consent, encumbrancer consent, and vesting after registration.

proposedGroups.titleSuggestion: Surrender of a registered lease
proposedGroups.reason: The subsections explain surrender by prescribed-form registration, required consents, and vesting after surrender.
proposedGroups.approximateLearningGoal: Describe how a registered lease may be surrendered and what follows.

proposals.reason: Cohesive assignment rule for registered mortgages, leases, and debentures and the rights passing to assignees.

proposedGroups.titleSuggestion: Assignment of registered mortgages, leases, and debentures
proposedGroups.reason: The subsections address assignment by registration, charged mortgagee interests, rights and obligations passing, right to sue and recover, and trusts.
proposedGroups.approximateLearningGoal: Explain what registration of an assignment does for mortgages, leases, debentures, and related rights.

proposals.reason: Focused caveat registration workflow covering notice, Registrar General inquiry, and improper caveat withdrawal orders.

proposedGroups.titleSuggestion: Registration and review of caveats
proposedGroups.reason: The subsections cover registering a caveat, notifying affected parties, forwarding and examining it, and ordering withdrawal if improperly registered.
proposedGroups.approximateLearningGoal: Explain how a caveat is registered, reviewed, and ordered withdrawn if improper.

proposals.reason: Explains the effect of caveat registration and assignment of caveator claims.

proposedGroups.titleSuggestion: Effect and assignment of a registered caveat
proposedGroups.reason: The subsections state that a caveat does not create an interest but affects later registrations, and that claims may be assigned.
proposedGroups.approximateLearningGoal: Describe what a registered caveat does and how caveator claims may be assigned.

proposals.reason: Focused notice-and-expiry process for withdrawing caveats unless court extension orders are filed.

proposedGroups.titleSuggestion: Notice request and expiry of caveat registration
proposedGroups.reason: The subsections cover notice requests, thirty-day expiry, court extension orders, and further extensions.
proposedGroups.approximateLearningGoal: Explain how a caveat ceases to be registered after a withdrawal request unless extended.

proposals.reason: Remedies for wrongful, vexatious, unreasonable, or unsupported caveat registration.

proposedGroups.titleSuggestion: Damages and restraining orders for improper caveats
proposedGroups.reason: The subsections create a cause of action and allow a restraining order after removal or refusal to extend.
proposedGroups.approximateLearningGoal: Identify the damages action and restraining order available for improper caveats.

proposals.reason: Focused stop-order process to block registration where errors, fraud, or improper dealings must be prevented.

proposedGroups.titleSuggestion: Stop orders prohibiting registration of instruments
proposedGroups.reason: The subsections cover issuing and registering stop orders, notice to owners, duration, and court review if withdrawal is refused.
proposedGroups.approximateLearningGoal: Explain when a stop order may block registration and how notice, duration, and court review work.

proposals.reason: Owner affidavit process to prevent registration in special circumstances and damages for wrongful affidavits.

proposedGroups.titleSuggestion: Affidavit preventing registration of an instrument
proposedGroups.reason: The subsections allow registration of an owner affidavit to block an instrument and create damages liability for wrongful, vexatious, or unsupported affidavits.
proposedGroups.approximateLearningGoal: Explain how an owner affidavit can prevent registration and what liability may follow.

proposals.reason: Focused application workflow for registering a money judgment against registered land.

proposedGroups.titleSuggestion: Application to register a memorial of judgment
proposedGroups.reason: The subsections identify who applies, joint-tenancy effect, acceptable name or land-description differences, multi-parcel applications, judgment copy attachment, and registration when in order.
proposedGroups.approximateLearningGoal: Explain how a judgment creditor applies to register a money judgment against registered land.

proposals.reason: The section separates notice and expiry or extension of judgment registration from assignment of a registered judgment.

proposedGroups.titleSuggestion: Notice to judgment creditor and expiry or extension of registration
proposedGroups.reason: These subsections cover notice requests, affidavit grounds, notice to the creditor, ninety-day cessation, court extension, and further extension.
proposedGroups.approximateLearningGoal: Explain how notice to a judgment creditor can lead to cessation or extension of registration.

proposedGroups.titleSuggestion: Assignment of a registered judgment
proposedGroups.reason: These subsections allow assignment registration and pass the assignor interest, rights, powers, privileges, and limitations to the assignee.
proposedGroups.approximateLearningGoal: State how a registered judgment may be assigned and what passes to the assignee.

proposals.reason: Damages action for improper judgment registration and deemed wrongful registration where debtor-owner matching was not reasonably checked.

proposedGroups.titleSuggestion: Damages against judgment creditor for improper registration
proposedGroups.reason: The subsections create a cause of action and deem registration wrongful if reasonable steps were not taken to match debtor and owner.
proposedGroups.approximateLearningGoal: Identify when damages may be claimed against a judgment creditor for improper registration.

proposals.reason: Focused filing and registration rule for powers of attorney and instruments executed under them.

proposedGroups.titleSuggestion: Registration or filing of powers of attorney
proposedGroups.reason: The subsections cover registration or filing, registrar recognition, proof by statutory declaration, and electronic-instrument exceptions.
proposedGroups.approximateLearningGoal: Explain how powers of attorney are filed or registered and used to prove execution.

proposals.reason: The section separates registration and notice effect of conditions or covenants from limits and discharge.

proposedGroups.titleSuggestion: Registration and notice effect of land conditions or covenants
proposedGroups.reason: These subsections allow registration and bind successive owners with notice if the condition or covenant runs with land, subject to court modification or discharge grounds.
proposedGroups.approximateLearningGoal: Explain how registering a condition or covenant affects successive owners.

proposedGroups.titleSuggestion: Limits and discharge of registered conditions or covenants
proposedGroups.reason: These subsections clarify registration does not determine whether a covenant runs with land or is enforceable and allow discharge by registered instrument.
proposedGroups.approximateLearningGoal: State the limits of registration and how conditions or covenants may be discharged.

proposals.reason: Cohesive bankruptcy registration workflow and notice-based correction if the bankrupt is not the owner.

proposedGroups.titleSuggestion: Bankruptcy proceedings affecting registered land
proposedGroups.reason: The subsections cover trustee registration, notices, owner requests, affidavit grounds, thirty-day cessation, court confirmation, and ownership restoration.
proposedGroups.approximateLearningGoal: Explain how bankruptcy orders or assignments are registered and corrected if the bankrupt is not the owner.

proposals.reason: Focused tax sale workflow for certificates, redemption notices, cancellation, and purchaser title registration.

proposedGroups.titleSuggestion: Tax sale proceedings for registered land
proposedGroups.reason: The subsections address certificate registration, redemption notice and cancellation, and registration of purchaser title without inquiry into irregularities.
proposedGroups.approximateLearningGoal: Explain how tax sale certificates, redemptions, and purchaser title registration work.

proposals.reason: Focused process for registering a claimant as owner where entitlement comes from judgment, enactment, sale, mortgage default, or another proceeding.

proposedGroups.titleSuggestion: Registration of claimant as owner
proposedGroups.reason: The subsections identify when documents are filed and forwarded and when the Registrar General orders claimant registration.
proposedGroups.approximateLearningGoal: Explain how a claimant may be registered as owner of land, an estate, or an interest.

proposals.reason: Transmission on death has distinct registration, personal-representative authority, purchaser-protection, and approval topics.

proposedGroups.titleSuggestion: Registration of transmission on death
proposedGroups.reason: These subsections require registration in the personal representative name, prescribed application and documents, interest-only registration, and Registrar General approval.
proposedGroups.approximateLearningGoal: Explain how registered land or an interest is transmitted on death.

proposedGroups.titleSuggestion: Personal representative instruments and purchaser protection
proposedGroups.reason: These subsections restrict instruments executed by personal representatives unless rights are established and protect good-faith value purchasers.
proposedGroups.approximateLearningGoal: Describe when a personal representative may execute instruments and how purchasers from a personal representative are protected.

proposedGroups.titleSuggestion: Devolution of Estates Act provisions for transmission
proposedGroups.reason: Subsection 53(8) separately applies specified Devolution of Estates Act sections to transmission on death.
proposedGroups.approximateLearningGoal: Identify the external devolution provisions applied to transmission on death.

proposals.reason: The implied-covenants section separates specific implied covenants from their general force, joint liability, and pleading effect.

proposedGroups.titleSuggestion: Implied covenants in transfers and mortgages
proposedGroups.reason: These subsections imply covenants to give effect to instruments, further transfer or mortgage land, and assume mortgage obligations on transfer.
proposedGroups.approximateLearningGoal: Identify the covenants implied in registered transfers and mortgages.

proposedGroups.titleSuggestion: Force, joint liability, and pleading of implied covenants
proposedGroups.reason: These subsections give implied covenants force as if written, bind multiple parties jointly and severally unless modified, and allow pleading them as expressed.
proposedGroups.approximateLearningGoal: Explain how implied covenants are enforced, bind parties, and may be pleaded.

proposals.reason: Proof of execution divides into signing and proof requirements, who may take affidavits or certificates, and exceptions or electronic-instrument treatment.

proposedGroups.titleSuggestion: Signing and proof of execution for registration
proposedGroups.reason: These subsections set signing or corporate seal requirements and proof by affidavit or certificate in prescribed form.
proposedGroups.approximateLearningGoal: Explain the execution and proof documents generally required for registration.

proposedGroups.titleSuggestion: Exceptions, Registrar General direction, and electronic instrument proof
proposedGroups.reason: These subsections exempt listed instruments, allow Registrar General direction where due execution is satisfactory, and apply paper proof rules to electronic-instrument source documents.
proposedGroups.approximateLearningGoal: Identify exceptions to execution proof and how electronic instrument source documents are treated.

proposals.reason: Focused address-for-service rule for registered or filed instruments and changes of name or address.

proposedGroups.titleSuggestion: Address for service in land titles filings
proposedGroups.reason: The subsections require addresses, allow name or address change notices, and make the last address on file the service address.
proposedGroups.approximateLearningGoal: State how addresses for service are supplied and updated for land titles notices.

proposals.reason: Focused method-of-service rule for specified Registrar General or registrar notices and other Act notices or documents.

proposedGroups.titleSuggestion: Method of service for land titles notices and documents
proposedGroups.reason: The subsections use Rules of Court personal service methods or directions by the Registrar General.
proposedGroups.approximateLearningGoal: Explain how required land titles notices and documents are served.

proposals.reason: Trust registration rule requiring in-trust registration and Registrar General satisfaction before trust dispositions.

proposedGroups.titleSuggestion: Registered land held in trust
proposedGroups.reason: The subsections require registration followed by in trust and block dispositions unless consistent with the trust.
proposedGroups.approximateLearningGoal: Explain how registered land taken in trust is registered and later disposed of.

proposals.reason: Focused paper-instrument rule about execution without seal or consideration and corporate seal exception.

proposedGroups.titleSuggestion: Seals and consideration for prescribed paper instruments
proposedGroups.reason: The subsections allow prescribed paper instruments without seal or stated consideration, give them sealed-instrument effect, and preserve corporate seal requirements.
proposedGroups.approximateLearningGoal: Explain when paper instruments may be executed without seal or stated consideration and when corporate seals are required.

proposals.reason: Central protection rule for persons dealing with registered owners against unregistered interests and Personal Property Registry registrations, subject to fraud.

proposedGroups.titleSuggestion: Effect of unregistered instruments, interests, and Personal Property Registry registrations
proposedGroups.reason: The subsections state non-inquiry and no-notice rules for unregistered claims, knowledge not being fraud by itself, and similar treatment for Personal Property Registry registrations.
proposedGroups.approximateLearningGoal: Explain how unregistered interests and Personal Property Registry registrations affect persons dealing with registered owners.

proposals.reason: Focused certificate-of-registered-ownership rule covering who may require it, contents, and evidentiary effect.

proposedGroups.titleSuggestion: Certificate of registered ownership
proposedGroups.reason: The subsections address issuance on request and fee, certificate contents, and evidentiary status.
proposedGroups.approximateLearningGoal: Explain how certificates of registered ownership are issued and used as evidence.

proposals.reason: Focused No Survivorship entry rule limiting dispositions and authorizing court orders for protection of beneficial interests.

proposedGroups.titleSuggestion: Entry of No Survivorship on the title register
proposedGroups.reason: The subsections allow the entry, define No Survivorship, and describe court notice and transfer or protective orders.
proposedGroups.approximateLearningGoal: Explain the effect of a No Survivorship entry and the court order process.

proposals.reason: Focused court rectification rule listing when the court may direct title-register rectification and how applications are made.

proposedGroups.titleSuggestion: Court orders directing rectification of the title register
proposedGroups.reason: The subsections list entitlement, aggrieved-entry, fraud, wrongful act, and mistake grounds and point applications to section 79.
proposedGroups.approximateLearningGoal: Explain when the court may order rectification of the title register.

proposals.reason: Focused notation rule for rectification and when the rectification is deemed effective.

proposedGroups.titleSuggestion: Notation and timing of title-register rectification
proposedGroups.reason: The subsections require notation without erasing erroneous entries and deem rectification effective from the original error or omission time.
proposedGroups.approximateLearningGoal: Explain how rectification is noted and when it is deemed to have taken effect.

proposals.reason: Indemnification on rectification has separate entitlement and exception rules and a special forged-disposition damage rule.

proposedGroups.titleSuggestion: Indemnity for rectification, errors, omissions, or lost documents
proposedGroups.reason: Subsection 73(1) states when damaged persons are entitled to indemnity and lists exceptions for fraud, negligence, available recovery actions, notice, trust breach, and necessary delay.
proposedGroups.approximateLearningGoal: Identify when a person is entitled to indemnity and the main exceptions.

proposedGroups.titleSuggestion: Forged disposition deemed damage on rectification
proposedGroups.reason: Subsection 73(2) deems a good-faith value owner under a forged disposition to have suffered damage when the title register is rectified.
proposedGroups.approximateLearningGoal: State how a forged disposition affects deemed damage for indemnity.

proposals.reason: Focused indemnity-award process through the Registrar General or court.

proposedGroups.titleSuggestion: Award of indemnity by Registrar General or court
proposedGroups.reason: The subsections allow Registrar General determination and award with approvals and consent, and court application if an award is not made.
proposedGroups.approximateLearningGoal: Explain how a claimant may obtain an indemnity award.

proposals.reason: Valuation rule for indemnity where damage involves loss of an estate, interest, or encumbrance, including good-faith improvements.

proposedGroups.titleSuggestion: Time of valuation for indemnity
proposedGroups.reason: The subsections cap indemnity by fair market value at the relevant error or rectification time and include good-faith later improvements.
proposedGroups.approximateLearningGoal: Explain how indemnity value is timed and when improvements are included.

proposals.reason: Court application section separates decision reasons and applications, notice and title-register effects, and timing or hearing powers.

proposedGroups.titleSuggestion: Reasons and applications to court for decisions or rectification
proposedGroups.reason: These subsections define decision, allow written reasons requests, and authorize court applications for rectification or dissatisfaction with a decision.
proposedGroups.approximateLearningGoal: Explain who may seek reasons or apply to court about rectification or a land titles decision.

proposedGroups.titleSuggestion: Notice of proposed court application and effect on dealings
proposedGroups.reason: These subsections require notice to the Registrar General, registrar notation, dealings subject to notice, and protection for prior good-faith value dispositions.
proposedGroups.approximateLearningGoal: Describe the notice procedure before a court application and its effect on dealings with land.

proposedGroups.titleSuggestion: Time limit, evidence, and court orders on applications
proposedGroups.reason: These subsections set the thirty-day application limit, allow relevant evidence, and authorize orders and costs subject to section 71.
proposedGroups.approximateLearningGoal: State the time limit, evidence rule, and order power for land titles court applications.

proposals.reason: Fees section separates registration and assurance fees, value evidence, and accounting or indemnity payment funds.

proposedGroups.titleSuggestion: Registration, electronic payment, and assurance fees
proposedGroups.reason: These subsections require prescribed fees before registrar action, electronic payment for electronic instruments, assurance fees, and Crown-transfer assurance fee exemptions.
proposedGroups.approximateLearningGoal: Identify fee, electronic payment, assurance fee, and Crown-transfer exemption rules.

proposedGroups.titleSuggestion: Affidavit or declaration of value for transfers
proposedGroups.reason: These subsections require value affidavits or electronic declarations, apply related statutes, and allow evaluator certificates if value is not satisfactory.
proposedGroups.approximateLearningGoal: Explain how land value is established before a transfer is registered.

proposedGroups.titleSuggestion: Registrar accounts and funds for indemnity payments
proposedGroups.reason: These subsections govern registrar accounts, payment of indemnity from a dedicated account or fund, and Consolidated Fund payment if needed.
proposedGroups.approximateLearningGoal: Describe how registrar money and indemnity payment funds are handled.

proposals.reason: Focused public request rule for registered information, fees, and registrar liability limits.

proposedGroups.titleSuggestion: Requests for registered land information
proposedGroups.reason: The subsections require information access on request, prescribed fee payment, and limit registrar liability unless information is certified.
proposedGroups.approximateLearningGoal: Explain how registered information is requested and when registrar liability can arise.

proposals.reason: The opening section separates core definitions from rules about when a claim is brought and what counts as a limitation period under the Act.

proposedGroups.titleSuggestion: Claim, claimant, and defendant definitions
proposedGroups.reason: Subsection 1(1) defines the central persons and claim concept used throughout the limitation regime.
proposedGroups.approximateLearningGoal: Identify claim, claimant, and defendant under the Act.

proposedGroups.titleSuggestion: When a claim is brought and limitation-period references
proposedGroups.reason: Subsections 1(2) and 1(3) specify when a claim is brought and exclude the section 22 period from references to limitation periods established by the Act.
proposedGroups.approximateLearningGoal: Explain when a claim is brought and how limitation-period references exclude section 22.

proposals.reason: Focused application rule for claims brought after commencement, including added claims in older proceedings.

proposedGroups.titleSuggestion: Application of the Limitation of Actions Act
proposedGroups.reason: The operative subsection states the Act applies to claims brought after commencement, including claims added to pre-commencement proceedings.
proposedGroups.approximateLearningGoal: State which claims the Limitation of Actions Act applies to.

proposals.reason: Conflict rule distinguishing public Act conflicts from private Act conflicts.

proposedGroups.titleSuggestion: Conflict rules for public and private Acts
proposedGroups.reason: The subsections say other public Acts prevail over this Act, while this Act prevails over conflicting private Acts.
proposedGroups.approximateLearningGoal: Explain which Act prevails when the Limitation of Actions Act conflicts with public or private Acts.

proposals.reason: Core limitation-period rule combining a two-year discovery period and fifteen-year ultimate period with a discovery test.

proposedGroups.titleSuggestion: General limitation periods and discovery of claims
proposedGroups.reason: The subsections state the earlier of two years from discovery and fifteen years from the act or omission, and define discovery by knowledge of injury, causation, and defendant act or omission.
proposedGroups.approximateLearningGoal: Explain the general limitation periods and when a claim is discovered.

proposals.reason: Focused limitation and title-extinguishment rule for converted personal property.

proposedGroups.titleSuggestion: Recovery of converted personal property and extinguishment of title
proposedGroups.reason: The subsections set different deadlines for good-faith value purchasers and other cases, and extinguish claimant title when the period expires.
proposedGroups.approximateLearningGoal: Explain the limitation periods for recovering converted personal property and the effect of expiry.

proposals.reason: Conversion damages rule applying Part 2 subject to a multiple-conversion bar tied to section 9 possession recovery.

proposedGroups.titleSuggestion: Limitation rule for damages for conversion
proposedGroups.reason: The subsections apply Part 2 to conversion damages and bar claims after multiple conversions if section 9 possession recovery against that defendant is unavailable.
proposedGroups.approximateLearningGoal: Explain when damages claims for conversion are governed by Part 2 or barred by section 9.

proposals.reason: Secured debt includes separate rules for Part 2 application, principal recovery, part payments, and redemption claims.

proposedGroups.titleSuggestion: Claims for payment or principal of secured debt
proposedGroups.reason: Subsections 12(1) and 12(2) apply Part 2 subject to a fifteen-year limit on principal recovery from when security is taken.
proposedGroups.approximateLearningGoal: Explain the limitation rule for claims to recover principal of secured debt.

proposedGroups.titleSuggestion: Part payments and redemption claims for secured debt
proposedGroups.reason: Subsections 12(3) and 12(4) treat payments as part payments of principal and interest and set a fifteen-year period for debtor redemption after creditor possession.
proposedGroups.approximateLearningGoal: Explain how secured-debt payments and creditor possession affect limitation periods.

proposals.reason: Contribution has a general settlement or judgment limitation rule and a separate Tortfeasors Act contribution rule.

proposedGroups.titleSuggestion: General limitation periods for contribution claims
proposedGroups.reason: Subsection 14(1) sets the earlier of two years from knowledge of contribution liability and the later of fifteen years from the underlying act or five years from payment, settlement, or judgment.
proposedGroups.approximateLearningGoal: Explain the limitation periods for general contribution claims after payment, settlement, or judgment.

proposedGroups.titleSuggestion: Tortfeasors Act contribution limitation period
proposedGroups.reason: Subsection 14(2) gives a separate rule for contribution under paragraph 2(c) of the Tortfeasors Act, based on knowledge after settlement or pleading service and a fifteen-year ultimate period.
proposedGroups.approximateLearningGoal: Explain the limitation period for Tortfeasors Act contribution claims.

proposals.reason: Section 15 has two distinct deemed-knowledge rules, one for agents of principals and one for successors in property-related claims.

proposedGroups.titleSuggestion: Agent knowledge attributed to principal
proposedGroups.reason: Subsection 15(1) deems a principal to know specified matters based on an agent with actual knowledge and a communication duty.
proposedGroups.approximateLearningGoal: Recall when an agent's actual knowledge is deemed to be the principal's knowledge.

proposedGroups.titleSuggestion: Predecessor knowledge attributed to successor claimant
proposedGroups.reason: Subsection 15(2) deems a successor claimant to know specified matters based on a predecessor or the claimant.
proposedGroups.approximateLearningGoal: Recall when a predecessor's knowledge affects a successor claimant.

proposals.reason: Section 18 pairs the suspension of listed limitation periods during incapacity with an extension rule when less than one year remains.

proposedGroups.titleSuggestion: Incapacity suspension and one-year extension
proposedGroups.reason: Section 18 pairs the suspension of listed limitation periods during incapacity with an extension rule when less than one year remains.
proposedGroups.approximateLearningGoal: Recall how incapacity suspends listed limitation periods and how the one-year extension operates when suspension ends.

proposals.reason: Section 19 separates the effect of an acknowledgment, the required form and recipients, and exclusions for without-prejudice or reserved-rights correspondence.

proposedGroups.titleSuggestion: Acknowledgment restarts the limitation period
proposedGroups.reason: Subsection 19(1) states that a timely acknowledgment begins the limitation period again.
proposedGroups.approximateLearningGoal: Recall when an acknowledgment restarts the operation of a limitation period.

proposedGroups.titleSuggestion: Writing and recipient requirements for acknowledgment
proposedGroups.reason: Subsection 19(2) sets writing, maker, and recipient requirements for an acknowledgment.
proposedGroups.approximateLearningGoal: Recall who must make an acknowledgment, who may receive it, and that it must be in writing.

proposedGroups.titleSuggestion: Correspondence that is not an acknowledgment
proposedGroups.reason: Subsection 19(3) excludes without-prejudice admissions and statements reserving the limitation defence.
proposedGroups.approximateLearningGoal: Recall which settlement correspondence is not an acknowledgment.

proposals.reason: Section 20 separates the part-payment restart rule, who must make and receive the payment, and payments that do not restart time.

proposedGroups.titleSuggestion: Part payment restarts the limitation period
proposedGroups.reason: Subsection 20(1) states that a timely part payment of a monetary obligation begins the limitation period again.
proposedGroups.approximateLearningGoal: Recall when a part payment restarts the operation of a limitation period.

proposedGroups.titleSuggestion: Required payer and recipient for part payment
proposedGroups.reason: Subsection 20(2) identifies who must make and receive the part payment.
proposedGroups.approximateLearningGoal: Recall who must make a part payment and who may receive it.

proposedGroups.titleSuggestion: Payments excluded from the restart rule

proposals.reason: Section 23 defines non-judicial remedy and bars enforcement of that remedy when a limitation period prevents bringing the claim.

proposedGroups.reason: Section 23 defines non-judicial remedy and bars enforcement of that remedy when a limitation period prevents bringing the claim.

proposals.reason: Section 24 states when the Act applies to New Brunswick claims governed by another jurisdiction's substantive law and when another jurisdiction's limitations law bars the claim.

proposedGroups.titleSuggestion: Conflict of laws limitation rules
proposedGroups.reason: Section 24 states when the Act applies to New Brunswick claims governed by another jurisdiction's substantive law and when another jurisdiction's limitations law bars the claim.

proposals.reason: The target is a technical consequential amendment to the Defamation Act that repeals and updates cross-references rather than stating a standalone limitation rule.

proposedGroups.titleSuggestion: Fatal Accidents Act cross-reference to subsection 8(3.1)

proposedGroups.approximateLearningGoal: Recall that subsection 2(2) is amended to include subsection 8(3.1) as a subject provision.

proposedGroups.titleSuggestion: Death action barred by deceased expired claim and two-year or five-year deadline

proposedGroups.approximateLearningGoal: Recall how the Fatal Accidents Act amendments bar actions and set the two-year or five-year deadline.

proposals.reason: The target is a long omnibus amendment to the former Limitation of Actions Act with title, definition, repeal, substitution, and cross-reference changes that should be reviewed before grouping.

The target repeals a Regional Health Authorities Act heading and section without stating a new operative study rule.
Section 3 covers entitlement to equal division, the 60-day application limit, deemed spouse status after nullity, and extension grounds.

proposedGroups.titleSuggestion: Equal division triggers for marital property
proposedGroups.reason: Subsection 3(1) lists the circumstances in which a spouse may apply for equal division of marital property.
proposedGroups.approximateLearningGoal: Recall the divorce, nullity, separation, and marriage-breakdown triggers for equal division.

proposedGroups.titleSuggestion: Sixty-day limit after ceasing to be a spouse
proposedGroups.reason: Subsection 3(2) sets the 60-day limit after divorce or declaration of nullity, subject to extension.
proposedGroups.approximateLearningGoal: Recall when the 60-day application limit applies.

proposedGroups.titleSuggestion: Nullity deemed-spouse rule and extension grounds
proposedGroups.reason: Subsections 3(3) and 3(4) address deemed spouse status after nullity and grounds for extending the limitation period.
proposedGroups.approximateLearningGoal: Recall how nullity affects spouse status and when the Court may extend the application period.

proposals.reason: Section 4 is a multi-part surviving-spouse scheme covering entitlement, deadlines, estate administration, elections, and limits on multiple remedies.

proposedGroups.titleSuggestion: Surviving spouse entitlement and vesting of home goods
proposedGroups.reason: Subsections 4(1) through 4(3) establish the surviving spouse application entitlement, vesting possibility, and court powers.
proposedGroups.approximateLearningGoal: Recall the surviving spouse entitlement to equal division and possible vesting of the marital home and household goods.

proposedGroups.titleSuggestion: Estate application timing and service
proposedGroups.reason: Subsections 4(4), 4(8), and 4(9) set service and application timing rules related to estate administration.
proposedGroups.approximateLearningGoal: Recall the timing and service rules for surviving spouse property division applications.

proposedGroups.titleSuggestion: Election and no double recovery rules
proposedGroups.reason: Subsections 4(5), 4(6), 4(7), and 4(10) address elections, barred applications, testamentary acceptance, and limits on combining claims.
proposedGroups.approximateLearningGoal: Recall how section 4 controls elections and prevents overlapping surviving-spouse property claims.

proposals.reason: Section 5 states when property division applications may continue by or against estates and when Survival of Actions Act does not apply.

proposedGroups.titleSuggestion: Survival of property division applications
proposedGroups.reason: Section 5 states when property division applications may continue by or against estates and when Survival of Actions Act does not apply.
proposedGroups.approximateLearningGoal: Recall how applications under sections 3 and 4 survive after a spouse dies.

proposals.reason: Section 15 abolishes the presumption of advancement between spouses and applies a resulting trust presumption with joint-tenancy and bank-account rules.

proposedGroups.titleSuggestion: Resulting trust presumption between spouses
proposedGroups.reason: Section 15 abolishes the presumption of advancement between spouses and applies a resulting trust presumption with joint-tenancy and bank-account rules.
proposedGroups.approximateLearningGoal: Recall the resulting-trust presumption and joint-tenancy proof rules between spouses.

proposals.reason: Section 16 defines when property is a marital home, including mixed-use property and multiple marital homes.

proposedGroups.titleSuggestion: Description of marital home
proposedGroups.reason: Section 16 defines when property is a marital home, including mixed-use property and multiple marital homes.
proposedGroups.approximateLearningGoal: Recall how property is identified as a marital home and how more than one marital home may result.

proposals.reason: Section 18 gives spouses equal possession rights in a marital home, subject to exclusive possession orders and domestic contracts, and states when the right ends.

proposedGroups.titleSuggestion: Spouses equal possession rights in marital home
proposedGroups.reason: Section 18 gives spouses equal possession rights in a marital home, subject to exclusive possession orders and domestic contracts, and states when the right ends.
proposedGroups.approximateLearningGoal: Recall the equal possession right in a marital home and when it terminates.

proposals.reason: Section 19 separates restrictions on disposition of a marital home, remedies for contravention, and status of required consent.

proposedGroups.titleSuggestion: When a spouse may dispose of an interest in a marital home
proposedGroups.reason: Subsection 19(1) lists the joinder, consent, release, court order, and authorization conditions for disposition.
proposedGroups.approximateLearningGoal: Recall the conditions that permit disposition of an interest in a marital home.

proposedGroups.titleSuggestion: Setting aside a contravening disposition
proposedGroups.reason: Subsection 19(2) allows a contravening disposition to be set aside except for value, good faith, and no notice.
proposedGroups.approximateLearningGoal: Recall when a disposition made in contravention of subsection 19(1) may be set aside.

proposedGroups.titleSuggestion: Consent does not give ownership interest
proposedGroups.reason: Subsection 19(3) states that joinder or consent does not of itself confer an ownership right, title, or interest.
proposedGroups.approximateLearningGoal: Recall the legal effect of joining in or consenting to a marital home disposition.

proposals.reason: Section 20 combines equal net-proceeds entitlement, unequal division, setting aside transfers, and no-notice purchaser protection.

proposedGroups.titleSuggestion: Equal entitlement to net proceeds from marital home disposition
proposedGroups.reason: Subsection 20(1) gives each spouse one-half of net proceeds, subject to court order and domestic contract.
proposedGroups.approximateLearningGoal: Recall the default equal entitlement to net proceeds from disposition of a marital home interest.

proposedGroups.titleSuggestion: Unequal division of net proceeds
proposedGroups.reason: Subsection 20(2) allows unequal division of net proceeds if equal division would be inequitable based on listed factors.
proposedGroups.approximateLearningGoal: Recall when the Court may divide net proceeds from a marital home unequally.

proposedGroups.titleSuggestion: Setting aside transfers and protecting no-notice purchasers
proposedGroups.reason: Subsections 20(3) through 20(5) address setting aside transfers, deemed notice, and protection for value, good faith, and no notice.
proposedGroups.approximateLearningGoal: Recall when transfers may be set aside and when a later acquirer is protected.

proposals.reason: Section 21 gives a spouse with possession rights the same redemption or relief-against-forfeiture rights and notice entitlement as the other spouse.

proposedGroups.titleSuggestion: Spouse redemption and relief against forfeiture rights
proposedGroups.reason: Section 21 gives a spouse with possession rights the same redemption or relief-against-forfeiture rights and notice entitlement as the other spouse.
proposedGroups.approximateLearningGoal: Recall the redemption, relief against forfeiture, notice, and payment-effect rights for a spouse with possession rights.

proposals.reason: Section 23 combines exclusive possession order powers, temporary relief, preconditions, and termination on death.

proposedGroups.titleSuggestion: Exclusive possession order powers
proposedGroups.reason: Subsection 23(1) lists the orders available for exclusive possession, release of property, payments, household goods, and maintenance obligations.
proposedGroups.approximateLearningGoal: Recall the orders the Court may make for exclusive possession of a marital home and household goods.

proposedGroups.titleSuggestion: Temporary relief and threshold for exclusive possession
proposedGroups.reason: Subsections 23(2) and 23(3) address temporary relief and the shelter or child-best-interests threshold.
proposedGroups.approximateLearningGoal: Recall when exclusive possession may be ordered as temporary relief and the conditions for making the order.

proposedGroups.titleSuggestion: Death terminates specified exclusive possession orders
proposedGroups.reason: Subsection 23(4) states when orders under paragraph 23(1)(a), (c), (d), or (e) cease.
proposedGroups.approximateLearningGoal: Recall which exclusive possession orders cease on death of either spouse.

proposals.reason: Section 24 allows discharge, variation, or suspension of specified orders after material change or when terms and conditions are no longer appropriate.

proposedGroups.titleSuggestion: Discharge variation or suspension of orders
proposedGroups.reason: Section 24 allows discharge, variation, or suspension of specified orders after material change or when terms and conditions are no longer appropriate.
proposedGroups.approximateLearningGoal: Recall when the Court may discharge, vary, or suspend exclusive-possession-related orders or terms.

proposals.reason: Section 26 gives each spouse equal possession rights in household goods subject to orders and domestic contracts, and states when the right ends.

proposedGroups.titleSuggestion: Spouses equal possession rights in household goods
proposedGroups.reason: Section 26 gives each spouse equal possession rights in household goods subject to orders and domestic contracts, and states when the right ends.
proposedGroups.approximateLearningGoal: Recall the equal possession right in household goods and when it terminates.

proposals.reason: Section 27 has distinct household goods topics: application, pending-disposal restriction, order powers, and exercise-of-power considerations.

proposedGroups.titleSuggestion: Application for household goods order
proposedGroups.reason: Subsection 27(1) allows a spouse to apply for an order respecting specified household goods not already covered by an exclusive possession order.
proposedGroups.approximateLearningGoal: Recall when a spouse may apply for a household goods order.

proposedGroups.titleSuggestion: Restriction on disposition while application pending
proposedGroups.reason: Subsection 27(2) bars the other spouse from disposing of specified household goods while the application is pending without consent or leave.
proposedGroups.approximateLearningGoal: Recall the restriction on disposing of household goods after notice of an application.

proposedGroups.titleSuggestion: Exclusive possession and non-disposition orders for household goods
proposedGroups.reason: Subsection 27(3) allows exclusive possession and non-disposition orders with incidental, supplemental, and consequential provisions.
proposedGroups.approximateLearningGoal: Recall the orders the Court may make for household goods after an application.

proposedGroups.titleSuggestion: Considerations for household goods orders
proposedGroups.reason: Subsection 27(4) directs the Court to consider daily-life needs, family responsibilities, and all other circumstances.
proposedGroups.approximateLearningGoal: Recall the considerations for exercising household goods order powers.

proposals.reason: Section 28 states when subsection 27(3) orders terminate and when the Court may vary, discharge, or suspend them.

proposedGroups.titleSuggestion: Termination or variation of household goods orders
proposedGroups.reason: Section 28 states when subsection 27(3) orders terminate and when the Court may vary, discharge, or suspend them.
proposedGroups.approximateLearningGoal: Recall when household goods orders terminate and when they may be varied, discharged, or suspended.

proposals.reason: Section 29 separates compensation for wrongful disposition of household goods, notice-based limits, and double-recovery prevention.

proposedGroups.titleSuggestion: Payment for loss of household goods use and enjoyment
proposedGroups.reason: Subsection 29(1) allows a fair and reasonable payment order when specified household goods were disposed of without consent and the Court would have made a household goods order.
proposedGroups.approximateLearningGoal: Recall when the Court may order payment for loss of use and enjoyment of household goods.

proposedGroups.titleSuggestion: No order against value good faith no-notice acquirer
proposedGroups.reason: Subsection 29(2) prevents orders against persons who acquired for value, in good faith, and without notice.
proposedGroups.approximateLearningGoal: Recall the protection for a person acquiring household goods for value, in good faith, and without notice.

proposedGroups.titleSuggestion: No further order after payment or satisfaction
proposedGroups.reason: Subsection 29(3) prevents another order under the section after payment or satisfaction of an order.
proposedGroups.approximateLearningGoal: Recall how section 29 prevents repeated payment orders for the same household goods.

proposals.reason: Section 30 allows registration, renewal, discharge, amendment, and cancellation of notice of household goods orders and deems registration to be notice.

proposedGroups.titleSuggestion: Registration and notice effect of household goods orders
proposedGroups.reason: Section 30 allows registration, renewal, discharge, amendment, and cancellation of notice of household goods orders and deems registration to be notice.
proposedGroups.approximateLearningGoal: Recall how notices of household goods orders are registered and how registration affects notice.

proposedGroups.reason: Section 34 authorizes marriage contracts about rights and obligations while barring agreement on parenting time or decision-making responsibility.
proposedGroups.approximateLearningGoal: Recall what may be included in a marriage contract and what parenting matters may not be agreed to.

proposedGroups.reason: Section 35 authorizes agreements between unmarried cohabitants, bars parenting-time and decision-making terms, and deems the agreement a marriage contract if the parties later marry.
proposedGroups.approximateLearningGoal: Recall the scope, parenting limits, and later-marriage effect of a domestic contract between cohabitants.

proposals.reason: Section 38 states when minors and representatives may enter domestic contracts or give waivers and consents.

proposedGroups.titleSuggestion: Capacity to contract and representative authority
proposedGroups.reason: Section 38 states when minors and representatives may enter domestic contracts or give waivers and consents.
proposedGroups.approximateLearningGoal: Recall the capacity and representative-approval rules for domestic contracts, waivers, and consents.

proposedGroups.reason: Subsection 46(1) states when Parts 1, 2, and 3 apply based on last common habitual residence or one spouse's last habitual residence in the Province.

proposedGroups.reason: Subsection 46(2) permits spouses outside subsection (1) to apply under section 44 and directs which law governs.

proposedGroups.reason: Subsection 46(3) lets the Court use section 44 order powers to give effect to rights under the applicable law.

proposedGroups.reason: Subsections 13(1) and 13(2) define the Board's exclusive jurisdiction and identify disputes and claims it may hear.

proposedGroups.reason: Subsections 14(1) and 14(2) establish Recorder offices and delegation to officers.

proposedGroups.titleSuggestion: Public access and practice rules
proposedGroups.reason: Subsections 14(5) and 14(6) address public inspection and Recorder rules of practice and procedure.
proposedGroups.approximateLearningGoal: Recall public access to Recorder records and the Recorder's rule-making power.

proposals.reason: Section 15 combines inspection orders, reports and certified copies, cancellation for non-compliance, and land withdrawal after cancellation.

proposedGroups.titleSuggestion: Inspection orders for mines claims and leases
proposedGroups.reason: Subsection 15(1) lets the Recorder order an officer to inspect mines, mineral claims, or mining leases for compliance.
proposedGroups.approximateLearningGoal: Recall when the Recorder may order inspections for compliance.

proposedGroups.titleSuggestion: Inspection reports and certified copies
proposedGroups.reason: Subsections 15(2) and 15(3) require written reports and allow certified copies on payment of the prescribed fee.

proposedGroups.reason: Subsection 19(1) defines interest to include shares in entities holding interests in mineral claims, mining leases, or mines.

proposedGroups.reason: Section 25 authorizes withdrawal of land from prospecting and registration and permits withdrawn land to be held or worked under Crown agreements.

proposedGroups.reason: Subsections 48(2) and 48(3) identify who may register claims or changes and in whose name registration may be made.

proposedGroups.titleSuggestion: Renewal terms and expiry of renewed mineral claims
proposedGroups.reason: Section 55 gives holders the right to renew for one, two, or three one-year terms, effective on expiry, and states expiry dates for renewed claims.
proposedGroups.approximateLearningGoal: Recall how mineral claim renewals take effect and when renewed claims expire.

proposals.reason: Section 56 is a detailed renewal requirement provision covering submissions, required work, excess work, fee treatment, reports, and conditions.

proposedGroups.titleSuggestion: Renewal submissions before and after claim expiry
proposedGroups.reason: Subsection 56(1) sets pre-expiry statement and fee submissions and post-renewal report and cost statement submissions.
proposedGroups.approximateLearningGoal: Recall the submissions required to register a mineral claim renewal.

proposedGroups.titleSuggestion: Required work and dollar value rules
proposedGroups.reason: Subsections 56(2) through 56(4) address prescribed required work, dollar value, and proof of performance.
proposedGroups.approximateLearningGoal: Recall how required work and dollar value are handled for mineral claim renewals.

proposedGroups.titleSuggestion: Excess work credits and allocation
proposedGroups.reason: Subsections 56(5) through 56(7) address crediting and allocating excess dollar value of work.
proposedGroups.approximateLearningGoal: Recall when excess work value may be credited or allocated.

proposedGroups.titleSuggestion: Non-compliance condition for renewal
proposedGroups.reason: Subsection 56(10) addresses a condition connected to renewal requirements when compliance is at issue.
proposedGroups.approximateLearningGoal: Recall the condition in subsection 56(10) for mineral claim renewal requirements.

proposals.reason: Section 57 prevents expiry when required reports are timely submitted despite consideration delays and requires notice of performed required work and excess credit.

proposedGroups.titleSuggestion: Delay while renewal report is considered
proposedGroups.reason: Section 57 prevents expiry when required reports are timely submitted despite consideration delays and requires notice of performed required work and excess credit.
proposedGroups.approximateLearningGoal: Recall the effect of delay in considering renewal work reports and cost statements.

proposals.reason: Section 58 requires annual work statements from mineral claim holders and allows statements to cover contiguous grouped claims.

proposedGroups.titleSuggestion: Annual statement of mineral claim work
proposedGroups.reason: Section 58 requires annual work statements from mineral claim holders and allows statements to cover contiguous grouped claims.
proposedGroups.approximateLearningGoal: Recall the annual statement duty for mineral claim work and grouped contiguous claims.

proposals.reason: Section 60 separates post-expiry removal rights, Crown vesting and disposal, continuing liability, and withdrawal of claim area.

proposedGroups.titleSuggestion: Removal of holder property after claim ends
proposedGroups.reason: Subsection 60(1) allows the former holder six months to remove structures, equipment, machinery, or other property after expiry, surrender, or cancellation.
proposedGroups.approximateLearningGoal: Recall the former holder's six-month removal right after a mineral claim ends.
