proposedGroups.titleSuggestion: Amusement device fees confiscation and regulation
proposedGroups.reason: This subsection lists fee, confiscation, location, use, and operation powers.
proposedGroups.approximateLearningGoal: Recall the fee, confiscation, location, use, and operation powers available for amusement-device by-laws.

proposals.reason: Section 92 separates the book licensing exemption and approval power from the offence for indicating approval.

proposedGroups.titleSuggestion: Book licence exemption and approval
proposedGroups.reason: These subsections address the licence exemption and Cabinet approval of books.
proposedGroups.approximateLearningGoal: Recall when approved books are exempt from municipal licensing and how Cabinet may approve a book for that purpose.

proposedGroups.titleSuggestion: Indicating book approval offence
proposedGroups.reason: This subsection creates the offence for indicating approval in the course of selling or soliciting orders.
proposedGroups.approximateLearningGoal: Recall the offence for indicating that a book has been approved by Cabinet while selling or soliciting orders.

proposals.reason: Section 94 separates code adoption and conflict rules from notice, inspection, and public-examination duties.

proposedGroups.titleSuggestion: Code adoption and approved-code conflicts
proposedGroups.reason: These subsections govern adopting approved codes, penalty clauses, and Minister approval for conflicts.
proposedGroups.approximateLearningGoal: Recall how council may adopt approved codes and how penalty clauses or conflicts with approved maintenance and occupancy codes are treated.

proposedGroups.titleSuggestion: Notice and public examination for codes
proposedGroups.reason: These subsections require newspaper notice, pre-passage inspection, and ongoing clerk availability.
proposedGroups.approximateLearningGoal: Recall the notice, inspection, and public-examination requirements for by-laws adopting codes.

proposals.reason: The section covers curfew by-laws, peace officer directions, Family Services Act handling, and parent offence liability.

proposedGroups.titleSuggestion: Curfew by-laws for children
proposedGroups.reason: All current subsections address curfew regulation for children and consequences.
proposedGroups.approximateLearningGoal: Recall the municipal curfew by-law power, peace officer response, and parent offence.

proposals.reason: Section 96 separates animal by-law powers from regulatory limits, construction and conflict rules, and the offence for violating an order.

proposedGroups.titleSuggestion: Animal by-law powers
proposedGroups.reason: These subsections define partial breed and list by-law powers over animals.
proposedGroups.approximateLearningGoal: Recall municipal animal by-law powers, including control, keeping, licensing, dangerous animals, seizure, and destruction or control orders.

proposedGroups.titleSuggestion: Animal by-law exceptions construction and conflicts
proposedGroups.reason: These subsections address exceptions, broad construction of paragraph (1)(j), and conflicts with superior instruments.
proposedGroups.approximateLearningGoal: Recall how regulatory exceptions, broad construction, and conflict rules limit or support municipal animal by-laws.

proposedGroups.titleSuggestion: Animal order offence and penalty
proposedGroups.reason: This subsection creates the offence for failing to comply with an animal order.
proposedGroups.approximateLearningGoal: Recall the offence category for failing to comply with an order made under an animal-keeping by-law.

proposals.reason: Section 97 separates retail closing authority and classes from mixed-business rules and statutory exceptions.

proposedGroups.titleSuggestion: Retail closing by-law authority and classes
proposedGroups.reason: These subsections define closed and authorize closing by-laws, classifications, and designations.
proposedGroups.approximateLearningGoal: Recall how council may regulate retail closing times, classify businesses, and designate businesses that may remain open.

proposedGroups.titleSuggestion: Mixed retail operations and exceptions
proposedGroups.reason: These subsections address multiple goods or services, customers present at closing, and Days of Rest Act exceptions.
proposedGroups.approximateLearningGoal: Recall how retail closing by-laws apply to mixed businesses, customers already present, and excepted businesses or activities.

proposals.reason: The section is a focused by-law power respecting precautions against enemy action.

proposedGroups.titleSuggestion: Enemy action prevention by-laws
proposedGroups.reason: The subsections address required equipment or acts, area limits, and non-compliance.
proposedGroups.approximateLearningGoal: Recall the by-law power to require equipment or acts to prevent enemy-action damage, area limits, and the offence.

proposals.reason: The section covers gravel pit safety by-laws, fine limits, safety work orders, and recovery as a debt.

proposedGroups.titleSuggestion: Gravel pit safety by-laws and work orders
proposedGroups.reason: Both subsections address safe operation and maintenance of gravel pits and council-ordered work.
proposedGroups.approximateLearningGoal: Recall the municipal power to regulate gravel pit safety, prescribe fines, order safety work, and recover expenses from the owner.

proposals.reason: Section 100 separates by-law offence and fine powers from prescribed payment in lieu of prosecution.

proposedGroups.titleSuggestion: By-law offence fines and special orders
proposedGroups.reason: These subsections list offence, fine, licence fee, bicycle, and animal-order enforcement powers.
proposedGroups.approximateLearningGoal: Recall municipal by-law powers for offences, fines, licence fee orders, bicycle impounding, animal disposition, and licence-fee treatment.

proposedGroups.titleSuggestion: Fine payment in lieu of prosecution
proposedGroups.reason: This subsection allows payment as prescribed by by-law to avoid prosecution.
proposedGroups.approximateLearningGoal: Recall when payment of a by-law fine prevents prosecution for the violation.

proposals.reason: The section covers clerk certificates as evidence in licensing by-law prosecutions.

proposedGroups.titleSuggestion: Licensing by-law certificate evidence
proposedGroups.reason: Both subsections govern certificates stating absence of a licence and name matching.
proposedGroups.approximateLearningGoal: Recall how a clerk certificate proves absence of a licence and how matching names are treated.

proposals.reason: Section 107 separates certified council records as evidence from judicial notice and appeal-record mechanics for by-laws.

proposedGroups.titleSuggestion: Certified council records as evidence
proposedGroups.reason: These subsections state the evidentiary effect of certified copies and stated dates.
proposedGroups.approximateLearningGoal: Recall how certified copies of council resolutions or by-laws prove passage, existence, and stated dates.

proposedGroups.titleSuggestion: Judicial notice and appeal record for by-laws
proposedGroups.reason: These subsections address filing certified by-laws for judicial notice and appeal or review records.
proposedGroups.approximateLearningGoal: Recall when a Provincial Court judge takes judicial notice of a by-law and what record must be transmitted on appeal or review.

proposals.reason: Section 109 separates fire by-law powers, non-fire rescue powers, order enforcement, and demolition compensation.

proposedGroups.titleSuggestion: Fire protection by-law powers
proposedGroups.reason: Subsection 109(1) lists by-law powers for preventing and extinguishing fires and protecting property.
proposedGroups.approximateLearningGoal: Recall municipal fire protection by-law powers for fire departments, fire zones, dangerous materials, inspections, demolition, and fire prevention enforcement.

proposedGroups.titleSuggestion: Non-fire rescue by-law powers
proposedGroups.reason: Subsection 109(1.1) separately authorizes by-laws for non-fire related rescue.
proposedGroups.approximateLearningGoal: Recall municipal by-law powers for non-fire rescue duties, vehicles and equipment, compensation, conduct, and assistance.

proposedGroups.titleSuggestion: Fire prevention orders and offences
proposedGroups.reason: These subsections address written service, Fire Prevention Act application, offences, and court orders.
proposedGroups.approximateLearningGoal: Recall how fire prevention orders are served and enforced, including offence categories and court compliance orders.

proposedGroups.titleSuggestion: Compensation for fire-control demolition
proposedGroups.reason: This subsection addresses compensation when a building or erection is demolished to prevent a fire from spreading.
proposedGroups.approximateLearningGoal: Recall when a municipality must compensate persons with interests in buildings or erections demolished to prevent fire spread.

proposals.reason: Section 111 separates housing project agreements from Cabinet-authorized implementation powers and rural-community application.

proposedGroups.titleSuggestion: Housing project agreements
proposedGroups.reason: These subsections authorize agreements for land, housing, clearance, replanning, rehabilitation, and modernization.
proposedGroups.approximateLearningGoal: Recall the housing project agreements a municipality may enter with the Province or Canada.

proposedGroups.titleSuggestion: Housing project borrowing services and rural communities
proposedGroups.reason: These subsections allow Cabinet to authorize implementation steps and apply the section to rural communities.
proposedGroups.approximateLearningGoal: Recall how Cabinet may authorize borrowing, capital funds, and municipal services for housing projects, and that the section applies to rural communities.

proposals.reason: The section is a focused provincial-licence prerequisite and municipal-licence statement rule.

proposedGroups.titleSuggestion: Provincial licence prerequisite for municipal licence
proposedGroups.reason: Both subsections address provincial licence production and stating that fact on the municipal licence.
proposedGroups.approximateLearningGoal: Recall when a provincial licence must be produced before a municipal licence is valid and what the municipal licence must state.

proposals.reason: The section lists classes of local improvement work and allows combined classes as one work.

proposedGroups.titleSuggestion: Authorized local improvement work
proposedGroups.reason: Both subsections address work classes and combining two or more classes.
proposedGroups.approximateLearningGoal: Recall the classes of work council may authorize as local improvements and that multiple classes may be undertaken as one work.

proposals.reason: Section 120 separates connections before paving or utility work, cost certification, and owner liability with recovery.

proposedGroups.titleSuggestion: Drain and water connections before paving
proposedGroups.reason: These subsections authorize council resolutions directing connections and service work.
proposedGroups.approximateLearningGoal: Recall when council may direct drain connections, water service pipes, stop-cocks, and private drain connections before paving, sewer, or water main work.

proposedGroups.titleSuggestion: Certificate of connection cost
proposedGroups.reason: These subsections govern cost certification, evidentiary effect, and measurement from the street centre.
proposedGroups.approximateLearningGoal: Recall how connection and service-pipe costs are certified, what the certificate proves, and how the cost is measured.

proposedGroups.titleSuggestion: Owner liability lien and recovery for installation
proposedGroups.reason: These subsections make costs payable by the owner, create a lien, and allow court recovery with interest.
proposedGroups.approximateLearningGoal: Recall when certified installation costs become payable, create a lien, and may be recovered from the owner with interest.

proposals.reason: The section governs special frontage assessment work initiated by owner petition.

proposedGroups.titleSuggestion: Petitioned special frontage assessment work
proposedGroups.reason: All subsections address petition support, thresholds, by-law vote, three-year timing, and partial work limits.
proposedGroups.approximateLearningGoal: Recall how a petition can support special frontage assessment work and the owner, value, council-vote, timing, and partial-work requirements.

proposals.reason: Section 123 separates the notice path for council-initiated work from the one-year restriction after opposition.

proposedGroups.titleSuggestion: Notice for council-initiated special frontage work
proposedGroups.reason: These subsections address published notice, prescribed form, opposition threshold, two-thirds vote, and three-year authorization.
proposedGroups.approximateLearningGoal: Recall the notice, opposition-petition, council-vote, and timing rules for council-initiated special frontage assessment work.

proposedGroups.titleSuggestion: One-year bar after opposition petition
proposedGroups.reason: This subsection prohibits a second notice within one year after a sufficient opposition petition, subject to section 124.
proposedGroups.approximateLearningGoal: Recall the one-year limit on a second notice after a sufficient petition against proposed special frontage assessment work.

proposals.reason: The section governs water or sewerage work ordered under the Health Act, including notice and authority despite opposition.

proposedGroups.titleSuggestion: Health Act ordered water or sewerage work
proposedGroups.reason: All subsections address notice for ordered work and authority to proceed despite a petition.
proposedGroups.approximateLearningGoal: Recall the notice and by-law process for Health Act ordered water or sewerage work and when council may proceed despite opposition.

proposals.reason: The section addresses filing, sufficiency, co-owner treatment, and withdrawal limits for petitions about work.

proposedGroups.titleSuggestion: Work petition filing sufficiency and withdrawal
proposedGroups.reason: All subsections govern petitions for or against work.
proposedGroups.approximateLearningGoal: Recall how petitions for or against work are filed, how the clerk determines sufficiency, how co-owners count, and when names cannot be withdrawn.

proposals.reason: Section 127 separates general metre-frontage assessment from domestic sewer and water main assessment rules.

proposedGroups.titleSuggestion: Metre frontage assessment and owners portion
proposedGroups.reason: These subsections set default special assessment by metre frontage and owners’ portion by-law authority.
proposedGroups.approximateLearningGoal: Recall the default metre-frontage basis for assessing local improvement work and the by-law power to prescribe the owners’ portion of cost.

proposedGroups.titleSuggestion: Domestic sewer outlet assessments and exemptions
proposedGroups.reason: These subsections govern outlet sewer exemptions, later connected parcel assessments, roll additions, and sewer account credits.
proposedGroups.approximateLearningGoal: Recall how domestic sewer outlet exemptions and later special frontage assessments for connected parcels are handled.

proposedGroups.titleSuggestion: Water main supply assessments and exemptions
proposedGroups.reason: These subsections govern water main exemptions, later connected parcel assessments, roll additions, and water supply account credits.
proposedGroups.approximateLearningGoal: Recall how water main exemptions and later special frontage assessments for connected parcels are handled.

proposals.reason: The section is a focused estimate and instalment rule for special frontage assessments.

proposedGroups.titleSuggestion: Special frontage assessment estimate and instalments
proposedGroups.reason: Both subsections address estimating cost, fixing instalments, and equal annual payment.
proposedGroups.approximateLearningGoal: Recall how council estimates work cost, fixes annual instalments, and requires equal annual payment of the owners’ portion of cost.

proposals.reason: Section 130 separates frontage assessment reductions from municipal payment and the clerk’s reduction role.

proposedGroups.titleSuggestion: Lot frontage assessment reductions
proposedGroups.reason: These subsections set actual metre frontage as default and describe lot reductions.
proposedGroups.approximateLearningGoal: Recall when abutting parcels are assessed by actual metre frontage and how reductions are made for corner, irregular, unfit, or double-abutting lots.

proposedGroups.titleSuggestion: Municipal payment and clerk reduction role
proposedGroups.reason: These subsections state who pays for reductions and that the clerk makes them.
proposedGroups.approximateLearningGoal: Recall that assessment reductions are paid by the municipality, entered on the roll, and made by the clerk.

proposals.reason: The section addresses liability of abutting parcels and treatment of exempt parcels.

proposedGroups.titleSuggestion: Abutting parcel liability for special frontage assessment
proposedGroups.reason: Both subsections address parcel liability and exempt parcel treatment.
proposedGroups.approximateLearningGoal: Recall which abutting parcels are liable for special frontage assessment and how exempt parcels are treated on the roll.

proposals.reason: The section covers required notice contents and delivery methods for special frontage assessments.

proposedGroups.titleSuggestion: Special frontage assessment notice
proposedGroups.reason: Both subsections address the ninety-day notice, required contents, and delivery.
proposedGroups.approximateLearningGoal: Recall the timing, contents, and delivery methods for notices of special frontage assessment.

proposals.reason: Section 136 separates the revision petition and clerk alteration process from notice of the clerk’s decision.

proposedGroups.titleSuggestion: Revision petition and clerk alterations
proposedGroups.reason: These subsections identify petitioners, revision matters, clerk review, and alterations.
proposedGroups.approximateLearningGoal: Recall who may seek revision of a local improvement assessment roll and how the clerk handles errors, reductions, and intended frontage changes.

proposedGroups.titleSuggestion: Revision decision notice
proposedGroups.reason: These subsections require notice to the applicant and affected owners and specify delivery.
proposedGroups.approximateLearningGoal: Recall who receives notice of the clerk’s revision decision and how that notice may be delivered.

proposals.reason: The section covers appeal rights and applicable court rules for revision decisions.

proposedGroups.titleSuggestion: Appeal of revision decision
proposedGroups.reason: Both subsections address appeal eligibility, timing, and Court of Queen’s Bench rules.
proposedGroups.approximateLearningGoal: Recall who may appeal a local improvement assessment roll revision decision, the fourteen-day deadline, and the applicable court rules.

proposals.reason: The section is a focused annual warrant of assessment rule.

proposedGroups.titleSuggestion: Warrant of assessment
proposedGroups.reason: Both subsections address the annual resolution, warrant, and execution under seal.
proposedGroups.approximateLearningGoal: Recall how council annually determines the owners’ portion of completed work and executes the warrant of assessment.

proposals.reason: Section 139 separates assessment-roll content and calculations from certification, validity, and delivery to the treasurer.

proposedGroups.titleSuggestion: Assessment roll columns and calculations
proposedGroups.reason: These subsections list roll columns, clerk calculations, form variation, and warrant attachment.
proposedGroups.approximateLearningGoal: Recall the required local improvement assessment roll columns and how the clerk enters frontage, rate, assessment, instalment, and warrant information.

proposedGroups.titleSuggestion: Roll certification validity and delivery to treasurer
proposedGroups.reason: These subsections address certification after appeals, validity, binding effect, and delivery to the treasurer.
proposedGroups.approximateLearningGoal: Recall when the local improvement assessment roll becomes valid and binding and what roll information the clerk delivers to the treasurer.

proposals.reason: The section governs issuing letters patent to local improvement associations and applying the Companies Act.

proposedGroups.titleSuggestion: Association letters patent and purposes
proposedGroups.reason: Both subsections address incorporation by letters patent, purposes, and Companies Act application.
proposedGroups.approximateLearningGoal: Recall who may receive letters patent for a local improvement association, the association’s purposes, and how the Companies Act applies.

proposals.reason: Section 159 separates the association transfer duty from the trust company duties and discharge rule, making two focused study groups clearer.

proposedGroups.titleSuggestion: Association transfer of income-only gifts to a trust company
proposedGroups.reason: Subsection 159(1) imposes the association duty to transfer income-only gifts, donations, bequests or devises to an authorized trust company.
proposedGroups.approximateLearningGoal: Recall when an association must transfer income-only gifts or bequests to an authorized trust company.

proposedGroups.titleSuggestion: Trust company investment, income payment, and discharge
proposedGroups.reason: Subsections 159(2) and 159(3) state what the trust company must do with the property and when payment of annual income discharges it.
proposedGroups.approximateLearningGoal: Explain the trust company duties for keeping or investing association gifts and paying annual income to the association.

proposals.reason: Section 162 has one study topic about by-law powers to create pension or superannuation plans and another about municipal payment and deduction duties once a plan operates.

proposedGroups.titleSuggestion: By-law powers for municipal pension or superannuation plans
proposedGroups.reason: Subsection 162(1) lists the plan adoption, employee definition, insurer contract, fund, employee contribution, and municipal contribution matters that may be provided by by-law.
proposedGroups.approximateLearningGoal: Recall the pension-plan matters a municipality may address by by-law, including plans, funds, insurers and contributions.

proposedGroups.titleSuggestion: Municipal deductions, fund payments, and pension payments after plan operation
proposedGroups.reason: Subsection 162(4) imposes operational duties once the plan comes into operation, including deductions, payments into the fund, and payments to former employees.
proposedGroups.approximateLearningGoal: Identify the municipality payment and deduction duties that begin when a pension plan comes into operation.

proposals.reason: Section 163 is a long pension provision with distinct topics: regulation-making for a uniform plan, limits and exceptions for local plans, amalgamation plan duties, and transfer or discontinuance mechanisms.

proposedGroups.titleSuggestion: Regulations creating and governing a uniform contributory pension plan
proposedGroups.reason: Subsection 163(1) authorizes regulations about the pension board, plan creation, purpose, fund, participation, termination, board duties, membership and administration.
proposedGroups.approximateLearningGoal: Recall the regulation subjects for establishing and administering a uniform contributory pension plan.

proposedGroups.titleSuggestion: Effect of a uniform plan on municipal pension by-laws
proposedGroups.reason: These subsections state the general bar on adopting section 162 plans after a uniform plan, the exception for replacement plans, retroactivity, and continuation of existing plans.
proposedGroups.approximateLearningGoal: Explain when a council may or may not adopt or continue a pension or superannuation plan after a uniform plan exists.

proposedGroups.titleSuggestion: Pension plan choices after amalgamation
proposedGroups.reason: These subsections require pension-plan action after amalgamation and allow either adoption of a former plan, designation of the uniform plan, provincial action in place of council, and retroactivity.
proposedGroups.approximateLearningGoal: Recall the pension-plan steps and options for amalgamated municipalities and when the Lieutenant-Governor in Council may act instead of council.

proposedGroups.titleSuggestion: Transfer to the uniform plan and discontinuance of contributions
proposedGroups.reason: Subsections 163(4) and 163(5) address agreements transferring assets and benefits to the uniform plan and ministerial discontinuance of contributions.
proposedGroups.approximateLearningGoal: Identify how pension assets and benefit obligations may be transferred to a uniform plan and when contributions may be discontinued.

proposals.reason: Section 164 covers definitions, parking by-law authorities, and two separate evidentiary rules for prosecutions involving meters and pay-and-display machines.

proposedGroups.titleSuggestion: Parking terms for meters, spaces, zones, streets, and vehicles
proposedGroups.reason: Subsection 164(1) defines the parking concepts used in the section and in by-laws made under it.
proposedGroups.approximateLearningGoal: Recall the defined parking terms that control section 164 and by-laws made under it.

proposedGroups.titleSuggestion: Municipal parking by-law powers and toll rules
proposedGroups.reason: Subsection 164(2) lists what council may regulate by by-law, including spaces, meters, pay-and-display machines, tolls, receipts, prohibitions, free periods, penalties and permits.
proposedGroups.approximateLearningGoal: Identify the parking-space, toll, receipt, penalty and permit matters that council may regulate by by-law.

proposedGroups.titleSuggestion: Meter-based prosecution evidence
proposedGroups.reason: Subsection 164(3) states when police or authorized-person evidence about a vehicle, meter, testing, and indicators proves unpaid or expired parking unless the contrary is proved.
proposedGroups.approximateLearningGoal: Recall what meter-related evidence can prove a parking violation in a prosecution.

proposedGroups.titleSuggestion: Pay-and-display prosecution evidence
proposedGroups.reason: Subsection 164(4) gives the parallel evidentiary rule for parking spaces in zones served by pay-and-display machines.
proposedGroups.approximateLearningGoal: Recall what pay-and-display evidence can prove unpaid or expired parking in a prosecution.

proposals.reason: Section 165 sets the municipal licence prerequisite for pawnbrokers, the annual expiry date, and the clerk limit on issue or renewal without council by-law authorization.

evidenceText: No person shall exercise the trade of a pawnbroker
expires on the thirty-first day of December
unless authorized by a by-law

proposedGroups.reason: Section 165 sets the municipal licence prerequisite for pawnbrokers, the annual expiry date, and the clerk limit on issue or renewal without council by-law authorization.
proposedGroups.approximateLearningGoal: Recall the licensing, expiry, and council authorization requirements for pawnbrokers in a municipality.

proposals.reason: Section 167 pairs the offence for acting as a pawnbroker without a licence with council power to regulate the trade by by-law.

proposedGroups.titleSuggestion: Unlicensed pawnbroker offence and by-law regulation power

evidenceText: without a pawnbroker
may make by-laws regulating the trade

proposedGroups.reason: Section 167 pairs the offence for acting as a pawnbroker without a licence with council power to regulate the trade by by-law.
proposedGroups.approximateLearningGoal: Identify the offence classification for unlicensed pawnbroking and the council by-law power over the pawnbroker trade.

proposals.reason: Section 168 authorizes licensing by-laws for peddling or hawking goods and then identifies categories of sellers to whom such a by-law does not apply.

proposedGroups.titleSuggestion: Pedlar licensing by-laws and exemptions

evidenceText: may provide for the licensing of persons who peddle or hawk
does not apply to

proposedGroups.reason: Section 168 authorizes licensing by-laws for peddling or hawking goods and then identifies categories of sellers to whom such a by-law does not apply.
proposedGroups.approximateLearningGoal: Recall council authority to license pedlars and the farm, fishing, and society-publication exemptions from those by-laws.

proposals.reason: Section 180 contains parallel powers for a municipality and a rural community to contract with Canada for RCMP policing on mutually agreed terms.

proposedGroups.titleSuggestion: RCMP policing contracts for municipalities and rural communities
proposedGroups.reason: Section 180 contains parallel powers for a municipality and a rural community to contract with Canada for RCMP policing on mutually agreed terms.
proposedGroups.approximateLearningGoal: Recall who may enter policing agreements with Canada for RCMP policing and on what basis.

proposals.reason: Section 187 combines a highway definition, municipal closure powers, public notice and objection procedure, and provincial approval for affected provincial highways.

proposedGroups.titleSuggestion: Highway definition and municipal closure powers
proposedGroups.reason: These subsections define highway and authorize full, partial, permanent, temporary, and vehicular-only closures, including effects on municipal interests and maintenance.
proposedGroups.approximateLearningGoal: Recall what counts as a highway and what types of highway closures council may make by by-law.

proposedGroups.titleSuggestion: Objection hearing and notice contents before highway closure
proposedGroups.reason: Subsections 187(6) and 187(7) require a time and place for objections, newspaper notice, hearing of objections, and specified notice contents before the by-law is passed.
proposedGroups.approximateLearningGoal: Identify the procedural notice and hearing steps required before a highway-closing by-law.

proposedGroups.titleSuggestion: Provincial highway approval requirement
proposedGroups.reason: Subsection 187(8) adds a validity condition where the closure by-law affects a provincial highway as defined in the Motor Vehicle Act.
proposedGroups.approximateLearningGoal: Recall when Lieutenant-Governor in Council approval is required for a highway closure by-law.

proposals.reason: Section 188 is best split between the accommodation-site definitions, the by-law subjects for mobile home sites and tourist or trailer camps, and the licence, zoning and fee limits.

proposedGroups.titleSuggestion: Mobile home, tourist camp, trailer camp, and space definitions
proposedGroups.reason: Subsection 188(1) defines the site and accommodation terms used by the regulatory by-law authority.
proposedGroups.approximateLearningGoal: Recall the defined terms for mobile homes, mobile home sites and parks, tourist camps, trailer camps, trailers and spaces.

proposedGroups.titleSuggestion: By-law regulation and licensing of mobile home and camp sites
proposedGroups.reason: Subsection 188(2) authorizes by-laws regulating mobile home sites and regulating and licensing tourist camps, trailer camps and mobile home parks, with listed area, temporary-location, lot-size, accommodation, safety, refuse and fee subjects.
proposedGroups.approximateLearningGoal: Identify the mobile home site, tourist camp, trailer camp and mobile home park matters that may be regulated or licensed by by-law.

proposedGroups.titleSuggestion: Licence duration, zoning condition, and annual fee ceiling
proposedGroups.reason: These subsections deal with the validity period for tourist or trailer camp licences, the zoning by-law condition for mobile home site designation, and the annual cap on licence or permit fees.
proposedGroups.approximateLearningGoal: Recall the licence duration, zoning prerequisite, and maximum annual fee rules in section 188.

proposals.reason: Section 189 is an oversized utility-finance provision with distinct learning topics for user-charge services, commissions and budgets, user-charge forms and collection, liens and debts, and connection or cost-allocation powers.

proposedGroups.titleSuggestion: Water, sewerage, and electric services on a user-charge basis
proposedGroups.reason: These subsections require or permit water, sewerage, local-improvement cost recovery and continued electric power services to operate on a user-charge basis, including classes, frontage calculations and cost-of-work content.
proposedGroups.approximateLearningGoal: Recall when municipal water, sewerage and electric services must or may be financed through user charges and how cost classes and frontage-based charges fit.

proposedGroups.titleSuggestion: Utility commissions, budgets, reserves, deficits, and surpluses
proposedGroups.reason: These subsections address establishing commissions, balanced budget requirements, budget submission, deficit and surplus treatment, reserve funds, and the meaning or deemed status of commissions.
proposedGroups.approximateLearningGoal: Explain how municipal utilities or commissions handle budgets, reserve funds, deficits, surpluses and commission status.

proposedGroups.titleSuggestion: User-charge types and by-law payment terms
proposedGroups.reason: Subsections 189(8) and 189(9) define what user-charge includes and excludes, and authorize by-laws prescribing payment, collection, discounts, penalties and default proceedings.
proposedGroups.approximateLearningGoal: Identify the permitted user-charge methods and the payment or enforcement terms council may prescribe by by-law.

proposedGroups.titleSuggestion: Water and sewer user-charge liens, debts, owner notice, and temporary borrowing
proposedGroups.reason: These subsections create a special lien for taxable land, a debt for non-taxable land, an owner-notice rule when another person owes the charges, and temporary borrowing authority for current utility expenditures.
proposedGroups.approximateLearningGoal: Recall how water and sewer charges become liens or debts, when owners must be notified, and how temporary borrowing for utilities is limited.

proposedGroups.titleSuggestion: Mandatory service connections, fire-protection water costs, gas pricing, and rural-community application
proposedGroups.reason: These subsections cover by-laws compelling connection or charging non-connecting owners, assessment of that charge, fire-protection allocation of water costs, gas-price limits, and application to rural communities.
proposedGroups.approximateLearningGoal: Identify the connection, non-connection charge, fire-protection water cost, gas-price, and rural-community application rules for section 189 services.

proposals.reason: Section 191 allows regulations respecting matters on which a municipality or rural community can make by-laws, applicable to unincorporated areas and rural communities without their own by-law.

proposedGroups.titleSuggestion: Provincial regulations mirroring municipal or rural-community by-law powers
proposedGroups.reason: Section 191 allows regulations respecting matters on which a municipality or rural community can make by-laws, applicable to unincorporated areas and rural communities without their own by-law.
proposedGroups.approximateLearningGoal: Identify when the Lieutenant-Governor in Council may make regulations for unincorporated areas and rural communities lacking a by-law.

proposals.reason: Section 192 is a broad regulation-making provision with distinct clusters for Act administration and forms, municipal finance and reserve matters, elections and officials, and extension or service-allocation powers.

proposedGroups.titleSuggestion: General regulation powers for administration, forms, offences, enforcement, and records
proposedGroups.reason: Paragraphs 192(1)(b), (c), (d), (e), (g), (g.1), (h), (h.1), (i), and (n) support a study group about forms, penalties, administrators, accounting, audits, public records, theatre operators, local boards, interest disclosure and general administration.
proposedGroups.approximateLearningGoal: Recall the general administrative, form, offence, enforcement, audit, record, local-board and disclosure subjects for regulations under section 192.

proposedGroups.titleSuggestion: Regulation powers for fees, interest, shared services, budgets, borrowing, and reserves
proposedGroups.reason: Paragraphs 192(1)(a), (a.1), (a.2), (a.3), (f), (j.1), (j.2), (k), (k.1), (k.2), and (k.3) concern financial and procedural regulation subjects, including fees, interest, procedural by-laws, shared services, estimates, borrowing percentages, reserve funds and generation-facility agreements.
proposedGroups.approximateLearningGoal: Identify the financial and procedural regulation subjects for fees, interest, shared services, budget dates, borrowing percentages, reserve funds and generation facilities.

proposedGroups.titleSuggestion: Election fees, municipal power extensions, and fire-protection water costs
proposedGroups.reason: Paragraphs 192(1)(j), (l), and (m) address election officer fees, extending municipal powers, and determining the portion of water costs charged against fire protection service.
proposedGroups.approximateLearningGoal: Recall the regulation powers for election officer fees, extending municipal powers, and allocating water costs to fire protection service.

proposals.reason: Section 193 deals with water or sewerage systems vested in the Minister: user-charge operation, applied utility rules, charge for unconnected land, Crown debt status, and transfer or alienation of the system.

proposedGroups.titleSuggestion: Ministerial operation and transfer of vested water or sewerage systems outside municipalities
proposedGroups.reason: Section 193 deals with water or sewerage systems vested in the Minister: user-charge operation, applied utility rules, charge for unconnected land, Crown debt status, and transfer or alienation of the system.
proposedGroups.approximateLearningGoal: Recall how the Minister operates, charges for, and may transfer vested water or sanitary sewerage systems outside municipalities.

proposals.reason: Section 196 continues by-laws in effect on January 1, 1967 until repeal, while making the Act prevail where a conflict exists.

proposedGroups.titleSuggestion: Continuation of pre-1967 by-laws subject to Act conflict
proposedGroups.reason: Section 196 continues by-laws in effect on January 1, 1967 until repeal, while making the Act prevail where a conflict exists.
proposedGroups.approximateLearningGoal: Recall how pre-1967 municipal by-laws continue and what happens if they conflict with the Act.

proposals.reason: Section 198 assigns category B, E and F offence classifications to specified violations involving association duties, pension duties, pawnbroker licensing authority, and trust-company transfer duties.

proposedGroups.titleSuggestion: Offence categories for association, pension, and pawnbroker violations
proposedGroups.reason: Section 198 assigns category B, E and F offence classifications to specified violations involving association duties, pension duties, pawnbroker licensing authority, and trust-company transfer duties.
proposedGroups.approximateLearningGoal: Identify the offence categories attached to violations of sections 158, 153, 162(4), 163(2), 165(3), 159(1), and 159(2).

proposals.reason: The target begins as commencement and repeal provisions but the operative target text also includes the First Schedule, Second Schedule, and proclamation notes under the same source key. The structure should be reviewed before approving study groups.

proposals.source: Occupational Health and Safety Act s. 2
proposals.reason: Section 2 contains the direct application rule that the Act binds the Crown; the remaining subsection is repealed.

proposedGroups.titleSuggestion: Crown bound by the Occupational Health and Safety Act
proposedGroups.reason: Section 2 contains the direct application rule that the Act binds the Crown; the remaining subsection is repealed.
proposedGroups.approximateLearningGoal: Recall that the Occupational Health and Safety Act binds the Crown.

proposals.source: Occupational Health and Safety Act s. 3
proposals.reason: Section 3 identifies where the Act does not apply, including private homes and exempted places, and permits written authorization to deviate from regulations where prescribed standards or equal-or-greater protection requirements are met.

proposedGroups.titleSuggestion: Private-home and regulatory exemptions plus authorized deviations
proposedGroups.reason: Section 3 identifies where the Act does not apply, including private homes and exempted places, and permits written authorization to deviate from regulations where prescribed standards or equal-or-greater protection requirements are met.
proposedGroups.approximateLearningGoal: Identify the Act exemptions for private homes or prescribed places and the conditions for authorized deviations from regulations.

proposals.source: Occupational Health and Safety Act s. 4
proposals.reason: Section 4 retains the Minister power, with Lieutenant-Governor in Council approval, to enter agreements with Canada, other provinces or local governments for administration of the Act.

proposedGroups.titleSuggestion: Ministerial administration agreements
proposedGroups.reason: Section 4 retains the Minister power, with Lieutenant-Governor in Council approval, to enter agreements with Canada, other provinces or local governments for administration of the Act.
proposedGroups.approximateLearningGoal: Recall who the Minister may make administration agreements with and what approval is required.

proposals.source: Occupational Health and Safety Act s. 5
proposals.reason: Section 5 authorizes the Commission board to appoint officers and designate the Chief Compliance Officer, requires identification cards, and permits designation of officers appointed by other governments.

proposedGroups.titleSuggestion: Appointment, identification, and interjurisdictional designation of occupational health and safety officers
proposedGroups.reason: Section 5 authorizes the Commission board to appoint officers and designate the Chief Compliance Officer, requires identification cards, and permits designation of officers appointed by other governments.
proposedGroups.approximateLearningGoal: Recall how occupational health and safety officers and the Chief Compliance Officer are appointed, identified and designated for interjurisdictional work.

proposals.source: Occupational Health and Safety Act s. 7
proposals.reason: Section 7 authorizes an inquiry under the Inquiries Act at the Commission request and requires commissioners to record and report evidence, findings and proceedings to the Commission for submission to the Lieutenant-Governor in Council.

proposedGroups.titleSuggestion: Commission-requested inquiries into occupational health and safety
proposedGroups.reason: Section 7 authorizes an inquiry under the Inquiries Act at the Commission request and requires commissioners to record and report evidence, findings and proceedings to the Commission for submission to the Lieutenant-Governor in Council.
proposedGroups.approximateLearningGoal: Recall how an occupational health and safety inquiry is initiated and reported.

proposals.source: Occupational Health and Safety Act s. 8
proposals.reason: Section 8 requires employers with 20 or more employees regularly employed in the Province to establish a written safety policy in consultation with employees, state responsibilities, keep it at each place of employment, and make it available to officers.

proposedGroups.titleSuggestion: Employer safety policy for workplaces with 20 or more employees
proposedGroups.reason: Section 8 requires employers with 20 or more employees regularly employed in the Province to establish a written safety policy in consultation with employees, state responsibilities, keep it at each place of employment, and make it available to officers.
proposedGroups.approximateLearningGoal: Recall when an employer must have a written safety policy and what it must cover and where it must be kept.

proposals.source: Occupational Health and Safety Act s. 9
proposals.reason: Section 9 is the core employer-duty provision and separates general compliance duties from specific hazard, information, supervision and equipment duties, plus inspection-program cooperation.

proposedGroups.titleSuggestion: General employer duties to protect employees and ensure compliance
proposedGroups.reason: Subsection 9(1) requires every employer to take reasonable precautions for employee health and safety, comply with the Act, regulations and orders, and ensure employee compliance.
proposedGroups.approximateLearningGoal: Recall the general employer duties to protect employee health and safety and ensure compliance with the Act, regulations and orders.

proposedGroups.titleSuggestion: Employer duties for safe systems, hazards, information, supervision, and protective equipment
proposedGroups.reason: Subsection 9(2) lists specific duties for safe systems and equipment, monthly inspections, hazard familiarization, information, instruction, training, competent and sufficient supervision, protective equipment, and cooperation.
proposedGroups.approximateLearningGoal: Identify the specific employer duties for workplace systems, hazards, inspections, training, supervision, protective equipment and cooperation.

proposedGroups.titleSuggestion: Employer inspection program and sharing of inspection results
proposedGroups.reason: Subsection 9(3) requires the employer to develop the monthly inspection program with the committee or health and safety representative and share each inspection result.
proposedGroups.approximateLearningGoal: Recall who must help develop the workplace inspection program and who receives inspection results.

proposals.source: Occupational Health and Safety Act s. 14
proposals.reason: Section 14 contains distinct committee topics: when a committee must be established and how it is composed, how meetings and records work, and how unresolved matters reach an officer.

proposedGroups.titleSuggestion: Non-project-site committee establishment, composition, representation, and co-chairs
proposedGroups.reason: These subsections exclude project sites, require committees for employers with 20 or more employees at a place of employment, and set size, equal representation, Chief Compliance Officer size-setting and co-chair rules.
proposedGroups.approximateLearningGoal: Recall when a non-project-site joint health and safety committee is required and how its membership and co-chairs are determined.

proposedGroups.titleSuggestion: Committee meetings, minutes, posting, retention, and Commission access
proposedGroups.reason: These subsections require monthly meetings, approved minutes, posting names and recent minutes, retaining signed minutes for three years and making them available to the Commission.
proposedGroups.approximateLearningGoal: Identify the meeting, minute, posting, retention and Commission-access duties for a committee.

proposedGroups.titleSuggestion: Officer resolution of committee deadlock
proposedGroups.reason: Subsection 14(13) requires a committee that cannot agree on a health and safety matter to call an officer to resolve the problem.
proposedGroups.approximateLearningGoal: Recall what a joint health and safety committee must do when it cannot agree on a health and safety matter.

proposals.source: Occupational Health and Safety Act s. 16
proposals.reason: Section 16 permits the Commission to reduce meeting frequency for low-risk employment if safety is not materially affected, and to schedule meeting times where scheduled meetings would disrupt operations.

proposedGroups.titleSuggestion: Commission changes to committee meeting frequency or timing
proposedGroups.reason: Section 16 permits the Commission to reduce meeting frequency for low-risk employment if safety is not materially affected, and to schedule meeting times where scheduled meetings would disrupt operations.
proposedGroups.approximateLearningGoal: Recall when the Commission may reduce committee meeting frequency or schedule meeting times.

proposals.source: Occupational Health and Safety Act s. 17
proposals.reason: Section 17 excludes project sites, requires a safety policy for employers with 5 to 19 employees that may include a representative, allows the Commission to require a representative policy for high-risk or high-accident workplaces, and requires election and posting where a representative is provided.

proposedGroups.titleSuggestion: Health and safety representatives for non-project sites
proposedGroups.reason: Section 17 excludes project sites, requires a safety policy for employers with 5 to 19 employees that may include a representative, allows the Commission to require a representative policy for high-risk or high-accident workplaces, and requires election and posting where a representative is provided.
proposedGroups.approximateLearningGoal: Recall when non-project workplaces use health and safety representatives and how representatives are elected and posted.

proposals.source: Occupational Health and Safety Act s. 18
proposals.reason: Section 18 lets a health and safety representative do what a committee may do under section 15, requires regular consultation with the employer, and requires calling an officer if no agreement is reached on a health or safety matter.

proposedGroups.titleSuggestion: Functions and dispute resolution for health and safety representatives
proposedGroups.reason: Section 18 lets a health and safety representative do what a committee may do under section 15, requires regular consultation with the employer, and requires calling an officer if no agreement is reached on a health or safety matter.
proposedGroups.approximateLearningGoal: Recall the representative functions, employer consultation duty, and officer referral rule for unresolved health and safety matters.

proposals.source: Occupational Health and Safety Act s. 20
proposals.reason: Section 20 is a staged refusal-to-work process with supervisor investigation, committee referral, officer referral and remedial orders, plus employee availability while investigations or appeals are pending.

proposedGroups.titleSuggestion: Supervisor investigation and remedial action after an employee safety report
proposedGroups.reason: These subsections require the employee to report the concern to the supervisor, supervisor investigation in the employee presence, remedial action or recommendation if reasonable grounds exist, and advice to do the act if not.
proposedGroups.approximateLearningGoal: Recall the supervisor-stage duties after an employee reports that an act may endanger health or safety.

proposedGroups.titleSuggestion: Committee investigation and recommendation after unresolved refusal
proposedGroups.reason: These subsections require referral to a committee or officer if unresolved, committee investigation, recommended remedial action if reasonable grounds exist, and advice to do the act if they do not.
proposedGroups.approximateLearningGoal: Explain the committee-stage process when the employee safety concern is not resolved with the supervisor.

proposedGroups.titleSuggestion: Officer findings, orders, written advice, appeal link, and employee availability
proposedGroups.reason: These subsections require officer referral if the committee stage is unresolved, written officer findings, remedial orders or written advice, application of appeal-related provisions, and employee availability at a safe place while investigation or appeal is pending.
proposedGroups.approximateLearningGoal: Identify the officer-stage findings, remedial order or advice, appeal connection, and employee availability requirements after a work refusal.

proposals.source: Occupational Health and Safety Act s. 21
proposals.reason: Section 21 states how long the right to refuse remains protected through supervisor, committee, officer and Chief Compliance Officer appeal stages, and prevents assigning another employee unless that employee is advised of the refusal, reasons and rights.

proposedGroups.titleSuggestion: Protection period for refused work and limits on assigning another employee
proposedGroups.reason: Section 21 states how long the right to refuse remains protected through supervisor, committee, officer and Chief Compliance Officer appeal stages, and prevents assigning another employee unless that employee is advised of the refusal, reasons and rights.
proposedGroups.approximateLearningGoal: Recall when an employee refusal remains protected and what an employer or supervisor must tell another employee before assigning the refused act.

proposals.source: Occupational Health and Safety Act s. 22
proposals.reason: Section 22 permits temporary reassignment to reasonably equivalent work while a protected refusal continues, with same wages and benefits, subject to any collective agreement.

proposedGroups.titleSuggestion: Temporary reassignment during protected work refusal
proposedGroups.reason: Section 22 permits temporary reassignment to reasonably equivalent work while a protected refusal continues, with same wages and benefits, subject to any collective agreement.
proposedGroups.approximateLearningGoal: Recall when and how an employee may be reassigned during a protected work refusal and what pay and agreement limits apply.

proposals.source: Occupational Health and Safety Act s. 24
proposals.reason: Section 24 prohibits employers, supervisors and unions from discriminatory action, threats, intimidation or coercion because an employee sought enforcement or complied with the Act, regulations, orders, or workplace-related Smoke-free Places Act requirements, and excludes section 22 reassignment from discriminatory action.

proposedGroups.titleSuggestion: Prohibition on discriminatory action for enforcing or complying with safety laws
proposedGroups.reason: Section 24 prohibits employers, supervisors and unions from discriminatory action, threats, intimidation or coercion because an employee sought enforcement or complied with the Act, regulations, orders, or workplace-related Smoke-free Places Act requirements, and excludes section 22 reassignment from discriminatory action.
proposedGroups.approximateLearningGoal: Identify the prohibited reprisals for safety-law enforcement or compliance and the reassignment exclusion.

proposals.source: Occupational Health and Safety Act s. 25
proposals.reason: Section 25 lets an employee complaining of a section 24 violation choose final and binding collective-agreement arbitration, if available, or file a written complaint with the Commission within one year, after which the Commission refers timely complaints to an appointed arbitrator.

proposedGroups.titleSuggestion: Complaint path and time limit for discriminatory action
proposedGroups.reason: Section 25 lets an employee complaining of a section 24 violation choose final and binding collective-agreement arbitration, if available, or file a written complaint with the Commission within one year, after which the Commission refers timely complaints to an appointed arbitrator.
proposedGroups.approximateLearningGoal: Recall how an employee brings a discriminatory-action complaint, the filing deadline, and the Commission referral duty.

proposals.source: Occupational Health and Safety Act s. 26
proposals.reason: Section 26 has distinct topics for arbitrator powers and remedies, written findings and clarification, court review and record transmission, and the definition of arbitrator.

proposedGroups.titleSuggestion: Arbitrator powers, discriminatory-action findings, and remedial orders
proposedGroups.reason: These subsections give the arbitrator Industrial Relations Act powers, authorize remedial orders after discriminatory findings, and require written findings with reasons and orders to be provided to the parties and Commission.
proposedGroups.approximateLearningGoal: Recall the arbitrator powers, available remedies, and written finding requirements for discriminatory-action complaints.

proposedGroups.titleSuggestion: Clarification requests and court review of arbitrator orders
proposedGroups.reason: These subsections allow a party to request clarification or omitted-matter treatment, permit court review for jurisdiction or legal error, require service and record delivery, and state possible court orders, effective-date orders and Rules of Court application.
proposedGroups.approximateLearningGoal: Identify how arbitrator orders may be clarified or reviewed by the Court of King Bench and what procedural rules apply.

proposedGroups.titleSuggestion: Meaning of arbitrator in discriminatory-action proceedings
proposedGroups.reason: Subsection 26(12) defines arbitrator for section 26 as the arbitrator appointed under subsection 25(2).
proposedGroups.approximateLearningGoal: Recall who counts as the arbitrator for section 26.

proposals.source: Occupational Health and Safety Act s. 27
proposals.reason: Section 27 permits the employee or Commission to file an arbitrator order in the Court of King Bench after the review period expires if a bound party fails to comply, and makes the filed order enforceable as a court judgment.

proposedGroups.titleSuggestion: Court filing and judgment enforcement of arbitrator orders
proposedGroups.reason: Section 27 permits the employee or Commission to file an arbitrator order in the Court of King Bench after the review period expires if a bound party fails to comply, and makes the filed order enforceable as a court judgment.
proposedGroups.approximateLearningGoal: Recall how an arbitrator order is filed and enforced as a judgment when a party does not comply.

proposals.source: Occupational Health and Safety Act s. 28
proposals.reason: Section 28 separates officer entry, inspection, document and investigation powers from technical-expert assistance and evidentiary use of certified copies.

proposedGroups.titleSuggestion: Officer entry, inspection, sampling, document, inquiry, investigation, and preservation powers
proposedGroups.reason: Subsection 28(1) authorizes officers to enter and inspect places of employment, conduct tests and examinations, require and copy records, remove materials for copying, sample products or equipment, make inquiries, investigate incidents and occupational disease, and order things left undisturbed.
proposedGroups.approximateLearningGoal: Identify the inspection, document, sampling, inquiry, investigation and preservation powers of occupational health and safety officers.

proposedGroups.titleSuggestion: Technical expert assistance and evidentiary use of certified copies
proposedGroups.reason: Subsections 28(2) and (3) allow technical experts to accompany officers and make certified copies admissible as prima facie proof of originals.
proposedGroups.approximateLearningGoal: Recall how technical experts may assist officers and how certified copies are used as evidence.

proposals.source: Occupational Health and Safety Act s. 31
proposals.reason: Section 31 allows an officer to give oral or written orders to any person for matters regulated, controlled or required by the Act or regulations, set a completion time, and requires oral orders to be written before the officer leaves the place of employment.

proposedGroups.titleSuggestion: Officer oral and written orders for Act or regulation matters
proposedGroups.reason: Section 31 allows an officer to give oral or written orders to any person for matters regulated, controlled or required by the Act or regulations, set a completion time, and requires oral orders to be written before the officer leaves the place of employment.
proposedGroups.approximateLearningGoal: Recall when an officer may give orders, how timing may be specified, and when an oral order must be reduced to writing.

proposals.source: Occupational Health and Safety Act s. 32
proposals.reason: Section 32 has one topic for orders addressing unsafe or unhealthy working conditions and service of those orders, and another for tool, equipment, machine or device non-compliance orders and warnings.

proposedGroups.titleSuggestion: Written officer orders for unsafe or unhealthy working conditions
proposedGroups.reason: These subsections authorize written orders to specified workplace parties to suspend work, control danger, protect health and safety, or ensure compliance, and set service methods.
proposedGroups.approximateLearningGoal: Recall who may receive a written officer order for unsafe conditions, what measures may be ordered, and how the order is served.

proposedGroups.titleSuggestion: Officer orders and warnings for non-compliant tools, equipment, machines, or devices
proposedGroups.reason: These subsections require an officer who finds non-compliant equipment to prohibit use, permit use only on safety conditions, or secure compliance, and to give written orders and attach warnings when use is prohibited.
proposedGroups.approximateLearningGoal: Identify the officer options for non-compliant tools, equipment, machines or devices and the warning requirement when use is prohibited.

proposals.source: Occupational Health and Safety Act s. 35
proposals.reason: Section 35 requires an officer who made a section 32 order to provide a copy to the committee or health and safety representative where one exists and permits posting; where neither exists, posting is mandatory.

proposedGroups.titleSuggestion: Providing or posting copies of section 32 officer orders
proposedGroups.reason: Section 35 requires an officer who made a section 32 order to provide a copy to the committee or health and safety representative where one exists and permits posting; where neither exists, posting is mandatory.
proposedGroups.approximateLearningGoal: Recall when copies of section 32 orders are provided to committees or representatives and when posting is required.
